abstract: We show analytically how the stability of two-dimensional lateral inhibition neural networks depends on the local connection topology. For various network topologies, we calculate the critical time delay for the onset of oscillation in continuous-time networks and present analytic phase diagrams characterizing the dynamics of discrete-time networks.
originalAbstract: We show analytically how the stability of two-dimensional lateral inhibition neural networks depends on the local connection topology. For various network topologies, we calculate the critical time delay for the onset of oscillation in continuous-time networks and present analytic phase diagrams characterizing the dynamics of discrete-time networks.

paragraphs: This paper studies how the arrangement of local connections affects the stability of two-dimensional lateral inhibition networks. In such networks, inhibitory interactions link nearby units. The central question is how changing which units interact changes the behavior of the network over time, particularly whether its activity remains stable or begins to oscillate.

For continuous-time networks, the authors calculate the critical delay at which oscillations begin for several connection topologies. A delay means that an interaction reflects earlier activity rather than acting immediately. The analysis connects the allowable delay before oscillation to the network’s local wiring, showing why temporal behavior must be considered together with connection structure.

The paper also analyzes discrete-time networks and presents phase diagrams describing their dynamics. These diagrams organize the behaviors associated with different conditions in the mathematical model. Together, the results provide an analytical account of how local topology shapes collective behavior in both continuous and discrete time, turning wiring choices into explicit questions about stability.
summary.tldr: Analytical results connect local inhibitory wiring to stability and the onset of oscillations in two-dimensional networks.

title: Connection Topology and Dynamics in Lateral Inhibition Networks

paragraphs: This paper investigates how organized feature maps can develop in the visual cortex. Cells selective for visual position, orientation, and ocular dominance form spatial patterns rather than an arbitrary arrangement. The researchers use a self-organizing neural network to study how such organization can arise and why the resulting maps have their observed spatial structure.

The model treats map formation as a reduction from a high-dimensional feature space to a two-dimensional lattice. Each feature combination has a location in the richer space, while cells occupy positions on the lattice. The organizing principle translates similarity between features into physical proximity between the cells that represent them.

The network reproduces several aspects of cortical map structure. This supports the usefulness of dimension reduction and similarity preservation as modeling principles for these arrangements. The result links development and spatial organization within one computational account: the process that builds the map also explains aspects of which feature-selective cells become neighbors. Its stated success concerns several structural features of cortical maps.
summary.tldr: A self-organizing model reproduces aspects of cortical feature maps by placing similar feature representations near one another on a two-dimensional lattice.

title: Development and Spatial Structure of Cortical Feature Maps: A Model Study

abstract: We propose a trajectory planning and control theory for continuous movements such as connected cursive handwriting and continuous natural speech. Its hardware is based on our previously proposed forward-inverse-relaxation neural network (Wada & Kawato, 1993). Computationally, its optimization principle is the minimum torque(cid:173) change criterion. Regarding the representation level, hard constraints satisfied by a trajectory are represented as a set of via-points extracted from a handwritten character. Accordingly, we propose a via-point estimation algorithm that estimates via-points by repeating the trajectory formation of a character and the via-point extraction from the character. In experiments, good quantitative agreement is found between human handwriting data and the trajectories generated by the theory. Finally, we propose a recognition schema based on the movement generation. We show a result in which the recognition schema is applied to the handwritten character recognition and can be extended to the phoneme timing estimation of natural speech.

paragraphs: This paper treats connected handwriting as a problem of planning and controlling continuous movement. Its central proposal is that a trajectory should minimize changes in torque, the turning forces that drive movement. This gives the model a physical optimization principle for producing a written path, implemented through a forward-inverse-relaxation neural network.

The intended character is represented through via-points: locations that the movement must pass through. These impose hard constraints while leaving the rest of the trajectory to the optimization process. The paper also proposes a way to estimate these points by repeatedly generating a character trajectory and extracting via-points from the resulting character.

The generated trajectories show good quantitative agreement with human handwriting data. The authors then use movement generation as the basis for a recognition scheme and demonstrate its application to handwritten characters. They also propose extending this approach to estimating phoneme timing in natural speech, connecting recognition with a model of how continuous actions are produced.
summary.tldr: A handwriting model generates human-like trajectories by minimizing torque changes while passing through estimated character-defining points.

title: A Computational Model for Cursive Handwriting Based on the Minimization Principle

abstract: Principal component analysis (PCA) is a commonly applied technique for dimensionality reduction. PCA implicitly minimizes a squared loss function, which may be inappropriate for data that is not real-valued, such as binary-valued data. This paper draws on ideas from the Exponen- tial family, Generalized linear models, and Bregman distances, to give a generalization of PCA to loss functions that we argue are better suited to other data types. We describe algorithms for minimizing the loss func- tions, and give examples on simulated data.
originalAbstract: Principal component analysis (PCA) is a commonly applied technique for dimensionality reduction. PCA implicitly minimizes a squared loss function, which may be inappropriate for data that is not real-valued, such as binary-valued data. This paper draws on ideas from the Exponen- tial family, Generalized linear models, and Bregman distances, to give a generalization of PCA to loss functions that we argue are better suited to other data types. We describe algorithms for minimizing the loss func- tions, and give examples on simulated data.

paragraphs: Principal component analysis reduces the dimensionality of data while implicitly measuring reconstruction errors with squared loss. This paper questions whether that measurement is appropriate for every kind of observation. Binary data provide the motivating example: a representation designed around real-valued errors may not reflect the structure of observations that take only two values.

The authors generalize PCA by drawing together ideas from exponential-family distributions, generalized linear models, and Bregman distances. These ingredients provide a route to alternative loss functions while retaining the goal of dimensionality reduction. The central change is therefore in what counts as a good approximation to the data, allowing that choice to reflect the data type.

The paper also describes algorithms for minimizing the resulting losses and illustrates the approach with simulated data. Its contribution combines a broader formulation with methods for fitting it. The authors argue that the alternative losses are better suited to other observation types; the abstract does not establish that one generalized version is best for all data.
summary.tldr: The paper generalizes PCA to alternative loss functions intended to better match data types such as binary observations.

title: A Generalization of Principal Components Analysis to the Exponential Family

abstract: The constraint classiﬁcation framework captures many ﬂavors of mul- ticlass classiﬁcation including winner-take-all multiclass classiﬁcation, multilabel classiﬁcation and ranking. We present a meta-algorithm for learning in this framework that learns via a single linear classiﬁer in high dimension. We discuss distribution independent as well as margin-based generalization bounds and present empirical and theoretical evidence showing that constraint classiﬁcation beneﬁts over existing methods of multiclass classiﬁcation.
originalAbstract: The constraint classiﬁcation framework captures many ﬂavors of mul- ticlass classiﬁcation including winner-take-all multiclass classiﬁcation, multilabel classiﬁcation and ranking. We present a meta-algorithm for learning in this framework that learns via a single linear classiﬁer in high dimension. We discuss distribution independent as well as margin-based generalization bounds and present empirical and theoretical evidence showing that constraint classiﬁcation beneﬁts over existing methods of multiclass classiﬁcation.

paragraphs: Classification problems can ask for different kinds of outputs: one winning class, several applicable labels, or a ranking. This paper brings these settings into a common constraint-classification framework. The central idea is to express their learning requirements in a form that a shared method can handle, despite the different outputs each task requests.

The authors present a meta-algorithm that learns within this framework using one linear classifier in a high-dimensional space. This gives the framework a concrete computational route rather than leaving it as a way to describe related problems. The high-dimensional representation supports a common learning mechanism across the included classification and ranking settings.

The paper also examines generalization through distribution-independent and margin-based bounds, linking the framework to theoretical questions about performance beyond the training examples. It reports both empirical and theoretical evidence of benefits over existing multiclass classification methods. Together, these contributions support constraint classification as a unified approach with demonstrated advantages, without establishing that it wins in every included task.
summary.tldr: Constraint classification unifies multiclass prediction, multilabel prediction, and ranking through a single high-dimensional linear classifier.

title: Constraint Classification for Multiclass Classification and Ranking

abstract: We consider the general problem of learning from labeled and unlabeled data, which is often called semi-supervised learning or transductive in- ference. A principled approach to semi-supervised learning is to design a classifying function which is suf(cid:2)ciently smooth with respect to the intrinsic structure collectively revealed by known labeled and unlabeled points. We present a simple algorithm to obtain such a smooth solution. Our method yields encouraging experimental results on a number of clas- si(cid:2)cation problems and demonstrates effective use of unlabeled data.
originalAbstract: We consider the general problem of learning from labeled and unlabeled data, which is often called semi-supervised learning or transductive in- ference. A principled approach to semi-supervised learning is to design a classifying function which is suf(cid:2)ciently smooth with respect to the intrinsic structure collectively revealed by known labeled and unlabeled points. We present a simple algorithm to obtain such a smooth solution. Our method yields encouraging experimental results on a number of clas- si(cid:2)cation problems and demonstrates effective use of unlabeled data.

paragraphs: This paper addresses classification when some examples have labels and others do not. The unlabeled examples still contribute information because their arrangement helps reveal the structure of the data. The authors use that collectively revealed structure to guide how a classification function should behave across the available points.

The central principle is smoothness with respect to the data’s intrinsic structure. A classifier should vary in a way that is consistent with that structure, using information from labeled and unlabeled examples together. The paper presents a simple algorithm for obtaining such a smooth solution, turning this principle into a concrete learning method.

Experiments on several classification problems produce encouraging results and demonstrate effective use of unlabeled data. These findings support the approach in the tested settings: observations without labels can help shape the classifier when their relationship to the rest of the data is incorporated. The contribution is a simple procedure organized around structural consistency as a basis for semi-supervised learning.
summary.tldr: A simple semi-supervised algorithm learns a classifier that is smooth with respect to structure revealed jointly by labeled and unlabeled data.

title: Learning with Local and Global Consistency

abstract: Many perceptual processes and neural computations, such as speech recognition, motor control and learning, depend on the ability to measure and mark the passage of time. However, the processes that make such temporal judgements possible are unknown. A number of different hypothetical mechanisms have been advanced, all of which depend on the known, temporally predictable evolution of a neural or psychological state, possibly through oscillations or the gradual decay of a memory trace. Alternatively, judgements of elapsed time might be based on observations of temporally structured, but stochastic processes. Such processes need not be specific to the sense of time; typical neural and sensory processes contain at least some statistical structure across a range of time scales. Here, we investigate the statistical properties of an estimator of elapsed time which is based on a simple family of stochastic process.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how elapsed time might be inferred from neural activity that is structured but random. Timing matters for processes such as speech recognition, movement, and learning, yet the mechanisms behind temporal judgments remain uncertain. Existing proposed mechanisms often rely on a state whose evolution is temporally predictable, such as an oscillation or a decaying memory trace.

The alternative explored here is that observations of a stochastic process could provide evidence about elapsed time. Randomness does not eliminate temporal structure: typical neural and sensory processes contain statistical relationships across multiple timescales. Such processes therefore need not be dedicated exclusively to timing to become candidates for temporal estimation.

The authors investigate the statistical properties of an elapsed-time estimator built from a simple family of stochastic processes. The contribution is an analysis of this alternative basis for timing, framed as a possible mechanism rather than an established account of human temporal judgments. It shifts the question toward how statistical structure in ongoing activity might carry information about the passage of time.
summary.tldr: The paper studies whether elapsed time can be estimated from the statistical structure of stochastic processes rather than a predictably evolving internal state.

title: Inferring Elapsed Time from Stochastic Neural Processes

abstract: When predicting class labels for objects within a relational database, it is often helpful to consider a model for relationships: this allows for information between class labels to be shared and to improve prediction performance. However, there are different ways by which objects can be related within a relational database. One traditional way corresponds to a Markov network structure: each existing relation is represented by an undirected edge. This encodes that, conditioned on input features, each object label is independent of other object labels given its neighbors in the graph. However, there is no reason why Markov networks should be the only representation of choice for symmetric dependence structures. Here we discuss the case when relationships are postulated to exist due to hidden com- mon causes. We discuss how the resulting graphical model differs from Markov networks, and how it describes different types of real-world relational processes. A Bayesian nonparametric classiﬁcation model is built upon this graphical repre- sentation and evaluated with several empirical studies.

paragraphs: When classifying objects in a relational database, relationships can help share information between their labels. A common representation places an undirected edge between related objects in a Markov network. This representation makes a particular assumption: given input features and neighboring labels, an object's label is independent of the remaining labels.

This paper examines another explanation for symmetric relationships: objects may be connected because of an unobserved common cause. The authors discuss how the resulting graphical model differs from a Markov network and how it represents different kinds of relational processes. The choice of representation therefore expresses an assumption about why related objects exhibit dependence.

The authors build a Bayesian nonparametric classification model around this common-cause representation and evaluate it through several empirical studies. The contribution is both a modeling perspective and an implemented classifier. It expands the set of assumptions available for relational learning, showing how hidden shared causes can serve as the basis for using relationships in prediction.
summary.tldr: A hidden-common-cause representation offers an alternative to Markov networks and supports a Bayesian nonparametric classifier for relational data.

title: Hidden Common Cause Relations in Relational Learning

abstract: We consider robust least-squares regression with feature-wise disturbance. We show that this formulation leads to tractable convex optimization problems, and we exhibit a particular uncertainty set for which the robust problem is equivalent to $\ell_1$ regularized regression (Lasso). This provides an interpretation of Lasso from a robust optimization perspective. We generalize this robust formulation to consider more general uncertainty sets, which all lead to tractable convex optimization problems. Therefore, we provide a new methodology for designing regression algorithms, which generalize known formulations. The advantage is that robustness to disturbance is a physical property that can be exploited: in addition to obtaining new formulations, we use it directly to show sparsity properties of Lasso, as well as to prove a general consistency result for robust regression problems, including Lasso, from a unified robustness perspective.

We show that this formulation leads to tractable convex optimization problems, and we exhibit a particular uncertainty set for which the robust problem is equivalent to $\ell_1$ regularized regression (Lasso). This provides an interpretation of Lasso from a robust optimization perspective. We generalize this robust formulation to consider more general uncertainty sets, which all lead to tractable convex optimization problems. paragraphs: The paper studies regression when input features may be disturbed. Instead of considering only the observed feature values, robust regression accounts for disturbances described by an uncertainty set. The authors show that this feature-wise formulation leads to tractable convex optimization problems, making the robustness objective computationally usable.

For one particular uncertainty set, the robust problem is equivalent to Lasso, the regression method that uses an absolute-value penalty on coefficients. This supplies a robustness interpretation of that penalty: under the specified disturbance model, it corresponds to protecting the regression against uncertain features. The equivalence depends on the chosen uncertainty set, rather than applying indiscriminately to every disturbance model.

The authors then consider more general uncertainty sets, obtaining further tractable convex regression formulations. This turns assumptions about disturbances into a way to design learning methods. They also use the robustness perspective to establish sparsity properties of Lasso and a general consistency result covering robust regression problems, including Lasso. The contribution therefore links algorithm design and theoretical properties through a shared treatment of uncertainty.
summary.tldr: Lasso is equivalent to robust regression under a particular feature-disturbance set, connecting regularization, sparsity, and consistency through robustness.

title: Robust Regression and Lasso

abstract: In visual recognition, the images are frequently modeled as sets of local features (bags). We show that bag of words, a common method to handle such cases, can be viewed as a special match kernel, which counts 1 if two local features fall into the same regions partitioned by visual words and 0 otherwise. Despite its simplicity, this quantization is too coarse. It is, therefore, appealing to design match kernels that more accurately measure the similarity between local features. However, it is impractical to use such kernels on large datasets due to their significant computational cost. To address this problem, we propose an efficient match kernel (EMK), which maps local features to a low dimensional feature space, average the resulting feature vectors to form a set-level feature, then apply a linear classifier. The local feature maps are learned so that their inner products preserve, to the best possible, the values of the specified kernel function. EMK is linear both in the number of images and in the number of local features. We demonstrate that EMK is extremely efficient and achieves the current state of the art performance on three difficult real world datasets: Scene-15, Caltech-101 and Caltech-256.

paragraphs: Images are often represented as collections of local features. A bag-of-words representation compares features coarsely: two features count as matching if they fall in the same visual-word region, and otherwise do not match. The paper interprets this rule as a match kernel and seeks a richer similarity measure without the expense of directly comparing large feature collections.

The proposed efficient match kernel learns a low-dimensional mapping of individual features. Inner products between mapped features are trained to approximate a specified kernel's similarity values. The mapped features are then averaged into one representation for each image, which can be used by a linear classifier. This connects detailed local similarity to a compact image-level representation.

The method scales linearly with both the number of images and the number of local features. Experiments on Scene-15, Caltech-101, and Caltech-256 report strong computational efficiency and state-of-the-art recognition performance. These results demonstrate that approximating richer feature comparisons can retain useful recognition information while making the computation practical.
summary.tldr: Learned low-dimensional feature maps make richer image match kernels efficient and achieve state-of-the-art results on three recognition datasets.

title: Efficient Match Kernel between Sets of Features for Visual Recognition

abstract: The success of machine learning, particularly in supervised settings, has led to numerous attempts to apply it in adversarial settings such as spam and malware detection. The core challenge in this class of applications is that adversaries are not static data generators, but make a deliberate effort to evade the classifiers deployed to detect them. We investigate both the problem of modeling the objectives of such adversaries, as well as the algorithmic problem of accounting for rational, objective-driven adversaries. In particular, we demonstrate severe shortcomings of feature reduction in adversarial settings using several natural adversarial objective functions, an observation that is particularly pronounced when the adversary is able to substitute across similar features (for example, replace words with synonyms or replace letters in words). We offer a simple heuristic method for making learning more robust to feature cross-substitution attacks. We then present a more general approach based on mixed-integer linear programming with constraint generation, which implicitly trades off overfitting and feature selection in an adversarial setting using a sparse regularizer along with an evasion model. Our approach is the first method for combining an adversarial classification algorithm with a very general class of models of adversarial classifier evasion. We show that our algorithmic approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art alternatives.

paragraphs: The paper examines classification when the objects being classified are deliberately changed to evade detection. In settings such as spam or malware detection, an adversary responds to the classifier rather than supplying fixed data. The authors investigate how to model these adversaries' objectives and how learning algorithms can account for their goal-directed behavior.

A central finding is that reducing the feature set can have severe weaknesses under several natural adversarial objectives. These weaknesses are especially pronounced when an attacker can substitute similar features, such as replacing words with synonyms or changing letters. The paper proposes a simple robustness heuristic and a broader method that explicitly incorporates an evasion model.

The broader method uses mixed-integer linear programming with constraint generation. A sparsity regularizer and the evasion model jointly govern the tradeoff involving feature selection and overfitting. The authors describe their method as the first to combine adversarial classification with this broad class of evasion models, and report significant improvements over state-of-the-art alternatives in their evaluation.
summary.tldr: Modeling attackers' ability to substitute similar features exposes weaknesses in feature reduction and supports more robust adversarial classification.

title: Feature Cross-Substitution in Adversarial Classification

abstract: Knowledge tracing, where a machine models the knowledge of a student as they interact with coursework, is an established and significantly unsolved problem in computer supported education.In this paper we explore the benefit of using recurrent neural networks to model student learning.This family of models have important advantages over current state of the art methods in that they do not require the explicit encoding of human domain knowledge,and have a far more flexible functional form which can capture substantially more complex student interactions.We show that these neural networks outperform the current state of the art in prediction on real student data,while allowing straightforward interpretation and discovery of structure in the curriculum.These results suggest a promising new line of research for knowledge tracing.
originalAbstract: Knowledge tracing, where a machine models the knowledge of a student as they interact with coursework, is an established and significantly unsolved problem in computer supported education.In this paper we explore the benefit of using recurrent neural networks to model student learning.This family of models have important advantages over current state of the art methods in that they do not require the explicit encoding of human domain knowledge,and have a far more flexible functional form which can capture substantially more complex student interactions.We show that these neural networks outperform the current state of the art in prediction on real student data,while allowing straightforward interpretation and discovery of structure in the curriculum.These results suggest a promising new line of research for knowledge tracing.

paragraphs: Knowledge tracing means modeling a student’s knowledge as they interact with coursework. The paper explores recurrent neural networks for this task, treating learning as an evolving process reflected in a sequence of student interactions. Its aim is to improve how educational systems predict student behavior from that history.

The authors emphasize two advantages of the proposed model family. It does not require human domain knowledge to be explicitly encoded, and its flexible mathematical form can capture substantially more complex patterns in student interactions. This shifts part of the modeling work toward learning relationships from data, allowing the representation of student learning to accommodate richer dependencies.

On real student data, the networks outperform the existing state of the art in prediction. The authors also report that the models permit straightforward interpretation and discovery of curriculum structure. These results support recurrent networks as a promising direction for knowledge tracing; the demonstrated improvement concerns prediction and modeling, rather than an established improvement in students’ learning outcomes.
summary.tldr: Recurrent neural networks improve student-performance prediction while learning patterns in student interactions and curriculum structure.

title: Deep Knowledge Tracing

abstract: The mutual information is a core statistical quantity that has applications in all areas of machine learning, whether this is in training of density models over multiple data modalities, in maximising the efficiency of noisy transmission channels, or when learning behaviour policies for exploration by artificial agents. Most learning algorithms that involve optimisation of the mutual information rely on the Blahut-Arimoto algorithm --- an enumerative algorithm with exponential complexity that is not suitable for modern machine learning applications. This paper provides a new approach for scalable optimisation of the mutual information by merging techniques from variational inference and deep learning. We develop our approach by focusing on the problem of intrinsically-motivated learning, where the mutual information forms the definition of a well-known internal drive known as empowerment. Using a variational lower bound on the mutual information, combined with convolutional networks for handling visual input streams, we develop a stochastic optimisation algorithm that allows for scalable information maximisation and empowerment-based reasoning directly from pixels to actions.

Most learning algorithms that involve optimisation of the mutual information rely on the Blahut-Arimoto algorithm --- an enumerative algorithm with exponential complexity that is not suitable for modern machine learning applications. This paper provides a new approach for scalable optimisation of the mutual information by merging techniques from variational inference and deep learning. We develop our approach by focusing on the problem of intrinsically-motivated learning, where the mutual information forms the definition of a well-known internal drive known as empowerment. paragraphs: Mutual information measures statistical dependence and appears in learning objectives across many domains. Optimizing it can be computationally difficult: the paper highlights an established enumerative algorithm whose exponential complexity is unsuitable for modern large-scale applications. The authors seek a scalable approach that combines variational inference with deep learning.

They develop the method through intrinsically motivated reinforcement learning, focusing on empowerment, an internal drive defined using mutual information. Instead of directly handling the full information objective through enumeration, they optimize a variational lower bound. Convolutional networks process visual input streams, connecting this information-based objective to observations supplied as images.

The resulting stochastic optimization algorithm supports scalable information maximization and empowerment-based reasoning from pixels to actions. The lower-bound formulation is an essential part of the claim: the method makes a tractable objective available for learning without asserting exact optimization of the full mutual information. Its significance is to bring an information-theoretic internal motivation into a computational form that can work with visual inputs and action decisions.
summary.tldr: A variational mutual-information bound and convolutional networks enable scalable empowerment-based learning from pixels to actions.

title: Variational Information Maximisation for Intrinsically Motivated Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Recent work on scaling up Gaussian process regression (GPR) to large datasets has primarily focused on sparse GPR, which leverages a small set of basis functions to approximate the full Gaussian process during inference. However, the majority of these approaches are batch methods that operate on the entire training dataset at once, precluding the use of datasets that are streaming or too large to fit into memory. Although previous work has considered incrementally solving variational sparse GPR, most algorithms fail to update the basis functions and therefore perform suboptimally. We propose a novel incremental learning algorithm for variational sparse GPR based on stochastic mirror ascent of probability densities in reproducing kernel Hilbert space. This new formulation allows our algorithm to update basis functions online in accordance with the manifold structure of probability densities for fast convergence. We conduct several experiments and show that our proposed approach achieves better empirical performance in terms of prediction error than the recent state-of-the-art incremental solutions to variational sparse GPR.
originalAbstract: Recent work on scaling up Gaussian process regression (GPR) to large datasets has primarily focused on sparse GPR, which leverages a small set of basis functions to approximate the full Gaussian process during inference. However, the majority of these approaches are batch methods that operate on the entire training dataset at once, precluding the use of datasets that are streaming or too large to fit into memory. Although previous work has considered incrementally solving variational sparse GPR, most algorithms fail to update the basis functions and therefore perform suboptimally. We propose a novel incremental learning algorithm for variational sparse GPR based on stochastic mirror ascent of probability densities in reproducing kernel Hilbert space. This new formulation allows our algorithm to update basis functions online in accordance with the manifold structure of probability densities for fast convergence. We conduct several experiments and show that our proposed approach achieves better empirical performance in terms of prediction error than the recent state-of-the-art incremental solutions to variational sparse GPR.

paragraphs: Sparse Gaussian process regression approximates a full Gaussian process using a small set of basis functions. This can reduce inference costs, but batch methods still require access to the whole training dataset. The paper addresses incremental learning for datasets that arrive as streams or are too large to fit into memory.

A central issue is whether the basis functions themselves can adapt as new observations arrive. The authors note that many earlier incremental methods leave them unchanged, leading to suboptimal performance. Their algorithm uses stochastic mirror ascent over probability densities in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, enabling online basis-function updates that respect the geometric structure of those densities.

The formulation is designed to support fast convergence while adapting the approximation throughout learning. Across several experiments, it achieves lower prediction error than recent state-of-the-art incremental variational sparse Gaussian process methods. The empirical finding supports updating the representation itself as part of incremental inference, alongside the other quantities needed for prediction.
summary.tldr: An incremental sparse Gaussian process algorithm updates basis functions online and achieves better prediction error than the compared incremental methods.

title: Incremental Variational Sparse Gaussian Process Regression

abstract: In many applications such as advertisement placement or automated dialog systems, an intelligent system optimizes performance over a sequence of interactions with each user. Such tasks often involve many states and potentially time-dependent transition dynamics, and can be modeled well as episodic Markov decision processes (MDPs). In this paper, we present a PAC algorithm for reinforcement learning in episodic finite MDPs with time-dependent transitions that acts epsilon-optimal in all but O(S A H^3 / epsilon^2 log(1 / delta)) episodes. Our algorithm has a polynomial computational complexity, and our sample complexity bound accounts for the fact that we may only be able to approximately solve the internal planning problems. In addition, our PAC sample complexity bound has only linear dependency on the number of states S and actions A and strictly improves previous bounds with S^2 dependency in this setting. Compared against other methods for infinite horizon reinforcement learning with linear state space sample complexity our method has much lower dependency on the (effective) horizon. Indeed, our bound is optimal up to a factor of H.

paragraphs: Some reinforcement-learning tasks consist of repeated, finite interactions, such as a dialogue or a sequence of advertisement decisions. Their transition dynamics may depend on the stage of the interaction. This paper develops a probably approximately correct algorithm for finite episodic Markov decision processes that allows this time dependence.

Its guarantee bounds the number of episodes in which behavior is more than ε away from optimal. With confidence controlled by δ, that number is O(SAH³/ε² log(1/δ)), where S counts states, A counts actions, and H is the episode horizon. The algorithm has polynomial computational complexity, and the analysis accommodates approximate solutions to its internal planning problems.

The bound depends linearly on both the number of states and the number of actions, improving earlier quadratic state dependence in this setting. It also has lower horizon dependence than the cited infinite-horizon methods with linear state dependence. The resulting sample complexity is optimal up to a factor of H, identifying the remaining gap in the guarantee.
summary.tldr: A polynomial-time episodic reinforcement-learning algorithm achieves a PAC sample bound linear in states and actions and optimal up to one horizon factor.

title: Only H is left: Near-tight Episodic PAC RL

abstract: We study the application of min-max propagation, a variation of belief propagation, for approximate min-max inference in factor graphs. We show that for “any” high-order function that can be minimized in O(ω), the min-max message update can be obtained using an efficient O(K(ω + log(K)) procedure, where K is the number of variables. We demonstrate how this generic procedure, in combination with efficient updates for a family of high-order constraints, enables the application of min-max propagation to efficiently approximate the NP-hard problem of makespan minimization, which seeks to distribute a set of tasks on machines, such that the worst case load is minimized.

paragraphs: Some optimization problems aim to reduce the worst outcome rather than a sum of costs. This paper studies min-max propagation, a variation of belief propagation, for approximate inference of that kind in factor graphs. The computational focus is on updating messages involving high-order functions, which depend on multiple variables.

The main result connects the cost of a message update to the cost of minimizing the underlying function. For a high-order function that can be minimized in O(omega) time, the paper gives a generic update procedure requiring O(K(omega + log K)) time, with K the number of variables. This makes an efficient minimization routine useful as a building block for message passing.

The authors combine the generic procedure with efficient updates for a family of high-order constraints and apply it to makespan minimization. That problem assigns tasks to machines to reduce the largest machine load. The resulting method efficiently approximates this NP-hard scheduling problem; the efficient local updates do not constitute a claim of exact global optimization.
summary.tldr: Efficient min-max message updates enable an approximate factor-graph approach to minimizing the worst machine load in scheduling.

title: Min-Max Propagation

abstract: We present improved algorithm for properly learning convex polytopes in the realizable PAC setting from data with a margin. Our learning algorithm constructs a consistent polytope as an intersection of about t log t halfspaces with margins in time polynomial in t (where t is the number of halfspaces forming an optimal polytope). We also identify distinct generalizations of the notion of margin from hyperplanes to polytopes and investigate how they relate geometrically; this result may be of interest beyond the learning setting.

We also identify distinct generalizations of the notion of margin from hyperplanes to polytopes and investigate how they relate geometrically; this result may be of interest beyond the learning setting.

paragraphs: A convex polytope can be described by intersecting halfspaces, with each halfspace imposing a linear boundary. This paper studies how to learn such a shape from labeled data when the data have a margin. It works in the realizable PAC setting, where a suitable target polytope can account for the labels.

The proposed algorithm properly learns the class: its output is itself a polytope. If an optimal polytope uses t halfspaces, the algorithm constructs a consistent polytope using about t log t halfspaces with margins, in time polynomial in t. Thus, the guarantee permits a more complex output boundary than the optimal polytope while retaining consistency with the supplied data.

The paper also examines what a margin should mean for a polytope. A definition familiar from a single hyperplane does not yield only one possible extension to an intersection of halfspaces. The authors identify distinct generalizations and study their geometric relationships. This analysis helps specify the learning assumptions precisely and may also be useful for geometric questions beyond learning.
summary.tldr: Under realizability and margin assumptions, the algorithm learns a consistent polytope with about t log t halfspaces in time polynomial in t.

title: Learning convex polytopes with margin

abstract: Box filters computed using integral images have been part of the computer vision toolset for a long time. Here, we show that a convolutional layer that computes box filter responses in a sliding manner can be used within deep architectures, whereas the dimensions and the offsets of the sliding boxes in such a layer can be learned as part of an end-to-end loss minimization. Crucially, the training process can make the size of the boxes in such a layer arbitrarily large without incurring extra computational cost and without the need to increase the number of learnable parameters. Due to its ability to integrate information over large boxes, the new layer facilitates long-range propagation of information and leads to the efficient increase of the receptive fields of downstream units in the network. By incorporating the new layer into existing architectures for semantic segmentation, we are able to achieve both the increase in segmentation accuracy as well as the decrease in the computational cost and the number of learnable parameters.

paragraphs: The paper brings box filters computed with integral images into trainable deep networks. Its proposed convolutional layer slides boxes across the input and computes their filter responses. The dimensions and offsets of these boxes are learned through the network's end-to-end training objective, allowing the spatial extent of the operation to adapt during learning.

The key computational property is that enlarging a box does not add computational cost or require more learnable parameters. A layer can therefore integrate information over a much larger area without paying a size-dependent cost for that expansion. This facilitates long-range information propagation and enlarges the receptive fields of downstream units, meaning those units can draw on a broader portion of the input.

The authors incorporate box-convolution layers into existing semantic segmentation architectures. In these experiments, segmentation accuracy increases while computational cost and parameter count decrease. The results show how a spatially adaptable filtering operation can improve both efficiency and prediction quality in the evaluated networks, with large-area aggregation providing the link between the architectural change and its intended benefit.
summary.tldr: Learnable box convolutions expand spatial context without size-dependent computation and improve the tested segmentation networks' accuracy and efficiency.

title: Deep Neural Networks with Box Convolutions

abstract: We study the problem of off-policy policy evaluation (OPPE) in RL. In contrast to prior work, we consider how to estimate both the individual policy value and average policy value accurately. We draw inspiration from recent work in causal reasoning, and propose a new finite sample generalization error bound for value estimates from MDP models. Using this upper bound as an objective, we develop a learning algorithm of an MDP model with a balanced representation, and show that our approach can yield substantially lower MSE in common synthetic benchmarks and a HIV treatment simulation domain.
originalAbstract: We study the problem of off-policy policy evaluation (OPPE) in RL. In contrast to prior work, we consider how to estimate both the individual policy value and average policy value accurately. We draw inspiration from recent work in causal reasoning, and propose a new finite sample generalization error bound for value estimates from MDP models. Using this upper bound as an objective, we develop a learning algorithm of an MDP model with a balanced representation, and show that our approach can yield substantially lower MSE in common synthetic benchmarks and a HIV treatment simulation domain.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates how a policy would perform using experience gathered under another policy. This paper considers accuracy for both individual policy values and average policy values. That dual focus asks the evaluation procedure to capture individual outcomes as well as aggregate performance, rather than assessing only the overall average.

Drawing inspiration from causal reasoning, the authors derive a finite-sample generalization-error bound for value estimates produced by Markov decision process models. They then use this upper bound as a learning objective. The resulting algorithm learns an MDP model with a balanced representation, connecting its representation-learning criterion directly to an analysis of policy-value estimation error.

The authors show that the approach can substantially reduce mean squared error on common synthetic benchmarks and in an HIV treatment simulation domain. These findings support using the error bound to guide model learning for off-policy evaluation. The simulation result is evidence about policy-value estimation in that domain; the stated outcome is lower estimation error, rather than a demonstrated improvement in real-world treatment.
summary.tldr: A causal-inspired error bound guides balanced MDP representation learning and can substantially improve off-policy value estimation.

title: Representation Balancing MDPs for Off-policy Policy Evaluation

abstract: A central problem to understanding intelligence is the concept of generalisation. This allows previously learnt structure to be exploited to solve tasks in novel situations differing in their particularities. We take inspiration from neuroscience, specifically the hippocampal-entorhinal system known to be important for generalisation. We propose that to generalise structural knowledge, the representations of the structure of the world, i.e. how entities in the world relate to each other, need to be separated from representations of the entities themselves. We show, under these principles, artificial neural networks embedded with hierarchy and fast Hebbian memory, can learn the statistics of memories and generalise structural knowledge. Spatial neuronal representations mirroring those found in the brain emerge, suggesting spatial cognition is an instance of more general organising principles. We further unify many entorhinal cell types as basis functions for constructing transition graphs, and show these representations effectively utilise memories. We experimentally support model assumptions, showing a preserved relationship between entorhinal grid and hippocampal place cells across environments.

paragraphs: Generalization requires reusing learned relationships when the particular entities involved change. Inspired by the hippocampal-entorhinal system, this paper proposes separating representations of entities from representations of how those entities relate. The aim is to preserve reusable structure while allowing the specific contents of an experience to vary across situations.

The authors build neural networks with hierarchy and fast Hebbian memory around this principle. They show that these networks can learn statistical patterns in memories and generalize structural knowledge. Spatial representations resembling those observed in the brain emerge in the models, suggesting that spatial cognition may reflect organizing principles with applications beyond physical space.

The work also interprets multiple entorhinal cell types as basis functions for constructing graphs of possible transitions, and shows that these representations use memories effectively. Experiments support a model assumption by finding a preserved relationship between entorhinal grid cells and hippocampal place cells across environments. This evidence connects the proposed computational separation to an observed relationship in the biological system.
summary.tldr: Separating relational structure from entity representations enables structural generalization in memory-based networks and yields brain-like spatial representations.

title: Generalisation of structural knowledge in the hippocampal-entorhinal system

abstract: Several algorithms build on the perfect phylogeny model to infer evolutionary trees. This problem is particularly hard when evolutionary trees are inferred from the fraction of genomes that have mutations in different positions, across different samples. Existing algorithms might do extensive searches over the space of possible trees. At the center of these algorithms is a projection problem that assigns a fitness cost to phylogenetic trees. In order to perform a wide search over the space of the trees, it is critical to solve this projection problem fast. In this paper, we use Moreau's decomposition for proximal operators, and a tree reduction scheme, to develop a new algorithm to compute this projection. Our algorithm terminates with an exact solution in a finite number of steps, and is extremely fast. In particular, it can search over all evolutionary trees with fewer than 11 nodes, a size relevant for several biological problems (more than 2 billion trees) in about 2 hours.

The observations are mutation frequencies: fractions of genomes carrying mutations at different positions across samples. Finding a suitable tree can require searching a large space of possibilities, making the cost of evaluating each candidate especially important.

At the center of that evaluation is a projection problem that assigns a fitness cost to a candidate tree. The authors develop a new projection algorithm using Moreau’s decomposition for proximal operators together with a tree reduction scheme. The algorithm reaches an exact solution after finitely many steps, providing a precise evaluation procedure for the surrounding tree search.

The reported computational result illustrates why this inner operation matters: the method enables a search over more than two billion evolutionary trees with fewer than 11 nodes in about two hours. That size is relevant to several biological problems described by the authors. The contribution is therefore an exact and fast building block that makes extensive exploration of candidate phylogenies more practical.
summary.tldr: An exact, finite-step projection algorithm makes extensive searches over small perfect-phylogeny trees practical.

title: Efficient Projection onto the Perfect Phylogeny Model

abstract: An agent that has well understood the environment should be able to apply its skills for any given goals, leading to the fundamental problem of learning the Universal Value Function Approximator (UVFA). A UVFA learns to predict the cumulative rewards between all state-goal pairs. However, empirically, the value function for long-range goals is always hard to estimate and may consequently result in failed policy. This has presented challenges to the learning process and the capability of neural networks. We propose a method to address this issue in large MDPs with sparse rewards, in which exploration and routing across remote states are both extremely challenging. Our method explicitly models the environment in a hierarchical manner, with a high-level dynamic landmark-based map abstracting the visited state space, and a low-level value network to derive precise local decisions. We use farthest point sampling to select landmark states from past experience, which has improved exploration compared with simple uniform sampling. Experimentally we showed that our method enables the agent to reach long-range goals at the early training stage, and achieve better performance than standard RL algorithms for a number of challenging tasks.

paragraphs: A universal value function approximator predicts cumulative rewards for different combinations of starting states and goals. Estimating values for distant goals is empirically difficult and can lead to unsuccessful policies. This paper addresses that difficulty in large Markov decision processes with sparse rewards, where both exploration and routing between remote states are challenging.

The method represents the environment hierarchically. A dynamic map of landmark states provides a high-level description of the visited state space, while a low-level value network supplies precise local decisions. This separates the broad problem of navigating across the environment from the more local decisions needed along the way.

Landmarks are selected from past experience using farthest point sampling. The authors report that this improves exploration compared with uniform sampling. Experiments show agents reaching distant goals early in training and outperforming standard reinforcement-learning algorithms on several challenging tasks. The findings support using an explicit landmark map to complement local value estimation when long-range value predictions are difficult to learn directly.
summary.tldr: A dynamic landmark map combined with local value estimation helps agents explore and reach distant goals in sparse-reward environments.

title: Mapping State Space using Landmarks for Universal Goal Reaching

abstract: The fundamental learning theory behind neural networks remains largely open. What classes of functions can neural networks actually learn? Why doesn't the trained network overfit when it is overparameterized? In this work, we prove that overparameterized neural networks can learn some notable concept classes, including two and three-layer networks with fewer parameters and smooth activations. Moreover, the learning can be simply done by SGD (stochastic gradient descent) or its variants in polynomial time using polynomially many samples. The sample complexity can also be almost independent of the number of parameters in the network. On the technique side, our analysis goes beyond the so-called NTK (neural tangent kernel) linearization of neural networks in prior works. We establish a new notion of quadratic approximation of the neural network, and connect it to the SGD theory of escaping saddle points.

paragraphs: This paper studies what overparameterized neural networks can provably learn and why having many parameters need not force excessive sample requirements. Its guarantees cover particular concept classes, including functions represented by smaller two- and three-layer networks with smooth activations. The result concerns identifiable families of learnable functions rather than every possible prediction problem.

The authors prove that stochastic gradient descent or its variants can learn these classes in polynomial time using polynomially many samples. They also show that sample complexity can be almost independent of the number of parameters in the learning network. This separates the size of the model used for optimization from the amount of data needed for the stated learning guarantees.

The analysis goes beyond the linear approximation associated with neural tangent kernel arguments. It introduces a quadratic approximation of the network and connects that approximation with theory about stochastic gradient descent escaping saddle points. This additional structure provides a route to learning and generalization guarantees that extend beyond the earlier linearized treatment.
summary.tldr: A quadratic network analysis proves efficient learning of specified function classes with sample requirements almost independent of the overparameterized model's size.

title: Learning and Generalization in Overparameterized Neural Networks, Going Beyond Two Layers

abstract: We present high quality image synthesis results using diffusion probabilistic models, a class of latent variable models inspired by considerations from nonequilibrium thermodynamics. Our best results are obtained by training on a weighted variational bound designed according to a novel connection between diffusion probabilistic models and denoising score matching with Langevin dynamics, and our models naturally admit a progressive lossy decompression scheme that can be interpreted as a generalization of autoregressive decoding. On the unconditional CIFAR10 dataset, we obtain an Inception score of 9.46 and a state-of-the-art FID score of 3.17. On 256x256 LSUN, we obtain sample quality similar to ProgressiveGAN.

paragraphs: This paper demonstrates high-quality image generation with diffusion probabilistic models, a family of latent variable models motivated by nonequilibrium thermodynamics. Its contribution combines a training formulation with empirical image synthesis results. The central question is how to train these models so that their generated images achieve strong quality.

The best results use a weighted variational bound whose design follows a newly identified connection to denoising score matching with Langevin dynamics. This connection links the diffusion modeling approach to another framework for learning and generating from distributions. The authors also show that the models naturally support progressive lossy decompression, giving image generation an interpretation as a generalization of autoregressive decoding.

On LSUN at 256 by 256 resolution, it reports sample quality similar to ProgressiveGAN. Together, these findings establish strong image synthesis performance in the stated evaluations, while the decompression interpretation offers another way to understand the model's generation process.
summary.tldr: Diffusion probabilistic models achieve strong image synthesis results using a training objective connected to denoising score matching.

title: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models

abstract: Deep convolutional networks (DCNs) learn meaningful representations where data that share the same abstract characteristics are positioned closer and closer. Understanding these representations and how they are generated is of unquestioned practical and theoretical interest. In this work we study the evolution of the probability density of the ImageNet dataset across the hidden layers in some state-of-the-art DCNs. We find that the initial layers generate a unimodal probability density getting rid of any structure irrelevant for classification. In subsequent layers density peaks arise in a hierarchical fashion that mirrors the semantic hierarchy of the concepts. Density peaks corresponding to single categories appear only close to the output and via a very sharp transition which resembles the nucleation process of a heterogeneous liquid. This process leaves a footprint in the probability density of the output layer where the topography of the peaks allows reconstructing the semantic relationships of the categories.

paragraphs: Deep convolutional networks place examples with shared abstract characteristics closer together in their learned representations. This paper examines how that organization develops across hidden layers by studying the probability density of ImageNet representations in several state-of-the-art networks. The focus is on the changing arrangement of data, rather than solely on final classification performance.

The authors find a sequence of structural changes. Early layers produce a single-peaked density while removing structure irrelevant to classification. Later layers develop multiple density peaks in a hierarchical pattern that reflects semantic relationships. Peaks associated with individual categories emerge only near the output, through a particularly sharp transition.

The paper compares this abrupt formation of category-specific peaks to nucleation in a heterogeneous liquid. The analogy describes the observed emergence of organized regions in representation space. That process leaves a detectable pattern in the output density: the arrangement of its peaks allows semantic relationships among categories to be reconstructed. The findings connect the internal geometry of the studied networks with the conceptual hierarchy of their categories.
summary.tldr: The studied convolutional networks organize representations through hierarchical density peaks, with category-specific peaks appearing sharply near the output.

title: Hierarchical nucleation in deep neural networks

abstract: Convolution is one of the most essential components of modern architectures used in computer vision. As machine learning moves towards reducing the expert bias and learning it from data, a natural next step seems to be learning convolution-like structures from scratch. This, however, has proven elusive. For example, current state-of-the-art architecture search algorithms use convolution as one of the existing modules rather than learning it from data. In an attempt to understand the inductive bias that gives rise to convolutions, we investigate minimum description length as a guiding principle and show that in some settings, it can indeed be indicative of the performance of architectures. To find architectures with small description length, we propose beta-LASSO, a simple variant of LASSO algorithm that, when applied on fully-connected networks for image classification tasks, learns architectures with local connections and achieves state-of-the-art accuracies for training fully-connected networks on CIFAR-10 (84.50%), CIFAR-100 (57.76%) and SVHN (93.84%) bridging the gap between fully-connected and convolutional networks.

paragraphs: Convolution is usually supplied as a predefined building block in vision architectures, including those found through architecture search. This paper asks whether convolution-like structure can instead emerge from learning. Its focus is the inductive bias that could encourage a fully connected image classifier to develop useful connection patterns.

The authors investigate minimum description length as a guiding principle and show that, in some settings, it can indicate architecture performance. To seek architectures with short descriptions, they introduce beta-LASSO, a simple variation of LASSO. These findings narrow the performance gap between fully connected and convolutional networks. The stated achievement is learning useful locality and improving fully connected classifiers; the description-length evidence is explicitly limited to some settings.
summary.tldr: Beta-LASSO encourages short-description architectures that learn local connections and improve fully connected image classifiers.

title: Towards Learning Convolutions from Scratch

abstract: In this paper, we study the problem of learning the skill distribution of a population of agents from observations of pairwise games in a tournament. These games are played among randomly drawn agents from the population. The agents in our model can be individuals, sports teams, or Wall Street fund managers. Formally, we postulate that the likelihoods of outcomes of games are governed by the parametric Bradley-Terry-Luce (or multinomial logit) model, where the probability of an agent beating another is the ratio between its skill level and the pairwise sum of skill levels, and the skill parameters are drawn from an unknown, non-parametric skill density of interest. The problem is, in essence, to learn a distribution from noisy, quantized observations. We propose a surprisingly simple and tractable algorithm that learns the skill density with near-optimal minimax mean squared error scaling as $n^{-1+\varepsilon}$, for any $\varepsilon>0$, so long as the density is smooth. Our approach brings together prior work on learning skill parameters from pairwise comparisons with kernel density estimation from non-parametric statistics. Furthermore, we prove information theoretic lower bounds which establish minimax optimality of the skill parameter estimation technique used in our algorithm. These bounds utilize a continuum version of Fano's method along with a careful covering argument. We apply our algorithm to various soccer leagues and world cups, cricket world cups, and mutual funds. We find that the entropy of a learnt distribution provides a quantitative measure of skill, which in turn provides rigorous explanations for popular beliefs about perceived qualities of sporting events, e.g., soccer league rankings. Finally, we apply our method to assess the skill distributions of mutual funds. Our results shed light on the abundance of low quality funds prior to the Great Recession of 2008, and the domination of the industry by more skilled funds after the financial crisis.

title: Estimation of Skill Distribution from a Tournament

abstract: Contemporary machine learning applications often involve classification tasks with many classes. Despite their extensive use, a precise understanding of the statistical properties and behavior of classification algorithms is still missing, especially in modern regimes where the number of classes is rather large. In this paper, we take a step in this direction by providing the first asymptotically precise analysis of linear multiclass classification. Our theoretical analysis allows us to precisely characterize how the test error varies over different training algorithms, data distributions, problem dimensions as well as number of classes, inter/intra class correlations and class priors. Specifically, our analysis reveals that the classification accuracy is highly distribution-dependent with different algorithms achieving optimal performance for different data distributions and/or training/features sizes. Unlike linear regression/binary classification, the test error in multiclass classification relies on intricate functions of the trained model (e.g., correlation between some of the trained weights) whose asymptotic behavior is difficult to characterize. This challenge is already present in simple classifiers, such as those minimizing a square loss. Our novel theoretical techniques allow us to overcome some of these challenges. The insights gained may pave the way for a precise understanding of other classification algorithms beyond those studied in this paper.

paragraphs: The paper develops an asymptotically precise analysis of linear classifiers with multiple classes. It asks how test error changes with the training algorithm, data distribution, problem dimensions, and number of classes. The analysis also accounts for class frequencies and correlations within and between classes, making it possible to examine several sources of classification difficulty together.

A major obstacle is that multiclass test error depends on complicated properties of the trained model, including correlations between learned weight vectors. This difficulty appears even when training minimizes a simple squared loss. The authors introduce theoretical techniques that overcome some of these obstacles and characterize the relevant asymptotic behavior.

Different algorithms can be optimal for different distributions or different amounts of training data and features. Thus, conclusions about which method performs best depend on the statistical setting being analyzed. The work provides precise results for the studied linear classifiers and suggests a possible foundation for analyzing additional classification algorithms.
summary.tldr: An asymptotically precise theory of linear multiclass classification shows how test error and the best-performing algorithm depend on the data and problem dimensions.

title: Theoretical Insights Into Multiclass Classification: A High-dimensional Asymptotic View

abstract: Localization by image retrieval is inexpensive and scalable due to its simple mapping and matching techniques. The localization accuracy, however, depends on the quality of the underlying image features, often obtained using contrastive learning. Most contrastive learning strategies learn features that distinguish between different classes. In the context of localization, however, there is no natural definition of classes. Therefore, images are artificially separated into positive/negative classes with respect to the chosen anchor images, based on some geometric proximity measure. In this paper, we show why such divisions are problematic for learning localization features. We argue that any artificial division based on a proximity measure is undesirable due to the inherently ambiguous supervision for images near the proximity threshold. To avoid this problem, we propose a novel technique that uses soft positive/negative assignments of images for contrastive learning. Our soft assignment makes a gradual distinction between close and far images in both geometric and feature space. Experiments on four large-scale benchmark datasets demonstrate the superiority of our soft contrastive learning over the state-of-the-art method for retrieval-based visual localization.

paragraphs: Image-retrieval localization estimates location by matching an image against other images, making the quality of its learned features crucial. Contrastive learning usually organizes examples into positive and negative relationships. For localization, however, there is no natural class boundary, so those relationships are commonly imposed using geometric proximity.

The paper identifies a problem near the chosen threshold: images with almost the same proximity can receive opposite training assignments. Such a sharp division creates ambiguous supervision for learning location-sensitive features. The proposed method replaces binary assignments with soft ones, gradually distinguishing close and far images in both geometric space and the learned feature space.

Experiments on four large-scale benchmark datasets report better retrieval-based localization than the state-of-the-art method used for comparison. The contribution is a change in how supervision expresses similarity, allowing the training signal to reflect degrees of proximity. This matters because the geometry of the localization task is gradual, and treating its artificial threshold as an absolute distinction can hinder feature learning.
summary.tldr: Soft contrastive assignments replace sharp proximity thresholds to improve learned image features for retrieval-based localization.

title: Soft Contrastive Learning for Visual Localization

abstract: A wide range of reinforcement learning (RL) problems --- including robustness, transfer learning, unsupervised RL, and emergent complexity --- require specifying a distribution of tasks or environments in which a policy will be trained. However, creating a useful distribution of environments is error prone, and takes a significant amount of developer time and effort. We propose Unsupervised Environment Design (UED) as an alternative paradigm, where developers provide environments with unknown parameters, and these parameters are used to automatically produce a distribution over valid, solvable environments. Existing approaches to automatically generating environments suffer from common failure modes: domain randomization cannot generate structure or adapt the difficulty of the environment to the agent's learning progress, and minimax adversarial training leads to worst-case environments that are often unsolvable. To generate structured, solvable environments for our protagonist agent, we introduce a second, antagonist agent that is allied with the environment-generating adversary. The adversary is motivated to generate environments which maximize regret, defined as the difference between the protagonist and antagonist agent's return. We call our technique Protagonist Antagonist Induced Regret Environment Design (PAIRED). Our experiments demonstrate that PAIRED produces a natural curriculum of increasingly complex environments, and PAIRED agents achieve higher zero-shot transfer performance when tested in highly novel environments.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning agent's abilities depend on the environments it encounters during training. Designing a useful collection by hand takes effort, while random variation may fail to create structure or track the agent's progress. Making environments maximally difficult can also produce tasks that cannot be solved.

The paper proposes Unsupervised Environment Design, in which developers leave environment parameters unspecified and a learning process chooses them. Its PAIRED method uses three participants: a protagonist learning to act, an adversary designing environments, and an antagonist allied with that adversary. The environment designer is rewarded for producing a gap between the agents' returns, using the antagonist's performance to expose challenges that the protagonist has not yet mastered.

This regret-based objective gives the designer a reason to create tasks that another agent can handle while the protagonist struggles. In the reported experiments, PAIRED generates a curriculum whose environments become increasingly complex. Agents trained this way also perform better when transferred directly to highly unfamiliar environments, connecting adaptive task generation with the measured transfer benefit.
summary.tldr: PAIRED automatically generates increasingly complex training environments by rewarding performance gaps between two agents, improving reported zero-shot transfer.

title: Emergent Complexity and Zero-shot Transfer via Unsupervised Environment Design

abstract: We propose a novel graph cross network (GXN) to achieve comprehensive feature learning from multiple scales of a graph. Based on trainable hierarchical representations of a graph, GXN enables the interchange of intermediate features across scales to promote information flow. Two key ingredients of GXN include a novel vertex infomax pooling (VIPool), which creates multiscale graphs in a trainable manner, and a novel feature-crossing layer, enabling feature interchange across scales. The proposed VIPool selects the most informative subset of vertices based on the neural estimation of mutual information between vertex features and neighborhood features. The intuition behind is that a vertex is informative when it can maximally reflect its neighboring information. The proposed feature-crossing layer fuses intermediate features between two scales for mutual enhancement by improving information flow and enriching multiscale features at hidden layers. The cross shape of feature-crossing layer distinguishes GXN from many other multiscale architectures. Experimental results show that the proposed GXN improves the classification accuracy by 2.12% and 1.15% on average for graph classification and vertex classification, respectively. Based on the same network, the proposed VIPool consistently outperforms other graph-pooling methods.
