paragraphs: A graph can contain useful patterns at several scales, from individual neighborhoods to larger structures. Graph Cross Networks, or GXN, learn representations at multiple scales and exchange intermediate features between them. This exchange lets information developed at one resolution contribute to learning at another while the network is still building its representations.

The first component, vertex infomax pooling, learns which vertices to retain when constructing smaller graphs. It uses a neural estimate of mutual information between a vertex's features and its neighborhood's features. The guiding idea is to retain vertices that reflect their surroundings well. A feature-crossing layer then combines intermediate features between two scales to enrich both representations.

The experiments report average classification accuracy improvements of 2.12% for whole graphs and 1.15% for individual vertices. With the surrounding network held the same, the proposed pooling method also consistently outperforms other graph-pooling methods. These results support both parts of the design: selecting informative vertices to construct multiple scales and allowing those scales to exchange information throughout feature learning.
summary.tldr: GXN combines informative vertex selection with feature exchange across graph scales to improve graph and vertex classification.

title: Graph Cross Networks with Vertex Infomax Pooling

abstract: Langevin dynamics (LD) has been proven to be a powerful technique for optimizing a non-convex objective as an efficient algorithm to find local minima while eventually visiting a global minimum on longer time-scales. LD is based on the first-order Langevin diffusion which is reversible in time. We study two variants that are based on non-reversible Langevin diffusions: the underdamped Langevin dynamics (ULD) and the Langevin dynamics with a non-symmetric drift (NLD). Adopting the techniques of Tzen et al. (2018) for LD to non-reversible diffusions, we show that for a given local minimum that is within an arbitrary distance from the initialization, with high probability, either the ULD trajectory ends up somewhere outside a small neighborhood of this local minimum within a recurrence time which depends on the smallest eigenvalue of the Hessian at the local minimum or they enter this neighborhood by the recurrence time and stay there for a potentially exponentially long escape time. The ULD algorithm improves upon the recurrence time obtained for LD in Tzen et al. (2018) with respect to the dependency on the smallest eigenvalue of the Hessian at the local minimum. Similar results and improvements are obtained for the NLD algorithm. We also show that non-reversible variants can exit the basin of attraction of a local minimum faster in discrete time when the objective has two local minima separated by a saddle point and quantify the amount of improvement. Our analysis suggests that non-reversible Langevin algorithms are more efficient to locate a local minimum as well as exploring the state space.

For a specified local minimum, the authors establish a high-probability alternative. summary.tldr: Two non-reversible Langevin variants improve theoretical recurrence-time bounds and can escape local basins faster in an analyzed two-minimum setting.

title: Breaking Reversibility Accelerates Langevin Dynamics for Non-Convex Optimization

abstract: Deep Reinforcement Learning (RL) is successful in solving many complex Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) problems. However, agents often face unanticipated environmental changes after deployment in the real world. These changes are often spurious and unrelated to the underlying problem, such as background shifts for visual input agents. Unfortunately, deep RL policies are usually sensitive to these changes and fail to act robustly against them. This resembles the problem of domain generalization in supervised learning. In this work, we study this problem for goal-conditioned RL agents. We propose a theoretical framework in the Block MDP setting that characterizes the generalizability of goal-conditioned policies to new environments. Under this framework, we develop a practical method PA-SkewFit that enhances domain generalization. The empirical evaluation shows that our goal-conditioned RL agent can perform well in various unseen test environments, improving by 50\% over baselines.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning agent may encounter an unfamiliar visual background after deployment even though its underlying task has not changed. Policies can react poorly to these irrelevant differences. This paper studies that problem for goal-conditioned agents, whose behavior depends on the goal they are asked to achieve.

The authors develop a theoretical framework within the Block Markov decision process setting to characterize generalization to new environments. This gives the study an explicit modeling setting for reasoning about environmental variation. Building on the framework, they propose PA-SkewFit, a practical method intended to improve domain generalization for goal-conditioned reinforcement learning.

In the reported evaluation, the agent performs well across several unseen test environments and improves by 50% over baselines. That result supports the method's usefulness for the environmental changes tested. The broader contribution is to connect a theoretical treatment of goal-conditioned generalization with a working algorithm, addressing situations where superficial changes in observations can otherwise disrupt an agent's behavior.
summary.tldr: PA-SkewFit builds on a Block MDP framework to improve goal-conditioned agents' performance in unseen environments.

title: Learning Domain Invariant Representations in Goal-conditioned Block MDPs

abstract: We consider the problem of finding a saddle point for the convex-concave objective $\min_x \max_y f(x) + \langle Ax, y\rangle - g^*(y)$, where $f$ is a convex function with locally Lipschitz gradient and $g$ is convex and possibly non-smooth. We propose an adaptive version of the Condat-Vũ algorithm, which alternates between primal gradient steps and dual proximal steps. The method achieves stepsize adaptivity through a simple rule involving $\|A\|$ and the norm of recently computed gradients of $f$. Under standard assumptions, we prove an $\mathcal{O}(k^{-1})$ ergodic convergence rate. Furthermore, when $f$ is also locally strongly convex and $A$ has full row rank we show that our method converges with a linear rate. Numerical experiments are provided for illustrating the practical performance of the algorithm.

The method achieves stepsize adaptivity through a simple rule involving $\|A\|$ and the norm of recently computed gradients of $f$. paragraphs: This paper studies a convex optimization problem expressed as a saddle point: one set of variables is minimized while another is maximized. Its structure combines a smooth convex function, a linear interaction between the variables, and a convex term that may be nonsmooth. The central question is how to adapt optimization steps to the smoothness encountered during the calculation.

The authors modify the Condat–Vũ algorithm, which alternates gradient updates for the primal variables with proximal updates for the dual variables. Their step-size rule uses the norm of the linear operator and recently computed gradients. This makes the update sizes responsive to local information, fitting a setting where the smooth function's gradient is locally Lipschitz.

Under standard assumptions, they prove an O(1/k) convergence rate for averaged iterates after k iterations. A stronger, linear rate holds when the smooth function is also locally strongly convex and the linear operator has full row rank. Numerical experiments illustrate practical performance. The faster guarantee therefore depends on additional structure, rather than following from adaptivity alone.
summary.tldr: An adaptive primal-dual algorithm uses recent gradients to choose step sizes, with stronger convergence guarantees under additional structural assumptions.

title: A first-order primal-dual method with adaptivity to local smoothness

abstract: Reward is the driving force for reinforcement-learning agents. This paper is dedicated to understanding the expressivity of reward as a way to capture tasks that we would want an agent to perform. We frame this study around three new abstract notions of “task” that might be desirable: (1) a set of acceptable behaviors, (2) a partial ordering over behaviors, or (3) a partial ordering over trajectories. Our main results prove that while reward can express many of these tasks, there exist instances of each task type that no Markov reward function can capture. We then provide a set of polynomial-time algorithms that construct a Markov reward function that allows an agent to optimize tasks of each of these three types, and correctly determine when no such reward function exists. We conclude with an empirical study that corroborates and illustrates our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning uses rewards to specify what an agent should accomplish, but that raises a basic question: which tasks can a reward function actually express? This paper investigates the representational power of Markov rewards by defining three kinds of task specifications and asking whether each can be captured by such a reward.

The task types are a set of acceptable behaviors, a partial ordering over behaviors, and a partial ordering over trajectories. These distinguish simply accepting certain outcomes from expressing preferences among possible behaviors or paths. The authors prove that Markov rewards can represent many such tasks, but that each category also contains instances that no Markov reward function can express.

The paper complements these impossibility results with polynomial-time algorithms. For each task type, the algorithms construct a suitable Markov reward when one exists and correctly recognize when none does. An empirical study illustrates and corroborates the theory. The practical conceptual consequence is that difficulty encoding a task can reflect a genuine representational constraint, and the proposed procedures can distinguish that situation from one where an appropriate reward is available.
summary.tldr: Some task specifications cannot be expressed by Markov rewards, and the paper gives efficient algorithms to construct suitable rewards or detect impossibility.

title: On the Expressivity of Markov Reward

abstract: Deep neural networks have achieved impressive performance in many areas. Designing a fast and provable method for training neural networks is a fundamental question in machine learning. The classical training method requires paying $\Omega(mnd)$ cost for both forward computation and backward computation, where $m$ is the width of the neural network, and we are given $n$ training points in $d$-dimensional space. In this paper, we propose two novel preprocessing ideas to bypass this $\Omega(mnd)$ barrier:* First, by preprocessing the initial weights of the neural networks, we can train the neural network in $\widetilde{O}(m^{1-\Theta(1/d)} n d)$ cost per iteration.* Second, by preprocessing the input data points, we can train neural network in $\widetilde{O} (m^{4/5} nd )$ cost per iteration.From the technical perspective, our result is a sophisticated combination of tools in different fields, greedy-type convergence analysis in optimization, sparsity observation in practical work, high-dimensional geometric search in data structure, concentration and anti-concentration in probability. Our results also provide theoretical insights for a large number of previously established fast training methods.In addition, our classical algorithm can be generalized to the Quantum computation model. Interestingly, we can get a similar sublinear cost per iteration but avoid preprocessing initial weights or input data points.

paragraphs: The paper investigates whether preprocessing can reduce the computational cost of training over-parameterized neural networks. In the classical calculation considered, forward and backward computation each cost at least on the order of mnd, where m is network width, n is the number of training examples, and d is their dimension.

Two preprocessing strategies yield improved per-iteration bounds. Preprocessing the initial weights gives a cost of approximately m raised to 1 minus Theta(1/d), multiplied by nd. Preprocessing the input examples instead gives approximately m raised to 4/5, multiplied by nd. Both expressions suppress logarithmic factors. The improvement concerns dependence on width per iteration, with preprocessing as a separate part of the approach.

The analysis combines optimization arguments, sparsity, geometric search data structures, and probabilistic tools. It also offers theoretical insight into previously developed fast training methods. Finally, the authors extend the algorithmic ideas to quantum computation, obtaining similar sublinear dependence on width per iteration without preprocessing either the initial weights or the inputs.
summary.tldr: Preprocessing weights or inputs yields provably lower per-iteration training costs with sublinear dependence on network width.

title: Does Preprocessing Help Training Over-parameterized Neural Networks?

abstract: The growing literature on "benign overfitting" in overparameterized models has been mostly restricted to regression or binary classification settings; however, most success stories of modern machine learning have been recorded in multiclass settings. Motivated by this discrepancy, we study benign overfitting in multiclass linear classification. Specifically, we consider the following popular training algorithms on separable data: (i) empirical risk minimization (ERM) with cross-entropy loss, which converges to the multiclass support vector machine (SVM) solution; (ii) ERM with least-squares loss, which converges to the min-norm interpolating (MNI) solution; and, (iii) the one-vs-all SVM classifier. Our first key finding is that under a simple sufficient condition, all three algorithms lead to classifiers that interpolate the training data and have equal accuracy. When the data is generated from Gaussian mixtures or a multinomial logistic model, this condition holds under high enough effective overparameterization. Second, we derive novel error bounds on the accuracy of the MNI classifier, thereby showing that all three training algorithms lead to benign overfitting under sufficient overparameterization. Ultimately, our analysis shows that good generalization is possible for SVM solutions beyond the realm in which typical margin-based bounds apply.

paragraphs: Benign overfitting describes situations where a model fits its training data exactly yet still generalizes well. This paper studies that possibility in multiclass linear classification, extending attention beyond regression and binary classification. It considers separable data and compares three common ways of training classifiers.

The methods are cross-entropy training, which converges to a multiclass support vector machine solution; least-squares training, which converges to a minimum-norm interpolating solution; and one-vs-all support vector machines. Under a sufficient condition, all three produce classifiers that interpolate the training data and have equal accuracy. For Gaussian-mixture and multinomial-logistic data models, sufficiently high effective overparameterization makes that condition hold.

The authors then derive accuracy bounds for the minimum-norm interpolating classifier. Combined with the equivalence result, these bounds establish benign overfitting for all three methods under sufficient overparameterization. The findings show that support vector machine solutions can generalize well in regimes beyond those explained by typical margin-based bounds. They do not assert that interpolation guarantees good generalization for arbitrary data.
summary.tldr: Under sufficient overparameterization and stated data conditions, three multiclass linear classifiers interpolate training data while generalizing well.

title: Benign Overfitting in Multiclass Classification: All Roads Lead to Interpolation

abstract: We address the estimation of conditional average treatment effects (CATEs) for structured treatments (e.g., graphs, images, texts). Given a weak condition on the effect, we propose the generalized Robinson decomposition, which (i) isolates the causal estimand (reducing regularization bias), (ii) allows one to plug in arbitrary models for learning, and (iii) possesses a quasi-oracle convergence guarantee under mild assumptions. In experiments with small-world and molecular graphs we demonstrate that our approach outperforms prior work in CATE estimation.
originalAbstract: We address the estimation of conditional average treatment effects (CATEs) for structured treatments (e.g., graphs, images, texts). Given a weak condition on the effect, we propose the generalized Robinson decomposition, which (i) isolates the causal estimand (reducing regularization bias), (ii) allows one to plug in arbitrary models for learning, and (iii) possesses a quasi-oracle convergence guarantee under mild assumptions. In experiments with small-world and molecular graphs we demonstrate that our approach outperforms prior work in CATE estimation.

paragraphs: The paper studies causal effects when a treatment has internal structure, such as a graph, image, or piece of text. Its target is the conditional average treatment effect: how an average causal effect varies with the conditions being considered. This extends the estimation problem beyond treatments represented by a simple category or numerical dose.

Under a weak condition on the effect, the authors propose a generalized Robinson decomposition. The decomposition separates the causal quantity of interest from other parts of the learning problem, reducing bias introduced by regularization. It also allows arbitrary learning models to be plugged into the framework, making the estimation strategy compatible with different ways of representing structured inputs.

Under mild assumptions, the method has a quasi-oracle convergence guarantee, providing theoretical support for its estimation behavior. Experiments involving small-world graphs and molecular graphs show better treatment-effect estimation than prior work. The contribution combines flexibility in the models used for learning with an explicit focus on protecting the causal target from regularization bias.
summary.tldr: A generalized Robinson decomposition enables flexible causal-effect estimation for structured treatments while reducing regularization bias.

title: Causal Effect Inference for Structured Treatments

abstract: We introduce implicit Deep Adaptive Design (iDAD), a new method for performing adaptive experiments in real-time with implicit models. iDAD amortizes the cost of Bayesian optimal experimental design (BOED) by learning a design policy network upfront, which can then be deployed quickly at the time of the experiment. The iDAD network can be trained on any model which simulates differentiable samples, unlike previous design policy work that requires a closed form likelihood and conditionally independent experiments. At deployment, iDAD allows design decisions to be made in milliseconds, in contrast to traditional BOED approaches that require heavy computation during the experiment itself. We illustrate the applicability of iDAD on a number of experiments, and show that it provides a fast and effective mechanism for performing adaptive design with implicit models.

The iDAD network can be trained on any model which simulates differentiable samples, unlike previous design policy work that requires a closed form likelihood and conditionally independent experiments. At deployment, iDAD allows design decisions to be made in milliseconds, in contrast to traditional BOED approaches that require heavy computation during the experiment itself. We illustrate the applicability of iDAD on a number of experiments, and show that it provides a fast and effective mechanism for performing adaptive design with implicit models.

paragraphs: Adaptive experimental design chooses later experimental settings in response to earlier observations. Bayesian optimal experimental design can support these decisions, but traditional methods require substantial computation while the experiment is running. Implicit Deep Adaptive Design, or iDAD, shifts that computational work into an upfront training phase.

The method learns a neural network that acts as a design policy and can make decisions quickly during deployment. Its training requirement is a model capable of generating differentiable simulated samples. Unlike earlier design-policy work described in the abstract, it does not require a closed-form likelihood or conditionally independent experiments. This makes the approach applicable to implicit models whose behavior can be simulated.

At experiment time, the trained policy makes design decisions in milliseconds. The authors illustrate the method across several experiments and report that it provides a fast and effective way to perform adaptive design with implicit models. The central benefit is amortization: investing computation in learning a reusable policy reduces the computation needed for each decision during an experiment.
summary.tldr: iDAD learns experimental design policies from differentiable simulators upfront, enabling millisecond adaptive decisions without closed-form likelihoods.

title: Implicit Deep Adaptive Design: Policy-Based Experimental Design without Likelihoods

abstract: Early methods in the rapidly developing field of neural architecture search (NAS) required fully training thousands of neural networks. To reduce this extreme computational cost, dozens of techniques have since been proposed to predict the final performance of neural architectures. Despite the success of such performance prediction methods, it is not well-understood how different families of techniques compare to one another, due to the lack of an agreed-upon evaluation metric and optimization for different constraints on the initialization time and query time. In this work, we give the first large-scale study of performance predictors by analyzing 31 techniques ranging from learning curve extrapolation, to weight-sharing, to supervised learning, to zero-cost proxies. We test a number of correlation- and rank-based performance measures in a variety of settings, as well as the ability of each technique to speed up predictor-based NAS frameworks. Our results act as recommendations for the best predictors to use in different settings, and we show that certain families of predictors can be combined to achieve even better predictive power, opening up promising research directions. We release our code, featuring a library of 31 performance predictors.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search can be expensive when assessing candidates requires fully training many networks. Performance predictors reduce that burden by estimating how well architectures will ultimately perform. This paper addresses the difficulty of comparing those predictors when evaluation measures differ and methods are designed for different initialization and query-time budgets.

The study analyzes 31 techniques spanning learning-curve extrapolation, weight sharing, supervised prediction, and zero-cost proxies. It evaluates correlation-based and ranking-based measures across multiple settings. It also examines whether predictors actually speed up search frameworks that use them, connecting predictive quality to their intended role in architecture selection.

The findings provide recommendations that depend on the operating setting rather than identifying a single universally preferred predictor. They also show that combining certain predictor families can improve predictive power. A released library collects the 31 methods. The contribution is a broad comparative foundation for choosing and combining predictors while considering both prediction behavior and the computational constraints of the search process.
summary.tldr: A study of 31 architecture-performance predictors identifies useful choices for different settings and benefits from combining certain families.

title: How Powerful are Performance Predictors in Neural Architecture Search?

abstract: Pretrained language models (PLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance in various natural language processing tasks: Unidirectional PLMs (e.g., GPT) are well known for their superior text generation capabilities; bidirectional PLMs (e.g., BERT) have been the prominent choice for natural language understanding (NLU) tasks. While both types of models have achieved promising few-shot learning performance, their potential for zero-shot learning has been underexplored. In this paper, we present a simple approach that uses both types of PLMs for fully zero-shot learning of NLU tasks without requiring any task-specific data: A unidirectional PLM generates class-conditioned texts guided by prompts, which are used as the training data for fine-tuning a bidirectional PLM. With quality training data selected based on the generation probability and regularization techniques (label smoothing and temporal ensembling) applied to the fine-tuning stage for better generalization and stability, our approach demonstrates strong performance across seven classification tasks of the GLUE benchmark (e.g., 72.3/73.8 on MNLI-m/mm and 92.8 on SST-2), significantly outperforming zero-shot prompting methods and achieving even comparable results to strong few-shot approaches using 32 training samples per class.

paragraphs: This paper combines two kinds of pretrained language models to learn language-understanding tasks without task-specific data. A text-generating model creates examples, and a bidirectional model learns to classify them. The setup uses generation as a source of training material for a separate understanding model.

Prompts guide the generator to produce text associated with particular classes. The method selects training examples using their generation probabilities, then fine-tunes the bidirectional model on the selected synthetic data. Label smoothing and temporal ensembling are applied during fine-tuning to improve generalization and stability. These steps make data selection and the learning procedure both part of the approach.

Across seven GLUE classification tasks, the method substantially outperforms the zero-shot prompting methods evaluated. It also produces results comparable to strong few-shot approaches given 32 training examples per class. The result shows that, in these evaluations, zero-shot task learning can benefit from an intermediate synthetic dataset and model fine-tuning. Zero-shot here refers to the absence of task-specific data, even though the second model undergoes training.
summary.tldr: Prompt-generated training examples let a bidirectional language model achieve strong zero-shot classification results without task-specific data.

title: Generating Training Data with Language Models: Towards Zero-Shot Language Understanding

abstract: We present VAEL, a neuro-symbolic generative model integrating variational autoencoders (VAE) with the reasoning capabilities of probabilistic logic (L) programming. Besides standard latent subsymbolic variables, our model exploits a probabilistic logic program to define a further structured representation, which is used for logical reasoning. The entire process is end-to-end differentiable. Once trained, VAEL can solve new unseen generation tasks by (i) leveraging the previously acquired knowledge encoded in the neural component and (ii) exploiting new logical programs on the structured latent space. Our experiments provide support on the benefits of this neuro-symbolic integration both in terms of task generalization and data efficiency. To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first to propose a general-purpose end-to-end framework integrating probabilistic logic programming into a deep generative model.

Besides standard latent subsymbolic variables, our model exploits a probabilistic logic program to define a further structured representation, which is used for logical reasoning. paragraphs: VAEL combines a variational autoencoder with probabilistic logic programming to create a neuro-symbolic generative model. Alongside ordinary latent variables, it includes a structured representation defined through a probabilistic logic program. That additional representation supports logical reasoning within the generative process, connecting learned neural information with explicitly structured knowledge.

The entire process is differentiable from end to end. After training, the model can address previously unseen generation tasks by reusing knowledge acquired in its neural component and applying new logical programs to the structured latent space. The design gives the learned representation and the logical program complementary roles in determining what the model generates.

Experiments provide support for benefits in both task generalization and data efficiency. The central result is evidence that this integration can help a generative model use acquired knowledge under new logical specifications. The authors describe the framework, to their knowledge, as the first general-purpose end-to-end integration of probabilistic logic programming into a deep generative model. Its contribution includes both that integrated architecture and the demonstrated benefits of combining its components.
summary.tldr: VAEL combines variational autoencoders with probabilistic logic so learned neural knowledge can support new generation tasks specified through logical programs.

title: VAEL: Bridging Variational Autoencoders and Probabilistic Logic Programming

abstract: Despite the empirical successes of self-supervised learning (SSL) methods, it is unclear what characteristics of their representations lead to high downstream accuracies. In this work, we characterize properties that SSL representations should ideally satisfy. Specifically, we prove necessary and sufficient conditions such that for any task invariant to given data augmentations, probes (e.g., linear or MLP) trained on that representation attain perfect accuracy. These requirements lead to a unifying conceptual framework for improving existing SSL methods and deriving new ones. For contrastive learning, our framework prescribes simple but significant improvements to previous methods such as using asymmetric projection heads. For non-contrastive learning, we use our framework to derive a simple and novel objective. Our resulting SSL algorithms outperform baselines on standard benchmarks, including SwAV+multicrops on linear probing of ImageNet.
originalAbstract: Despite the empirical successes of self-supervised learning (SSL) methods, it is unclear what characteristics of their representations lead to high downstream accuracies. In this work, we characterize properties that SSL representations should ideally satisfy. Specifically, we prove necessary and sufficient conditions such that for any task invariant to given data augmentations, probes (e.g., linear or MLP) trained on that representation attain perfect accuracy. These requirements lead to a unifying conceptual framework for improving existing SSL methods and deriving new ones. For contrastive learning, our framework prescribes simple but significant improvements to previous methods such as using asymmetric projection heads. For non-contrastive learning, we use our framework to derive a simple and novel objective. Our resulting SSL algorithms outperform baselines on standard benchmarks, including SwAV+multicrops on linear probing of ImageNet.

paragraphs: Self-supervised learning can produce useful representations, but empirical success alone does not explain which representation properties make later prediction tasks easy. This paper approaches that question through an idealized target: representations on which a trained prediction head, such as a linear model or multilayer perceptron, can achieve perfect accuracy.

The authors prove necessary and sufficient conditions for this target across tasks that remain unchanged under specified data augmentations. That restriction is central to the result: the characterization concerns tasks invariant to the chosen transformations. The conditions provide a common framework for understanding and improving both contrastive and non-contrastive approaches to self-supervised learning.

For contrastive methods, the framework motivates changes including asymmetric projection heads. For non-contrastive methods, it leads to a new, simple training objective. The resulting algorithms outperform baselines on standard benchmarks, including SwAV with multiple crops in ImageNet linear probing. The paper thus connects a conditional mathematical characterization of ideal representations to practical changes with measured downstream benefits.
summary.tldr: A characterization of ideal representations yields improvements to contrastive and non-contrastive self-supervised learning with benchmark gains.

title: Improving Self-Supervised Learning by Characterizing Idealized Representations

abstract: Bilevel optimization has been shown to be a powerful framework for formulating multi-task machine learning problems, e.g., reinforcement learning (RL) and meta-learning, where the decision variables are coupled in both levels of the minimization problems. In practice, the learning tasks would be located at different computing resource environments, and thus there is a need for deploying a decentralized training framework to implement multi-agent and multi-task learning. We develop a stochastic linearized augmented Lagrangian method (SLAM) for solving general nonconvex bilevel optimization problems over a graph, where both upper and lower optimization variables are able to achieve a consensus. We also establish that the theoretical convergence rate of the proposed SLAM to the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) points of this class of problems is on the same order as the one achieved by the classical distributed stochastic gradient descent for only single-level nonconvex minimization problems. Numerical results tested on multi-agent RL problems showcase the superiority of SLAM compared with the benchmarks.
originalAbstract: Bilevel optimization has been shown to be a powerful framework for formulating multi-task machine learning problems, e.g., reinforcement learning (RL) and meta-learning, where the decision variables are coupled in both levels of the minimization problems. In practice, the learning tasks would be located at different computing resource environments, and thus there is a need for deploying a decentralized training framework to implement multi-agent and multi-task learning. We develop a stochastic linearized augmented Lagrangian method (SLAM) for solving general nonconvex bilevel optimization problems over a graph, where both upper and lower optimization variables are able to achieve a consensus. We also establish that the theoretical convergence rate of the proposed SLAM to the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) points of this class of problems is on the same order as the one achieved by the classical distributed stochastic gradient descent for only single-level nonconvex minimization problems. Numerical results tested on multi-agent RL problems showcase the superiority of SLAM compared with the benchmarks.

paragraphs: Bilevel optimization describes learning problems with two linked minimization tasks: decisions at one level depend on decisions at the other. This structure appears in reinforcement learning and meta-learning. When tasks run on different computing resources, solving the coupled problem also requires coordinating the participating agents.

The paper introduces SLAM, a stochastic linearized augmented Lagrangian method for nonconvex bilevel optimization over a communication graph. Its coordination mechanism allows agents to reach agreement on variables at both optimization levels. This matters because agreement on only one set of variables would leave part of the coupled learning problem unresolved.

The theoretical result concerns convergence to Karush-Kuhn-Tucker points, which satisfy constrained optimization conditions rather than necessarily being global minima. SLAM achieves a convergence rate of the same order as classical distributed stochastic gradient descent for single-level nonconvex problems. Numerical experiments on multi-agent reinforcement learning also show advantages over the tested benchmarks. Together, these results support decentralized bilevel learning without a worse convergence-rate order than the stated single-level comparison.
summary.tldr: SLAM coordinates decentralized bilevel learning and achieves convergence to KKT points at the same rate order as distributed single-level stochastic gradient descent.

title: A Stochastic Linearized Augmented Lagrangian Method for Decentralized Bilevel Optimization

abstract: While there has been progress in developing non-vacuous generalization bounds for deep neural networks, these bounds tend to be uninformative about why deep learning works. In this paper, we develop a compression approach based on quantizing neural network parameters in a linear subspace, profoundly improving on previous results to provide state-of-the-art generalization bounds on a variety of tasks, including transfer learning. We use these tight bounds to better understand the role of model size, equivariance, and the implicit biases of optimization, for generalization in deep learning. Notably, we find large models can be compressed to a much greater extent than previously known, encapsulating Occam’s razor.
originalAbstract: While there has been progress in developing non-vacuous generalization bounds for deep neural networks, these bounds tend to be uninformative about why deep learning works. In this paper, we develop a compression approach based on quantizing neural network parameters in a linear subspace, profoundly improving on previous results to provide state-of-the-art generalization bounds on a variety of tasks, including transfer learning. We use these tight bounds to better understand the role of model size, equivariance, and the implicit biases of optimization, for generalization in deep learning. Notably, we find large models can be compressed to a much greater extent than previously known, encapsulating Occam’s razor.

paragraphs: Generalization bounds aim to explain how well a trained model will perform beyond its training data. A bound can be non-vacuous yet still reveal little about why deep learning works. This paper seeks tighter bounds that can also help investigate the properties associated with successful generalization.

The proposed compression method quantizes neural network parameters within a linear subspace. Quantization represents parameters at a restricted level of precision, while the subspace supplies a constrained representation in which to encode them. The authors use this compression approach to obtain substantially improved, state-of-the-art generalization bounds across a variety of tasks, including transfer learning.

They then use the tight bounds to study model size, equivariance, and the implicit preferences of optimization procedures. A notable finding is that large models can be compressed much more than previously recognized. This connects their analysis to Occam's razor: a network's large parameter count can coexist with a much shorter compressed description. The contribution is both stronger bounds and a way to use them to examine generalization.
summary.tldr: Compressing neural network parameters through subspace quantization yields tighter generalization bounds and reveals substantial compressibility in large models.

title: PAC-Bayes Compression Bounds So Tight That They Can Explain Generalization

abstract: As part of the effort to understand implicit bias of gradient descent in overparametrized models, several results have shown how the training trajectory on the overparametrized model can be understood as mirror descent on a different objective. The main result here is a complete characterization of this phenomenon under a notion termed commuting parametrization, which encompasses all the previous results in this setting. It is shown that gradient flow with any commuting parametrization is equivalent to continuous mirror descent with a related mirror map. Conversely, continuous mirror descent with any mirror map can be viewed as gradient flow with a related commuting parametrization. The latter result relies upon Nash's embedding theorem.
originalAbstract: As part of the effort to understand implicit bias of gradient descent in overparametrized models, several results have shown how the training trajectory on the overparametrized model can be understood as mirror descent on a different objective. The main result here is a complete characterization of this phenomenon under a notion termed commuting parametrization, which encompasses all the previous results in this setting. It is shown that gradient flow with any commuting parametrization is equivalent to continuous mirror descent with a related mirror map. Conversely, continuous mirror descent with any mirror map can be viewed as gradient flow with a related commuting parametrization. The latter result relies upon Nash's embedding theorem.

paragraphs: A model's parameterization can affect the path followed during training, even when the underlying prediction problem is unchanged. This paper studies that effect through the connection between gradient-based training and mirror descent. Earlier results had shown that some overparameterized models follow trajectories that can be understood using a different optimization geometry.

The authors give a complete characterization under a condition they call commuting parameterization, which includes the earlier results in this setting. They prove that gradient flow under any such parameterization is equivalent to continuous mirror descent with a corresponding mirror map. This relates the choice of model coordinates to the geometry governing the optimization trajectory.

The correspondence also runs in reverse: continuous mirror descent with any mirror map can be represented as gradient flow under a related commuting parameterization. That direction uses Nash's embedding theorem. Together, the results provide a unified theoretical account of these connections. The equivalence concerns continuous-time dynamics and the stated parameterization framework, which define the scope of the characterization.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes a two-way equivalence between gradient flow with commuting parameterizations and continuous mirror descent.

title: Implicit Bias of Gradient Descent on Reparametrized Models: On Equivalence to Mirror Descent

abstract: This paper considers online convex optimization with hard constraints and analyzes achievable regret and cumulative hard constraint violation (violation for short). The problem distinguishes itself from online convex optimization with soft constraints, where a violation at one round can be compensated/cancelled by a conservative decision at a different round. We propose a RECtified Online Optimization algorithm (RECOO) and consider two settings: fixed constraints and adversarial constraints. Both settings have been considered in the literature. Compared with existing results, {\em RECOO achieves the best of two worlds and beyond.} For the fixed-constraints setting, RECOO achieves $O\left(\sqrt{T}\right)$ regret and $O(1)$ violation, where $T$ is the learning horizon. The best known results in this case are $O(\sqrt{T})$ regret and $O\left(T^{1/4}\right)$ violation. For the adversarial-constraints setting, it guarantees $O(\sqrt{T})$ regret and $O(T^{3/4})$ violation, which match the best existing results. When the loss functions are strongly convex, RECOO can guarantee $O(\log T)$ regret and $O(1)$ violation for fixed constraints, and $O(\log T)$ regret and $O(\sqrt{T\log T})$ violation for adversarial constraints. Both these results are order-wise better than the existing bounds. The regret and violation bounds mentioned above use the best fixed decision in hindsight as the baseline. This paper further considers a dynamic baseline where the comparator sequence is time-varying. This paper shows that RECOO not only improves the existing results in the fixed-constraints setting but also {\em for the first time,} guarantees dynamic regret and violation bounds in the adversarial-constraints setting. Our experiment results confirm that RECOO outperforms several existing algorithms for both fixed and adversarial constraints.

paragraphs: This paper studies online decisions with hard constraints, where violating a constraint now cannot be canceled by being conservative later. It tracks both regret, relative to a comparator's losses, and cumulative violation. The proposed RECOO algorithm handles constraints that stay fixed and constraints chosen adversarially over time.

With fixed constraints, RECOO guarantees regret growing as the square root of the learning horizon and bounded cumulative violation. This improves the previous violation bound while preserving the regret order. With adversarial constraints, it matches the best stated existing orders: square-root regret and violation growing as the horizon to the three-quarter power.

Stronger assumptions yield stronger results. For strongly convex losses, regret becomes logarithmic, with bounded violation for fixed constraints and a square-root-of-horizon-times-logarithm violation bound for adversarial constraints. These guarantees compare against the best fixed decision in hindsight. The paper also analyzes changing comparators, improving fixed-constraint results and providing its claimed first dynamic guarantees for adversarial constraints. Experiments report advantages over several existing algorithms in both constraint settings.
summary.tldr: RECOO improves or matches regret and cumulative hard-constraint violation bounds across fixed and adversarial constraint settings.

title: Online Convex Optimization with Hard Constraints: Towards the Best of Two Worlds and Beyond

abstract: Intelligence relies on an agent's knowledge of what it does not know.This capability can be assessed based on the quality of joint predictions of labels across multiple inputs.In principle, ensemble-based approaches can produce effective joint predictions, but the computational costs of large ensembles become prohibitive.We introduce the epinet: an architecture that can supplement any conventional neural network, including large pretrained models, and can be trained with modest incremental computation to estimate uncertainty.With an epinet, conventional neural networks outperform very large ensembles, consisting of hundreds or more particles, with orders of magnitude less computation.The epinet does not fit the traditional framework of Bayesian neural networks.To accommodate development of approaches beyond BNNs, such as the epinet, we introduce the epistemic neural network (ENN) as a general interface for models that produce joint predictions.
originalAbstract: Intelligence relies on an agent's knowledge of what it does not know.This capability can be assessed based on the quality of joint predictions of labels across multiple inputs.In principle, ensemble-based approaches can produce effective joint predictions, but the computational costs of large ensembles become prohibitive.We introduce the epinet: an architecture that can supplement any conventional neural network, including large pretrained models, and can be trained with modest incremental computation to estimate uncertainty.With an epinet, conventional neural networks outperform very large ensembles, consisting of hundreds or more particles, with orders of magnitude less computation.The epinet does not fit the traditional framework of Bayesian neural networks.To accommodate development of approaches beyond BNNs, such as the epinet, we introduce the epistemic neural network (ENN) as a general interface for models that produce joint predictions.

paragraphs: A useful uncertainty estimate should express how a model's uncertainty relates across multiple inputs. This paper evaluates that capability through joint predictions of labels, rather than considering each prediction in isolation. Large ensembles can provide such predictions, but running and training many constituent models can make the computational cost prohibitive.

The authors introduce the epinet, an architecture that can be added to a conventional neural network, including a large pretrained model. It is trained with modest additional computation to estimate uncertainty. In the reported comparisons, networks equipped with an epinet outperform very large ensembles containing hundreds or more particles while using orders of magnitude less computation.

The paper also introduces epistemic neural networks, or ENNs, as a general interface for models producing joint predictions. This broader interface accommodates the epinet, which does not fit the traditional Bayesian neural-network framework. The contribution therefore combines a concrete architecture for computationally efficient uncertainty estimation with a way to describe and develop a wider family of joint-prediction models.
summary.tldr: An epinet adds efficient joint uncertainty predictions to conventional networks, outperforming much larger ensembles in the reported comparisons.

title: Epistemic Neural Networks

abstract: When solving decision-making tasks, humans typically depend on information from two key sources: (1) Historical policy data, which provides interaction replay from the environment, and (2) Analytical insights in natural language form, exposing the invaluable thought process or strategic considerations. Despite this, the majority of preceding research focuses on only one source: they either use historical replay exclusively to directly learn policy or value functions, or engaged in language model training utilizing mere language corpus. In this paper, we argue that a powerful autonomous agent should cover both sources. Thus, we propose ChessGPT, a GPT model bridging policy learning and language modeling by integrating data from these two sources in Chess games. Specifically, we build a large-scale game and language dataset related to chess. Leveraging the dataset, we showcase two model examples ChessCLIP and ChessGPT, integrating policy learning and language modeling. Finally, we propose a full evaluation framework for evaluating language model's chess ability. Experimental results validate our model and dataset's effectiveness. We open source our code, model, and dataset at https://github.com/waterhorse1/ChessGPT.

paragraphs: Learning to make decisions can draw on records of what happened and explanations of why particular actions made sense. In chess, these correspond to game histories and natural-language analysis. This paper argues that autonomous agents should use both, bringing together policy learning from interactions and language modeling from written strategic information.

The authors build a large chess dataset containing both game data and language. They use it to present ChessCLIP and ChessGPT as two model examples that integrate the two sources. The contribution therefore includes a shared data resource as well as models: it creates a setting in which action sequences and linguistic analysis can jointly inform learned chess capabilities.

The paper also proposes a comprehensive framework for evaluating a language model's chess ability. Reported experiments support the effectiveness of the models and dataset. The broader significance is a concrete approach to studying how learning from decisions and learning from explanations can be combined, with chess supplying both a decision-making environment and a source of strategic language.
summary.tldr: ChessGPT combines chess game histories and natural-language analysis through a shared dataset, model examples, and an evaluation framework.

title: ChessGPT: Bridging Policy Learning and Language Modeling

abstract: Nonlinear independent component analysis (ICA) aims to uncover the true latent sources from their observable nonlinear mixtures. Despite its significance, the identifiability of nonlinear ICA is known to be impossible without additional assumptions. Recent advances have proposed conditions on the connective structure from sources to observed variables, known as Structural Sparsity, to achieve identifiability in an unsupervised manner. However, the sparsity constraint may not hold universally for all sources in practice. Furthermore, the assumptions of bijectivity of the mixing process and independence among all sources, which arise from the setting of ICA, may also be violated in many real-world scenarios. To address these limitations and generalize nonlinear ICA, we propose a set of new identifiability results in the general settings of undercompleteness, partial sparsity and source dependence, and flexible grouping structures. Specifically, we prove identifiability when there are more observed variables than sources (undercomplete), and when certain sparsity and/or source independence assumptions are not met for some changing sources. Moreover, we show that even in cases with flexible grouping structures (e.g., part of the sources can be divided into irreducible independent groups with various sizes), appropriate identifiability results can also be established. Theoretical claims are supported empirically on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Nonlinear independent component analysis seeks hidden sources from observations formed by mixing those sources nonlinearly. The central theoretical question is identifiability: whether the observations can determine the underlying sources. Without additional assumptions, this is impossible. Earlier work uses sparse connections between sources and observations, but practical settings may violate sparsity, source independence, or assumptions about the mixing process.

This paper develops identifiability results for broader settings. These include having more observed variables than sources, called undercompleteness, and allowing some sources to depart from sparsity or independence assumptions. It also examines flexible grouping structures, including cases where some sources form independent groups of different sizes that cannot be divided into smaller independent groups.

The contribution is a set of guarantees adapted to these structures, rather than an assumption-free solution to nonlinear source recovery. The authors support their theoretical claims with synthetic and real-world experiments. The findings expand the circumstances in which meaningful recovery guarantees can be established when the full collection of classical ICA assumptions does not hold.
summary.tldr: New identifiability results extend nonlinear source recovery to undercomplete settings, partial sparsity, some source dependence, and flexible independent groups.

title: Generalizing Nonlinear ICA Beyond Structural Sparsity

abstract: Data-driven machine learning approaches are being increasingly used to solve partial differential equations (PDEs). They have shown particularly striking successes when training an operator, which takes as input a PDE in some family, and outputs its solution. However, the architectural design space, especially given structural knowledge of the PDE family of interest, is still poorly understood. We seek to remedy this gap by studying the benefits of weight-tied neural network architectures for steady-state PDEs. To achieve this, we first demonstrate that the solution of most steady-state PDEs can be expressed as a fixed point of a non-linear operator. Motivated by this observation, we propose FNO-DEQ, a deep equilibrium variant of the FNO architecture that directly solves for the solution of a steady-state PDE as the infinite-depth fixed point of an implicit operator layer using a black-box root solver and differentiates analytically through this fixed point resulting in $\mathcal{O}(1)$ training memory. Our experiments indicate that FNO-DEQ-based architectures outperform FNO-based baselines with $4\times$ the number of parameters in predicting the solution to steady-state PDEs such as Darcy Flow and steady-state incompressible Navier-Stokes. Finally, we show FNO-DEQ is more robust when trained with datasets with more noisy observations than the FNO-based baselines, demonstrating the benefits of using appropriate inductive biases in architectural design for different neural network based PDE solvers. Further, we show a universal approximation result that demonstrates that FNO-DEQ can approximate the solution to any steady-state PDE that can be written as a fixed point equation.

paragraphs: Neural operators learn to map a partial differential equation from a family of equations to its solution. This paper asks how their architecture can reflect the structure of steady-state problems. Its starting observation is that solutions of most steady-state PDEs can be expressed as fixed points: states left unchanged by a suitable nonlinear operator.

FNO-DEQ builds this idea into a deep equilibrium version of the Fourier neural operator. Instead of explicitly applying a finite stack of layers, it uses a black-box root solver to find the fixed point of an implicit operator layer. Analytic differentiation through that fixed point gives constant training memory with respect to the implicit depth.

Experiments on Darcy flow and steady-state incompressible Navier–Stokes show better predictions than FNO baselines with four times as many parameters. FNO-DEQ also performs more robustly when training observations are noisier. Separately, a universal approximation result establishes that it can approximate solutions of steady-state PDEs expressible as fixed-point equations. That representational guarantee is conditional on the fixed-point formulation; the performance comparisons are empirical.
summary.tldr: FNO-DEQ exploits fixed-point structure to predict steady-state PDE solutions with constant-depth-related training memory and strong reported accuracy.

title: Deep Equilibrium Based Neural Operators for Steady-State PDEs

abstract: Previous work has shown that DNNs withlarge depth $L$ and $L_{2}$-regularization are biased towards learninglow-dimensional representations of the inputs, which can be interpretedas minimizing a notion of rank $R^{(0)}(f)$ of the learned function$f$, conjectured to be the Bottleneck rank. We compute finite depthcorrections to this result, revealing a measure $R^{(1)}$ of regularitywhich bounds the pseudo-determinant of the Jacobian $\left\|Jf(x)\right\|\_\+$and is subadditive under composition and addition. This formalizesa balance between learning low-dimensional representations and minimizingcomplexity/irregularity in the feature maps, allowing the networkto learn the `right' inner dimension. Finally, we prove the conjecturedbottleneck structure in the learned features as $L\to\infty$: forlarge depths, almost all hidden representations are approximately$R^{(0)}(f)$-dimensional, and almost all weight matrices $W_{\ell}$have $R^{(0)}(f)$ singular values close to 1 while the others are$O(L^{-\frac{1}{2}})$. Interestingly, the use of large learning ratesis required to guarantee an order $O(L)$ NTK which in turns guaranteesinfinite depth convergence of the representations of almost all layers.

paragraphs: Prior theory suggests that very deep networks with L2 regularization favor low-dimensional internal representations. This tendency can be described through a function-level rank quantity, whose identification with Bottleneck rank was conjectured. The paper examines how finite depth changes this picture, revealing a tradeoff between reducing dimension and keeping feature maps regular.

The authors derive a correction term measuring regularity. It bounds a quantity built from the Jacobian's nonzero singular values and is subadditive under both addition and composition. These properties formalize why representation dimension alone does not capture the full preference induced by regularization: the complexity of the maps producing those representations also matters.

The paper also proves a bottleneck structure in the infinite-depth limit. At large depths, almost all hidden representations are approximately as dimensional as the rank quantity. Almost all weight matrices have that many singular values near one, with the others shrinking at order L to the minus one-half. Within the analysis, large learning rates are required for a neural tangent kernel scaling that guarantees convergence of almost all layers' representations.
summary.tldr: The analysis shows how depth and L2 regularization balance low-dimensional features against regularity and produce an asymptotic bottleneck structure.

title: Bottleneck Structure in Learned Features: Low-Dimension vs Regularity Tradeoff

abstract: Cross-device Federated Learning (FL) faces significant challenges where low-end clients that could potentially make unique contributions are excluded from training large models due to their resource bottlenecks. Recent research efforts have focused on model-heterogeneous FL, by extracting reduced-size models from the global model and applying them to local clients accordingly. Despite the empirical success, general theoretical guarantees of convergence on this method remain an open question. This paper presents a unifying framework for heterogeneous FL algorithms with online model extraction and provides a general convergence analysis for the first time. In particular, we prove that under certain sufficient conditions and for both IID and non-IID data, these algorithms converge to a stationary point of standard FL for general smooth cost functions. Moreover, we introduce the concept of minimum coverage index, together with model reduction noise, which will determine the convergence of heterogeneous federated learning, and therefore we advocate for a holistic approach that considers both factors to enhance the efficiency of heterogeneous federated learning.

paragraphs: Federated learning can exclude resource-constrained devices when the shared model is too large for them to train. One response is to extract smaller models for different clients, allowing more devices to participate. Although this strategy has worked empirically, its convergence has lacked a general theoretical account. This paper develops a unified framework for algorithms that extract such reduced models during training.

The analysis establishes sufficient conditions under which these heterogeneous algorithms converge to a stationary point of the standard federated learning objective. It covers both identically distributed and non-identically distributed client data, for general smooth cost functions. A stationary point is the stated target of the guarantee; the result does not claim convergence to a globally optimal solution.

The authors introduce a minimum coverage index and consider it alongside noise caused by model reduction. Their analysis identifies both as factors governing convergence. The practical implication is that choosing smaller client models requires attention to more than local computational savings. How model extraction covers parameters and how much reduction disturbs learning must be considered together.
summary.tldr: A unified analysis gives sufficient conditions for federated learning with dynamically reduced client models to converge to a stationary point.

title: Every Parameter Matters: Ensuring the Convergence of Federated Learning with Dynamic Heterogeneous Models Reduction

abstract: We study the maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) in the multivariate deviated model where the data are generated from the density function $(1-\lambda^{\ast})h_{0}(x)+\lambda^{\ast}f(x|\mu^{\ast}, \Sigma^{\ast})$ in which $h_{0}$ is a known function, $\lambda^{\ast} \in [0,1]$ and $(\mu^{\ast}, \Sigma^{\ast})$ are unknown parameters to estimate. The main challenges in deriving the convergence rate of the MLE mainly come from two issues: (1) The interaction between the function $h_{0}$ and the density function $f$; (2) The deviated proportion $\lambda^{\ast}$ can go to the extreme points of $[0,1]$ as the sample size tends to infinity. To address these challenges, we develop the \emph{distinguishability condition} to capture the linear independent relation between the function $h_{0}$ and the density function $f$. We then provide comprehensive convergence rates of the MLE via the vanishing rate of $\lambda^{\ast}$ to zero as well as the distinguishability of two functions $h_{0}$ and $f$.

The main challenges in deriving the convergence rate of the MLE mainly come from two issues: (1) The interaction between the function $h_{0}$ and the density function $f$; (2) The deviated proportion $\lambda^{\ast}$ can go to the extreme points of $[0,1]$ as the sample size tends to infinity. paragraphs: The paper studies parameter estimation when observations come from a mixture of a known background density and a second density with unknown parameters. The mixture weight determines the proportion contributed by the second component. The authors analyze maximum likelihood estimation, which selects parameters that make the observed data most probable under this model.

Two features complicate the analysis. The background and the second density can interact in ways that make their contributions difficult to distinguish. Also, the mixture weight can approach either endpoint of its allowed range as the sample size grows. In particular, when the second component's proportion shrinks toward zero, increasing the dataset size changes both the amount and the composition of available evidence.

To describe the first issue, the authors introduce a distinguishability condition based on linear independence between the two functions. They then characterize convergence rates in relation to this condition and the speed at which the mixture weight vanishes. The result connects estimation accuracy to both component separability and the shrinking proportion of observations attributable to the unknown component.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes maximum-likelihood convergence rates through component distinguishability and how quickly an unknown mixture component's proportion vanishes.

title: Minimax Optimal Rate for Parameter Estimation in Multivariate Deviated Models

abstract: We examine the relationship between learnability and robust learnability for the problem of distribution learning.We show that learnability implies robust learnability if the adversary can only perform additive contamination (and consequently, under Huber contamination), but not if the adversary is allowed to perform subtractive contamination. Thus, contrary to other learning settings (e.g., PAC learning of function classes), realizable learnability does not imply agnostic learnability. We also explore related implications in the context of compression schemes and differentially private learnability.
originalAbstract: We examine the relationship between learnability and robust learnability for the problem of distribution learning.We show that learnability implies robust learnability if the adversary can only perform additive contamination (and consequently, under Huber contamination), but not if the adversary is allowed to perform subtractive contamination. Thus, contrary to other learning settings (e.g., PAC learning of function classes), realizable learnability does not imply agnostic learnability. We also explore related implications in the context of compression schemes and differentially private learnability.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether being able to learn a distribution from clean data also implies being able to learn it when an adversary contaminates the data. Its central finding is that the answer depends on the adversary’s allowed operation. Adding contamination and removing information lead to different theoretical relationships between ordinary learning and robust learning.

For additive contamination, the authors show that learnability implies robust learnability. The implication also covers Huber contamination. But it does not hold in general when the adversary can perform subtractive contamination. Thus, the positive result for added contamination cannot simply be carried over to a setting where an adversary can remove parts of the evidence.

This distinction also separates realizable from agnostic distribution learning: success when the target belongs to the assumed class does not imply success in the more general agnostic setting. The authors contrast this with other learning settings, including PAC learning of function classes. They additionally examine related implications for compression schemes and differentially private learnability.
summary.tldr: Distribution learnability implies robustness to additive contamination, but this implication fails in general for subtractive contamination.

title: Distribution Learnability and Robustness

abstract: While machine learning can myopically reinforce social inequalities, it may also be used to dynamically seek equitable outcomes. In this paper, we formalize long-term fairness as an online reinforcement learning problem for a policy affecting human populations. This formulation accommodates dynamical control objectives, such as achieving equitable population states, that cannot be incorporated into static formulations of fairness. We demonstrate that algorithmic solutions to the proposed fairness problem can adapt to unknown dynamics and, by sacrificing short-term incentives, drive the policy-population system towards more desirable equilibria. For the proposed setting, we develop an algorithm that adapts recent work in online learning and prove that this algorithm achieves simultaneous probabilistic bounds on cumulative loss and cumulative violations of fairness. In the classification setting subject to group fairness, we compare our proposed algorithm to several baselines, including the repeated retraining of myopic or distributionally robust classifiers, and to a deep reinforcement learning algorithm that lacks fairness guarantees. Our experiments model human populations according to evolutionary game theory and integrate real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Decisions made by a machine learning system can change the population on which future decisions are made. This paper treats fairness as a problem of controlling that evolving interaction. It formulates long-term fairness through online reinforcement learning, allowing objectives such as reaching equitable population states that static fairness formulations cannot express.

The proposed algorithm adapts ideas from online learning to a setting where population dynamics are initially unknown. The authors show that algorithmic solutions can learn those dynamics and move the policy-population system toward more desirable equilibria, potentially by giving up short-term incentives. They prove simultaneous probabilistic bounds on cumulative loss and cumulative fairness violations in their proposed setting.

Experiments examine classification with group fairness, using population models based on evolutionary game theory and incorporating real-world datasets. Comparisons include repeatedly retrained myopic classifiers, distributionally robust classifiers, and a deep reinforcement learning method without fairness guarantees. The contribution is a formulation and algorithm that make evolving population outcomes part of the learning objective while supplying cumulative guarantees.
summary.tldr: An online reinforcement learning formulation pursues long-term population fairness under unknown dynamics with probabilistic bounds on cumulative loss and fairness violations.

title: Long-Term Fairness with Unknown Dynamics

abstract: In an era of more diverse data modalities, multi-view clustering has become a fundamental tool for comprehensive data analysis and exploration. However, existing multi-view unsupervised learning methods often rely on strict assumptions on semantic consistency among samples. In this paper, we reformulate the multi-view clustering problem from an information-theoretic perspective and propose a general theoretical model. In particular, we define three desiderata under multi-view unsupervised learning in terms of mutual information, namely, comprehensiveness, concentration, and cross-diversity. The multi-view variational lower bound is then obtained by approximating the samples' high-dimensional mutual information. The Kullback–Leibler divergence is utilized to deduce sample assignments. Ultimately the information-based multi-view clustering model leverages deep neural networks and Stochastic Gradient Variational Bayes to achieve representation learning and clustering simultaneously. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real datasets with wide types demonstrate that the proposed method exhibits a more stable and superior clustering performance than state-of-the-art algorithms.

paragraphs: Multi-view clustering combines different views or modalities of data to discover groups without labels. Existing approaches often make restrictive assumptions about semantic consistency among samples. This paper reformulates the problem through information theory, providing a general model for learning representations and assigning samples to clusters within the same framework.

The authors express three desired properties—comprehensiveness, concentration, and cross-diversity—in terms of mutual information. They approximate high-dimensional mutual information to obtain a multi-view variational lower bound, creating a tractable objective for the model. Kullback–Leibler divergence is then used to derive sample assignments. Deep networks and Stochastic Gradient Variational Bayes bring these ingredients together for joint representation learning and clustering.

Experiments across varied synthetic and real datasets report more stable and better clustering performance than the state-of-the-art algorithms compared. The importance of the formulation is that it grounds multiple learning goals in one information-based objective and connects that objective to actual cluster assignments. The empirical results support the usefulness of this unified approach across the tested data types.
summary.tldr: An information-theoretic framework jointly learns multi-view representations and clusters, with improved stability and performance in the reported experiments.

title: Generalized Information-theoretic Multi-view Clustering

abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) has shown immense potential for learning to control systems through data alone. However, one challenge deep RL faces is that the full state of the system is often not observable. When this is the case, the policy needs to leverage the history of observations to infer the current state. At the same time, differences between the training and testing environments makes it critical for the policy not to overfit to the sequence of observations it sees at training time. As such, there is an important balancing act between having the history encoder be flexible enough to extract relevant information, yet be robust to changes in the environment. To strike this balance, we look to the PID controller for inspiration. We assert the PID controller's success shows that only summing and differencing are needed to accumulate information over time for many control tasks. Following this principle, we propose two architectures for encoding history: one that directly uses PID features and another that extends these core ideas and can be used in arbitrary control tasks. When compared with prior approaches, our encoders produce policies that are often more robust and achieve better performance on a variety of tracking tasks. Going beyond tracking tasks, our policies achieve 1.7x better performance on average over previous state-of-the-art methods on a suite of locomotion control tasks.

paragraphs: When a controller cannot observe the full state of a system, it must use past observations to infer what is happening now. A highly flexible history encoder can extract useful information, but it can also overfit to sequences encountered during training. This paper seeks a useful balance between expressiveness and robustness to environmental changes.

These findings support structured history processing as a useful design choice for partially observable control, with the reported benefits extending beyond the tracking setting that naturally motivates PID-inspired features.
summary.tldr: PID-inspired history encoders improve reported control performance and often robustness when reinforcement-learning policies cannot observe the full system state.

title: PID-Inspired Inductive Biases for Deep Reinforcement Learning in Partially Observable Control Tasks

abstract: Invisible watermarks safeguard images' copyrights by embedding hidden messages only detectable by owners. They also prevent people from misusing images, especially those generated by AI models.We propose a family of regeneration attacks to remove these invisible watermarks. The proposed attack method first adds random noise to an image to destroy the watermark and then reconstructs the image. This approach is flexible and can be instantiated with many existing image-denoising algorithms and pre-trained generative models such as diffusion models. Through formal proofs and extensive empirical evaluations, we demonstrate that pixel-level invisible watermarks are vulnerable to this regeneration attack.Our results reveal that, across four different pixel-level watermarking schemes, the proposed method consistently achieves superior performance compared to existing attack techniques, with lower detection rates and higher image quality.However, watermarks that keep the image semantically similar can be an alternative defense against our attacks.Our finding underscores the need for a shift in research/industry emphasis from invisible watermarks to semantic-preserving watermarks. Code is available at https://github.com/XuandongZhao/WatermarkAttacker
