paragraphs: Invisible image watermarks embed hidden messages intended to support ownership detection and discourage misuse. This paper examines how robust pixel-level watermarks remain when an image is regenerated. The authors propose a family of attacks that disrupt the hidden signal and then reconstruct the visible image using denoising algorithms or pretrained generative models.

The approach separates watermark destruction from image recovery: random noise damages the watermark, and reconstruction restores image quality. Its flexibility allows different denoising methods and generative models, including diffusion models, to instantiate the same general idea. Formal proofs and empirical evaluations establish vulnerability of pixel-level invisible watermarks to this regeneration approach.

Across four pixel-level watermarking schemes, the method achieves lower detection rates and higher image quality than existing attack techniques in the reported comparisons. The authors identify semantic-preserving watermarks as a possible alternative defense and advocate directing more research toward them. The findings therefore concern a specific weakness of pixel-level invisible signals, while the proposed defensive direction remains an alternative that may resist these attacks.
summary.tldr: Formal analysis and experiments show that regeneration attacks can remove pixel-level invisible watermarks while retaining high image quality.

title: Invisible Image Watermarks Are Provably Removable Using Generative AI

abstract: We consider the problem of privately estimating a parameter $\mathbb{E}[h(X_1,\dots,X_k)]$, where $X_1$, $X_2$, $\dots$, $X_k$ are i.i.d. data from some distribution and $h$ is a permutation-invariant function. Without privacy constraints, the standard estimators for this task are U-statistics, which commonly arise in a wide range of problems, including nonparametric signed rank tests, symmetry testing, uniformity testing, and subgraph counts in random networks, and are the unique minimum variance unbiased estimators under mild conditions. Despite the recent outpouring of interest in private mean estimation, privatizing U-statistics has received little attention. While existing private mean estimation algorithms can be applied in a black-box manner to obtain confidence intervals, we show that they can lead to suboptimal private error, e.g., constant-factor inflation in the leading term, or even $\Theta(1/n)$ rather than $O(1/n^2)$ in degenerate settings. To remedy this, we propose a new thresholding-based approach that reweights different subsets of the data using _local Hájek projections_. This leads to nearly optimal private error for non-degenerate U-statistics and a strong indication of near-optimality for degenerate U-statistics.

U-statistics are standard estimators for this setting and appear in tasks such as symmetry testing and subgraph counting. Under mild conditions, their non-private form is the unique minimum-variance unbiased estimator.

The loss can involve a constant-factor increase in the leading term. In degenerate settings, it can be more severe: error scaling as Θ(1/n) instead of O(1/n²).

The proposed remedy uses thresholding to reweight subsets of the data through local Hájek projections. This makes the privacy procedure responsive to the structure of the U-statistic rather than treating it as a generic mean-estimation problem. The method achieves nearly optimal private error for non-degenerate U-statistics. For degenerate U-statistics, the authors report strong evidence of near-optimality, a more qualified conclusion.
summary.tldr: A thresholding and reweighting method improves private U-statistic estimation, achieving nearly optimal error in the non-degenerate case.

title: On Differentially Private U Statistics

abstract: Although recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) have significantly improved their performance on various tasks, they still face challenges with complex and symbolic multi-step reasoning, particularly in mathematical reasoning. To bolster the mathematical reasoning capabilities of LLMs, most existing efforts concentrate on seeking assistance from either domain experts or GPT-4 for high-quality process-supervised data, which is not only expensive but also labor-intensive. In our study, we propose an innovative framework, AlphaMath, that bypasses the need for process annotations (from humans or GPTs) by leveraging Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS). This framework focuses on unleashing the potential of a well-pretrained LLM to autonomously enhance its mathematical reasoning. Specifically, we integrate a value model with the LLM, automatically generating both process supervision and step-level evaluation signals in MCTS. Furthermore, we propose an efficient inference strategy—step-level beam search, where the value model is crafted to assist the policy model (i.e., LLM) in navigating more effective reasoning paths, rather than solely relying on prior probabilities. The experimental results on both in-domain and out-of-domain datasets demonstrate that even without GPT-4 or human-annotated process supervision, our AlphaMath framework achieves comparable or superior results to previous state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Teaching language models mathematical reasoning often relies on annotated intermediate steps supplied by experts or stronger models. Producing those explanations is costly and labor-intensive. AlphaMath investigates whether a well-pretrained language model can improve its mathematical reasoning by generating its own process-level learning signals through search.

The framework combines the language model with a value model and Monte Carlo Tree Search. Search automatically produces both supervision for reasoning processes and evaluations of individual steps. This gives the system a way to assess possible continuations as it explores solutions, without requiring human-written or GPT-generated annotations of those intermediate reasoning steps.

At inference time, AlphaMath uses step-level beam search guided by the value model. Candidate reasoning paths are therefore assessed using more than the language model's prior probabilities. Experiments on both in-domain and out-of-domain datasets report performance comparable to or better than previous leading methods. The findings support search-generated process supervision as an effective route to improving mathematical reasoning from an already pretrained model.
summary.tldr: AlphaMath uses tree search and a value model to generate mathematical reasoning supervision without human or GPT annotations of intermediate steps.

title: AlphaMath Almost Zero: Process Supervision without Process

abstract: Reliable prediction of protein variant effects is crucial for both protein optimization and for advancing biological understanding. For practical use in protein engineering, it is important that we can also provide reliable uncertainty estimates for our predictions, and while prediction accuracy has seen much progress in recent years, uncertainty metrics are rarely reported. We here provide a Gaussian process regression model, Kermut, with a novel composite kernel for modeling mutation similarity, which obtains state-of-the-art performance for supervised protein variant effect prediction while also offering estimates of uncertainty through its posterior. An analysis of the quality of the uncertainty estimates demonstrates that our model provides meaningful levels of overall calibration, but that instance-specific uncertainty calibration remains more challenging.

paragraphs: Predicting how a protein mutation changes its effects is useful for protein engineering and biological understanding. Practical decisions also require knowing how much confidence to place in a prediction. The paper highlights an imbalance in this area: prediction accuracy has improved, while uncertainty quality is much less frequently reported.

Kermut is a Gaussian process regression model with a new composite kernel for expressing similarity between mutations. That similarity structure supports supervised prediction of protein variant effects. The model also provides uncertainty estimates through its posterior, placing the prediction and its uncertainty within the same modeling framework rather than assessing accuracy alone.

The reported experiments achieve state-of-the-art predictive performance and find meaningful overall uncertainty calibration. However, calibration for individual instances remains more difficult. This distinction matters because uncertainty can behave sensibly across a collection of predictions without being equally informative for each specific variant. Kermut therefore contributes both a strong predictor and an explicit examination of how far its uncertainty estimates support the confidence judgments needed in protein engineering.
summary.tldr: Kermut combines strong protein variant prediction with posterior uncertainty estimates, achieving meaningful overall calibration while leaving instance-level calibration challenging.

title: Kermut: Composite kernel regression for protein variant effects

abstract: Decision Transformer (DT), as one of the representative Reinforcement Learning via Supervised Learning (RvS) methods, has achieved strong performance in offline learning tasks by leveraging the powerful Transformer architecture for sequential decision-making. However, in adversarial environments, these methods can be non-robust, since the return is dependent on the strategies of both the decision-maker and adversary. Training a probabilistic model conditioned on observed return to predict action can fail to generalize, as the trajectories that achieve a return in the dataset might have done so due to a suboptimal behavior adversary. To address this, we propose a worst-case-aware RvS algorithm, the Adversarially Robust Decision Transformer (ARDT), which learns and conditions the policy on in-sample minimax returns-to-go. ARDT aligns the target return with the worst-case return learned through minimax expectile regression, thereby enhancing robustness against powerful test-time adversaries. In experiments conducted on sequential games with full data coverage, ARDT can generate a maximin (Nash Equilibrium) strategy, the solution with the largest adversarial robustness. In large-scale sequential games and continuous adversarial RL environments with partial data coverage, ARDT demonstrates significantly superior robustness to powerful test-time adversaries and attains higher worst-case returns compared to contemporary DT methods.

paragraphs: A Decision Transformer learns actions from recorded trajectories while conditioning on a desired return. In adversarial environments, however, a high recorded return may reflect a weak opponent rather than a strong strategy. Learning to reproduce actions associated with that return can therefore fail when a more capable adversary appears.

The Adversarially Robust Decision Transformer changes the return used for learning and conditioning. It estimates in-sample minimax returns-to-go through minimax expectile regression, aligning the policy’s target with a learned worst-case outcome. The central idea is to account for the adversary when interpreting what the recorded trajectories say about the quality of an action.

In sequential-game experiments with full data coverage, ARDT can produce a maximin strategy, corresponding to a Nash equilibrium in the studied setting. With partial coverage in larger games and continuous adversarial reinforcement-learning environments, it achieves higher worst-case returns and stronger robustness than contemporary Decision Transformer methods. The full-coverage result and the partial-coverage empirical improvements are distinct: the latter demonstrate better performance without establishing the same equilibrium outcome.
summary.tldr: ARDT conditions action selection on learned worst-case returns to improve robustness against stronger adversaries.

title: Adversarially Robust Decision Transformer

abstract: Knowledge transfer between multi-omic single-cell data aims to effectively transfer cell types from scRNA-seq data to unannotated scATAC-seq data. Several approaches aim to reduce the heterogeneity of multi-omic data while maintaining the discriminability of cell types with extensive annotated data. However, in reality, the cost of collecting both a large amount of labeled scRNA-seq data and scATAC-seq data is expensive. Therefore, this paper explores a practical yet underexplored problem of knowledge transfer across multi-omic single-cell data under cell type scarcity. To address this problem, we propose a semi-supervised knowledge transfer framework named Dual label scArcity elimiNation with Cross-omic multi-samplE Mixup (DANCE). To overcome the label scarcity in scRNA-seq data, we generate pseudo-labels based on optimal transport and merge them into the labeled scRNA-seq data. Moreover, we adopt a divide-and-conquer strategy which divides the scATAC-seq data into source-like and target-specific data. For source-like samples, we employ consistency regularization with random perturbations while for target-specific samples, we select a few candidate labels and progressively eliminate incorrect cell types from the label set for additional supervision. Next, we generate virtual scRNA-seq samples with multi-sample Mixup based on the class-wise similarity to reduce cell heterogeneity. Extensive experiments on many benchmark datasets suggest the superiority of our DANCE over a series of state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Transferring cell-type annotations from scRNA-seq to unannotated scATAC-seq is difficult when the two data types differ and labeled cells are scarce. DANCE addresses this setting with a semi-supervised framework that expands available supervision while treating different target samples according to their relationship with the source data.

For scRNA-seq, optimal transport supplies pseudo-labels that are merged with existing labeled examples. For scATAC-seq, the method separates source-like samples from target-specific ones. Source-like samples receive consistency regularization under random perturbations. Target-specific samples receive candidate label sets, from which incorrect cell types are progressively removed to create additional supervision.

DANCE also generates virtual scRNA-seq examples through multi-sample Mixup guided by class-wise similarity, with the aim of reducing cell heterogeneity. These components jointly address scarce labels and differences across the two measurement types. Experiments across multiple benchmark datasets suggest better performance than a range of state-of-the-art methods, supporting this differentiated approach to cross-omic transfer under cell-type scarcity.
summary.tldr: DANCE combines pseudo-labeling, sample-specific supervision, and Mixup to transfer cell types across omic data when labels are scarce.

title: Semi-supervised Knowledge Transfer Across Multi-omic Single-cell Data

abstract: How did humanity coax mathematics from the aether? We explore the Platonic view that mathematics can be discovered from its axioms---a game of conjecture and proof. We describe an agent that jointly learns to pose challenging problems for itself (conjecturing) and solve them (theorem proving). Given a mathematical domain axiomatized in dependent type theory, we first combine methods for constrained decoding and type-directed synthesis to sample valid conjectures from a language model. Our method guarantees well-formed conjectures by construction, even as we start with a randomly initialized model. We use the same model to represent a policy and value function for guiding proof search. Our agent targets generating hard but provable conjectures --- a moving target, since its own theorem proving ability also improves as it trains. We propose novel methods for hindsight relabeling on proof search trees to significantly improve the agent's sample efficiency in both tasks. Experiments on 3 axiomatic domains (propositional logic, arithmetic and group theory) demonstrate that our agent can bootstrap from only the axioms, self-improving in generating true and challenging conjectures and in finding proofs.

paragraphs: This paper explores an agent that learns mathematics by proposing its own conjectures and searching for proofs. Its starting point is a mathematical domain expressed through axioms in dependent type theory. The goal is a self-improving cycle in which the agent generates problems that are challenging enough to teach it something but remain provable.

Constrained decoding and type-directed synthesis ensure that sampled conjectures are well formed, even when the language model begins with random initialization. This construction guarantees valid form, rather than automatically guaranteeing that every conjecture is true. The same model supplies a policy and value function that guide proof search as its ability develops.

Across those domains, it improves at producing true, challenging conjectures and finding proofs, supporting an approach where the learning problems evolve with the learner.
summary.tldr: An agent learns to generate conjectures and prove theorems through a self-improving process that starts from mathematical axioms.

title: Learning Formal Mathematics From Intrinsic Motivation

abstract: Transformers, renowned for their self-attention mechanism, have achieved state-of-the-art performance across various tasks in natural language processing, computer vision, time-series modeling, etc. However, one of the challenges with deep Transformer models is the oversmoothing problem, where representations across layers converge to indistinguishable values, leading to significant performance degradation. We interpret the original self-attention as a simple graph filter and redesign it from a graph signal processing (GSP) perspective. We propose a graph-filter-based self-attention (GFSA) to learn a general yet effective one, whose complexity, however, is slightly larger than that of the original self-attention mechanism. We demonstrate that GFSA improves the performance of Transformers in various fields, including computer vision, natural language processing, graph-level tasks, speech recognition, and code classification.

We propose a graph-filter-based self-attention (GFSA) to learn a general yet effective one, whose complexity, however, is slightly larger than that of the original self-attention mechanism. paragraphs: Deep Transformers can suffer from oversmoothing: representations become increasingly alike across layers until useful distinctions are lost. This can substantially degrade performance even though self-attention is a powerful mechanism for exchanging information. The paper approaches this problem by reconsidering self-attention through graph signal processing.

The authors interpret ordinary self-attention as a simple graph filter and introduce graph-filter-based self-attention, or GFSA. The redesign learns a more general filter, expanding how attention processes information through the graph perspective. Its purpose is to enrich the transformation applied to representations rather than accepting the filtering behavior of the original attention mechanism.

Experiments report improved Transformer performance in computer vision, language processing, graph-level tasks, speech recognition, and code classification. This breadth supports the usefulness of the graph-filter formulation across several application types. The abstract also identifies a concrete cost: GFSA has slightly greater complexity than standard self-attention. The result is an empirical performance improvement accompanied by additional computation, rather than a claim that greater expressiveness is free.
summary.tldr: GFSA redesigns self-attention as a learnable graph filter, improving performance across several domains with slightly higher computational complexity.

title: Graph Convolutions Enrich the Self-Attention in Transformers!

abstract: Recent developments of vision large language models (LLMs) have seen remarkable progress, yet still encounter challenges towards multimodal generalists, such as coarse-grained instance-level understanding, lack of unified support for both images and videos, and insufficient coverage across various vision tasks. In this paper we present Vitron, a universal pixel-level vision LLM designed for comprehensive understanding, generating, segmenting, and editing of both static images and dynamic videos. Building on top of an LLM backbone, Vitron incorporates encoders for images, videos, and pixel-level regional visuals within its frontend modules, while employing state-of-the-art visual specialists as its backend, via which Vitron supports a spectrum of vision end tasks, spanning visual comprehension to visual generation, from low level to high level. To ensure an effective and precise message passing from LLM to backend modules for function invocation, we propose a novel hybrid method by simultaneously integrating discrete textual instructions and continuous signal embeddings. Further, we design various pixel-level spatiotemporal vision-language alignment learning for Vitron to reach the best fine-grained visual capability. Finally, a cross-task synergy module is advised to learn to maximize the task-invariant fine-grained visual features, enhancing the synergy between different visual tasks. Demonstrated over 12 visual tasks and evaluated across 22 datasets, Vitron showcases its extensive capabilities in the four main vision task clusters. Overall, this work illuminates the great potential of developing a more unified multimodal generalist.

paragraphs: Vitron aims to bring visual understanding, generation, segmentation, and editing into one system for both images and videos. Its focus on pixel-level information addresses the difficulty of working precisely with visual regions rather than relying only on coarse descriptions of objects or whole scenes.

The architecture combines a language-model backbone with frontend encoders for images, videos, and regional visual inputs. Specialized visual models serve as backend components. To invoke those components precisely, Vitron communicates through both discrete textual instructions and continuous signal embeddings. This hybrid interface lets the language model pass information in two complementary forms when coordinating visual tasks.

Training includes pixel-level spatial and temporal vision-language alignment, alongside a cross-task module intended to strengthen fine-grained features shared across tasks. The authors demonstrate the system on twelve visual tasks and evaluate it across twenty-two datasets, covering its four main task groups. The contribution is a unified architecture and training approach for coordinating broad visual capabilities while retaining detailed regional information.
summary.tldr: Vitron combines a language model with visual encoders and specialist backends to support detailed image and video understanding and creation.

title: Vitron: A Unified Pixel-level Vision LLM for Understanding, Generating, Segmenting, Editing

abstract: Although humans inherently have diverse values, current large language model (LLM) alignment methods often assume that aligning LLMs with the general public’s preferences is optimal. A major challenge in adopting a more individualized approach to LLM alignment is its lack of scalability, as it involves repeatedly acquiring preference data and training new reward models and LLMs for each individual’s preferences. To address these challenges, we propose a new paradigm where users specify what they value most within the system message, steering the LLM’s generation behavior to better align with the user’s intentions. However, a naive application of such an approach is non-trivial since LLMs are typically trained on a uniform system message (e.g., “You are a helpful assistant”), which limitstheir ability to generalize to diverse, unseen system messages. To improve this generalization, we create Multifaceted Collection, augmenting 66k user instructions into 197k system messages through hierarchical user value combinations. Using this dataset, we train a 7B LLM called Janus and test it on 921 prompts from 5 benchmarks (AlpacaEval 2.0, FLASK, Koala, MT-Bench, and Self-Instruct)by adding system messages that reflect unseen user values. JANUS achieves tie+win rate of 75.2%, 72.4%, and 66.4% against Mistral 7B Instruct v0.2, GPT-3.5 Turbo, and GPT-4, respectively. Unexpectedly, on three benchmarks focused on response helpfulness (AlpacaEval 2.0, MT-Bench, Arena Hard Auto v0.1), JANUS also outperforms LLaMA 3 8B Instruct by a +4.0%p, +0.1%p, +3.0%p margin, underscoring that training with a vast array of system messages could also enhance alignment to the general public’s preference as well. Our code, dataset, benchmark, and models are available at https://lklab.kaist.ac.kr/Janus/.

Unexpectedly, on three benchmarks focused on response helpfulness (AlpacaEval 2.0, MT-Bench, Arena Hard Auto v0.1), JANUS also outperforms LLaMA 3 8B Instruct by a +4.0%p, +0.1%p, +3.0%p margin, underscoring that training with a vast array of system messages could also enhance alignment to the general public’s preference as well. Our code, dataset, benchmark, and models are available at https://lklab.kaist.ac.kr/Janus/.

paragraphs: People want different things from an assistant, but tailoring alignment separately to each person requires repeated data collection and training. This paper instead lets users describe their values in the system message. The challenge is that models trained with a largely uniform system message may struggle to follow unfamiliar combinations of preferences.

The authors create Multifaceted Collection by expanding 66,000 user instructions into 197,000 system messages using hierarchical combinations of user values. They use this collection to train Janus, a model with seven billion parameters. Evaluation adds system messages expressing unseen values to 921 prompts from five benchmarks, testing whether this training transfers beyond the preferences encountered during training.

Janus records combined tie-and-win rates of 75.2%, 72.4%, and 66.4% against Mistral 7B Instruct v0.2, GPT-3.5 Turbo, and GPT-4, respectively. These figures include ties, rather than representing wins alone. Janus also exceeds LLaMA 3 8B Instruct on three helpfulness benchmarks. Together, the findings suggest that varied system-message training can support individualized behavior and may also improve alignment with broader preferences.
summary.tldr: Training Janus on diverse value-bearing system messages improves its ability to follow unseen user preferences and yields gains on several helpfulness benchmarks.

title: Aligning to Thousands of Preferences via System Message Generalization

abstract: Unsupervised skill discovery carries the promise that an intelligent agent can learn reusable skills through autonomous, reward-free interactions with environments. Existing unsupervised skill discovery methods learn skills by encouraging distinguishable behaviors that cover diverse states. However, in complex environments with many state factors (e.g., household environments with many objects), learning skills that cover all possible states is impossible, and naively encouraging state diversity often leads to simple skills that are not ideal for solving downstream tasks. This work introduces Skill Discovery from Local Dependencies (SkiLD), which leverages state factorization as a natural inductive bias to guide the skill learning process. The key intuition guiding SkiLD is that skills that induce \textbf{diverse interactions} between state factors are often more valuable for solving downstream tasks. To this end, SkiLD develops a novel skill learning objective that explicitly encourages the mastering of skills that effectively induce different interactions within an environment. We evaluate SkiLD in several domains with challenging, long-horizon sparse reward tasks including a realistic simulated household robot domain, where SkiLD successfully learns skills with clear semantic meaning and shows superior performance compared to existing unsupervised reinforcement learning methods that only maximize state coverage.

Encouraging diversity alone can therefore produce simple behaviors that contribute little to later tasks.

SkiLD uses the factorized structure of an environment to guide skill learning. The learning objective explicitly encourages mastering these varied interactions, making relationships between factors the organizing principle for exploration.

The authors evaluate the method on challenging tasks with long horizons and sparse rewards, including a realistic simulated household robot domain. SkiLD learns skills with clear semantic meaning and outperforms the tested unsupervised reinforcement learning methods that maximize state coverage alone. The results support interaction diversity as a useful guide for discovering reusable skills in the evaluated environments.
summary.tldr: SkiLD discovers useful reward-free skills by encouraging diverse interactions among state factors instead of focusing only on state coverage.

title: SkiLD: Unsupervised Skill Discovery Guided by Factor Interactions

abstract: Statistical heterogeneity in federated learning poses two major challenges: slow global training due to conflicting gradient signals, and the need of personalization for local distributions. In this work, we tackle both challenges by leveraging recent advances in \emph{linear mode connectivity} --- identifying a linearly connected low-loss region in the parameter space of neural networks, which we call solution simplex. We propose federated learning over connected modes (\textsc{Floco}), where clients are assigned local subregions in this simplex based on their gradient signals, and together learn the shared global solution simplex. This allows personalization of the client models to fit their local distributions within the degrees of freedom in the solution simplex and homogenizes the update signals for the global simplex training. Our experiments show that \textsc{Floco} accelerates the global training process, and significantly improves the local accuracy with minimal computational overhead in cross-silo federated learning settings.

paragraphs: Federated learning becomes harder when clients have different data distributions. Their training updates can conflict, slowing shared learning, and one common model may not fit every client well. Floco addresses these two problems together by learning a shared region of useful models that also allows local personalization.

The method builds on linear mode connectivity: the existence of linearly connected regions in neural-network parameter space with low loss. The authors call their shared region a solution simplex. Clients receive local subregions based on their gradient signals and jointly train the overall simplex. Each client can adjust its model within the available region to suit its own distribution.

This arrangement gives personalization a shared structure while making global update signals more consistent. Experiments in cross-silo federated learning report faster global training and significantly better local accuracy with minimal computational overhead. The results support learning a connected family of solutions as a way to accommodate client differences while preserving productive collaboration on a global model region.
summary.tldr: Floco learns a connected region of models that supports client personalization and speeds global federated training.

title: Federated Learning over Connected Modes

abstract: Diffusion models face significant challenges when employed for large-scale medical image reconstruction in real practice such as 3D Computed Tomography (CT).Due to the demanding memory, time, and data requirements, it is difficult to train a diffusion model directly on the entire volume of high-dimensional data to obtain an efficient 3D diffusion prior. Existing works utilizing diffusion priors on single 2D image slice with hand-crafted cross-slice regularization would sacrifice the z-axis consistency, which results in severe artifacts along the z-axis. In this work, we propose a novel framework that enables learning the 3D image prior through position-aware 3D-patch diffusion score blending for reconstructing large-scale 3D medical images. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to utilize a 3D-patch diffusion prior for 3D medical image reconstruction. Extensive experiments on sparse view and limited angle CT reconstructionshow that our DiffusionBlend method significantly outperforms previous methodsand achieves state-of-the-art performance on real-world CT reconstruction problems with high-dimensional 3D image (i.e., $256 \times 256 \times 500$). Our algorithm also comes with better or comparable computational efficiency than previous state-of-the-art methods. Code is available at https://github.com/efzero/DiffusionBlend.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a large three-dimensional CT image with diffusion models presents a difficult tradeoff. Training directly on whole volumes demands considerable memory, time, and data. Methods that instead learn from individual two-dimensional slices can lose consistency between slices, producing artifacts along the volume’s depth axis even when handcrafted cross-slice constraints are added.

DiffusionBlend learns a prior from three-dimensional patches and blends diffusion scores in a position-aware way. This gives the reconstruction method access to local three-dimensional structure without requiring diffusion training on each entire high-dimensional volume. The authors describe it, to their knowledge, as the first use of a three-dimensional patch diffusion prior for medical image reconstruction.

Experiments cover sparse-view and limited-angle CT, including volumes measuring 256 by 256 by 500. The authors report significant improvements over previous methods and state-of-the-art reconstruction performance, with computational efficiency that is better than or comparable to previous leading approaches. The findings support patch-based three-dimensional modeling as a practical route to stronger large-volume CT reconstruction.
summary.tldr: DiffusionBlend combines position-aware diffusion scores from 3D patches to improve large-volume CT reconstruction with competitive computational efficiency.

title: DiffusionBlend: Learning 3D Image Prior through Position-aware Diffusion Score Blending for 3D Computed Tomography Reconstruction

abstract: Existing diffusion-based text-to-3D generation methods primarily focus on producing visually realistic shapes and appearances, often neglecting the physical constraints necessary for downstream tasks. Generated models frequently fail to maintain balance when placed in physics-based simulations or 3D printed. This balance is crucial for satisfying user design intentions in interactive gaming, embodied AI, and robotics, where stable models are needed for reliable interaction. Additionally, stable models ensure that 3D-printed objects, such as figurines for home decoration, can stand on their own without requiring additional supports. To fill this gap, we introduce Atlas3D, an automatic and easy-to-implement method that enhances existing Score Distillation Sampling (SDS)-based text-to-3D tools. Atlas3D ensures the generation of self-supporting 3D models that adhere to physical laws of stability under gravity, contact, and friction. Our approach combines a novel differentiable simulation-based loss function with physically inspired regularization, serving as either a refinement or a post-processing module for existing frameworks. We verify Atlas3D's efficacy through extensive generation tasks and validate the resulting 3D models in both simulated and real-world environments.

paragraphs: A generated 3D object can look convincing while failing to stand upright. That gap matters when the object enters a physics simulation or becomes a physical print: appearance alone does not establish balance. Atlas3D addresses this problem by adding physical stability requirements to text-to-3D generation, with applications including interactive environments, robotics, and freestanding printed objects.

The method extends tools based on Score Distillation Sampling, or SDS. It combines a differentiable simulation-based loss with regularization inspired by physics. Together, these components bring gravity, contact, and friction into the process of shaping an object. The simulation loss makes physical behavior part of the optimization objective, connecting the generated geometry to how the object is expected to stand.

Atlas3D can serve as a refinement module or as post-processing for an existing generation framework. The authors evaluate it across generation tasks and validate resulting objects in simulated and real environments. Their stated result is self-supporting geometry, making physical balance an explicit generation goal alongside visual appearance and the user's design intent.
summary.tldr: Atlas3D adds differentiable physical stability objectives to text-to-3D tools so generated objects can stand on their own.

title: Atlas3D: Physically Constrained Self-Supporting Text-to-3D for Simulation and Fabrication

abstract: Bayesian optimization is a technique for efficiently optimizing unknown functions in a black-box manner. To handle practical settings where gathering data requires use of finite resources, it is desirable to explicitly incorporate function evaluation costs into Bayesian optimization policies. To understand how to do so, we develop a previously-unexplored connection between cost-aware Bayesian optimization and the Pandora's Box problem, a decision problem from economics. The Pandora's Box problem admits a Bayesian-optimal solution based on an expression called the Gittins index, which can be reinterpreted as an acquisition function. We study the use of this acquisition function for cost-aware Bayesian optimization, and demonstrate empirically that it performs well, particularly in medium-high dimensions. We further show that this performance carries over to classical Bayesian optimization without explicit evaluation costs. Our work constitutes a first step towards integrating techniques from Gittins index theory into Bayesian optimization.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization searches for good inputs to an unknown function by deciding which evaluations to perform. When evaluations consume limited resources, their costs should influence that choice. This paper investigates how to incorporate those costs by connecting Bayesian optimization to Pandora's Box, a decision problem from economics.

Pandora's Box has a Bayesian-optimal solution expressed through a Gittins index. The authors reinterpret that index as an acquisition function: a rule for selecting the next evaluation in Bayesian optimization. This supplies a principled source for a cost-sensitive selection rule. The optimality statement belongs to the Pandora's Box problem; the abstract evaluates the resulting Bayesian optimization approach empirically.

The experiments find that the acquisition function performs well, particularly in medium- to high-dimensional settings. Its favorable performance also carries over to conventional Bayesian optimization without explicit evaluation costs. These results suggest that the connection has value beyond the original resource-aware motivation, while the paper positions it as an initial step toward bringing Gittins index techniques into Bayesian optimization.
summary.tldr: A Gittins-index acquisition function derived from Pandora's Box performs well empirically in cost-aware and conventional Bayesian optimization.

title: Cost-aware Bayesian Optimization via the Pandora's Box Gittins Index

abstract: In this paper, we approach an overlooked yet critical task Graph2Image: generating images from multimodal attributed graphs (MMAGs). This task poses significant challenges due to the explosion in graph size, dependencies among graph entities, and the need for controllability in graph conditions. To address these challenges, we propose a graph context-conditioned diffusion model called InstructG2I. InstructG2I first exploits the graph structure and multimodal information to conduct informative neighbor sampling by combining personalized page rank and re-ranking based on vision-language features. Then, a graph QFormer encoder adaptively encodes the graph nodes into an auxiliary set of graph prompts to guide the denoising process of diffusion. Finally, we propose graph classifier-free guidance, enabling controllable generation by varying the strength of graph guidance and multiple connected edges to a node. Extensive experiments conducted on three datasets from different domains demonstrate the effectiveness and controllability of our approach. The code is available at https://github.com/PeterGriffinJin/InstructG2I.

paragraphs: Generating an image from a graph requires using both information attached to entities and the relationships between them. Large graphs make it difficult to select relevant context, while dependencies between entities complicate image generation. InstructG2I addresses this Graph2Image task with a diffusion model conditioned on graph context.

The method first chooses informative neighbors using personalized PageRank together with reranking based on vision-language features. A graph QFormer then encodes graph nodes into auxiliary prompts that guide diffusion denoising. These stages connect graph-based context selection to the image generator, giving the model a way to use selected structural and multimodal information during synthesis.

The authors also introduce graph classifier-free guidance to control generation. Users can vary the strength of graph guidance and the multiple edges connected to a node, changing how graph conditions influence the result. Experiments on three datasets from different domains support the method's effectiveness and controllability. The contribution combines context selection, graph encoding, and adjustable guidance within one image-generation approach.
summary.tldr: InstructG2I selects and encodes multimodal graph context to guide diffusion image generation with adjustable graph influence.

title: InstructG2I: Synthesizing Images from Multimodal Attributed Graphs

abstract: Accurately predicting conditional average treatment effects (CATEs) is crucial in personalized medicine and digital platform analytics. Since the treatments of interest often cannot be directly randomized, observational data is leveraged to learn CATEs, but this approach can incur significant bias from unobserved confounding. One strategy to overcome these limitations is to leverage instrumental variables (IVs) as latent quasi-experiments, such as randomized intent-to-treat assignments or randomized product recommendations. This approach, on the other hand, can suffer from low compliance, i.e., IV weakness. Some subgroups may even exhibit zero compliance, meaning we cannot instrument for their CATEs at all. In this paper, we develop a novel approach to combine IV and observational data to enable reliable CATE estimation in the presence of unobserved confounding in the observational data and low compliance in the IV data, including no compliance for some subgroups. We propose a two-stage framework that first learns \textit{biased} CATEs from the observational data, and then applies a compliance-weighted correction using IV data, effectively leveraging IV strength variability across covariates. We characterize the convergence rates of our method and validate its effectiveness through a simulation study. Additionally, we demonstrate its utility with real data by analyzing the heterogeneous effects of 401(k) plan participation on wealth.

paragraphs: The effect of a treatment can vary across people or groups. Estimating these differences from observational data is difficult when unobserved factors influence both treatment and outcome. Instrumental variables, such as randomized recommendations, offer another source of evidence, but they can be weak when people rarely respond to the assigned encouragement.

This paper combines observational and instrumental-variable data in a two-stage framework. It first learns conditional average treatment effects from observational data, accepting that these estimates may be biased. It then uses instrumental-variable evidence to make a correction weighted by compliance, taking advantage of differences in instrument strength across observed characteristics.

The proposed approach addresses settings with unobserved confounding and low compliance, including some subgroups with no compliance at all. The authors characterize convergence rates and evaluate the method in simulations. They also apply it to differences in the effects of 401(k) participation on wealth. The central idea is to combine broad observational information with corrective evidence whose strength varies across groups.
summary.tldr: A two-stage estimator corrects biased observational treatment-effect estimates using instrumental-variable evidence weighted by compliance.

title: Estimating Heterogeneous Treatment Effects by Combining Weak Instruments and Observational Data

abstract: Geometric graph neural networks (GNNs) have emerged as powerful tools for modeling molecular geometry. However, they encounter limitations in effectively capturing long-range interactions in large molecular systems. To address this challenge, we introduce **Neural P$^3$M**, a versatile enhancer of geometric GNNs to expand the scope of their capabilities by incorporating mesh points alongside atoms and reimaging traditional mathematical operations in a trainable manner. Neural P$^3$M exhibits flexibility across a wide range of molecular systems and demonstrates remarkable accuracy in predicting energies and forces, outperforming on benchmarks such as the MD22 dataset. It also achieves an average improvement of 22% on the OE62 dataset while integrating with various architectures. Codes are available at https://github.com/OnlyLoveKFC/Neural_P3M.

paragraphs: Neural P³M addresses the difficulty geometric graph neural networks face when modeling long-range interactions in large molecular systems. These networks represent molecular geometry, but their ability to capture interactions across a large structure can be limited. The paper introduces an enhancement intended to expand that capability across different molecular models.

The approach incorporates mesh points alongside the atoms and turns traditional mathematical operations into trainable components. The added mesh gives the model a representation beyond the atomic points alone, while trainable operations allow the interaction modeling to be learned. The framework is designed to integrate with multiple geometric GNN architectures.

Experiments report strong energy and force prediction accuracy, including improved results on MD22. On OE62, the method achieves an average improvement of 22% while being integrated with various architectures. These results support its role as a reusable enhancement for molecular prediction. The contribution links a broader representation of molecular interactions to measured improvements, rather than relying on a single replacement architecture for all molecular systems.
summary.tldr: Neural P³M adds mesh points and trainable operations to geometric GNNs to improve modeling of long-range molecular interactions.

title: Neural P$^3$M: A Long-Range Interaction Modeling Enhancer for Geometric GNNs

abstract: The success of pretrain-finetune paradigm brings about the release of numerous model weights. In this case, merging models finetuned on different tasks to enable a single model with multi-task capabilities is gaining increasing attention for its practicability. Existing model merging methods usually suffer from (1) significant performance degradation or (2) requiring tuning by additional data or training. In this paper, we rethink and analyze the existing model merging paradigm. We discover that using a single model's weights can hardly simulate all the models' performance. To tackle this issue, we propose Elect, Mask & Rescale-Merging (EMR-Merging). We first (a) elect a unified model from all the model weights and then (b) generate extremely lightweight task-specific modulators, including masks and rescalers, to align the direction and magnitude between the unified model and each specific model, respectively. EMR-Merging is tuning-free, thus requiring no data availability or any additional training while showing impressive performance. We find that EMR-Merging shows outstanding performance compared to existing merging methods under different classical and newly-established settings, including merging different numbers of vision models (up to 30), NLP models, PEFT models, and multi-modal models.

paragraphs: Many models begin with pretraining and are then fine-tuned for separate tasks. Combining their weights could produce a shared model with several capabilities, but existing merging methods often lose performance or require extra data and training. This paper identifies a central difficulty: one fixed set of weights struggles to reproduce every specialized model's behavior.

EMR-Merging addresses this by pairing a unified model with very lightweight task-specific modulators. It first elects unified weights from the available model weights. It then generates masks and rescalers that align the unified model with each task-specific model in direction and magnitude, respectively. Task-specific adjustments therefore remain part of the merged system.

The method requires neither additional training nor access to data for tuning. The authors report strong performance against existing merging methods across vision, language, parameter-efficient fine-tuned models, and multimodal models, including settings with up to 30 vision models. The findings support lightweight modulation as a practical way to retain task specialization within a shared model.
summary.tldr: EMR-Merging combines unified model weights with lightweight task-specific masks and rescalers, requiring no tuning data or additional training.

title: EMR-Merging: Tuning-Free High-Performance Model Merging

abstract: Preference learning methods make use of models of human choice in order to infer the latent utilities that underlie human behavior. However, accurate modeling of human choice behavior is challenging due to a range of context effects that arise from how humans contrast and evaluate options. Cognitive science has proposed several models that capture these intricacies but, due to their intractable nature, work on preference learning has, in practice, had to rely on tractable but simplified variants of the well-known Bradley-Terry model. In this paper, we take one state-of-the-art intractable cognitive model and propose a tractable surrogate that is suitable for deployment in preference learning. We then introduce a mechanism for fitting the surrogate to human data and extend it to account for data that cannot be explained by the original cognitive model. We demonstrate on large-scale human data that this model produces significantly better inferences on static and actively elicited data than existing Bradley-Terry variants. We further show in simulation that when using this model for preference learning, we can significantly improve utility in a range of real-world tasks.

paragraphs: Preference learning tries to infer the hidden utilities behind people's choices. That inference depends on how choices are modeled, but human decisions can change with the context in which options are compared. Cognitive models capture some of these effects, yet their computational difficulty has encouraged practical systems to use simpler Bradley-Terry variants.

This paper constructs a tractable surrogate for a state-of-the-art cognitive model. It introduces a procedure for fitting the surrogate to human observations and extends the model to handle data that the original cognitive account cannot explain. The aim is to retain richer descriptions of human choice while making them usable inside preference-learning systems.

On large-scale human data, the proposed model gives significantly better utility inferences than existing Bradley-Terry variants, both with fixed datasets and with actively elicited observations. Separately, simulations show significant utility improvements across a range of real-world task settings. The evidence links better modeling of contextual choice behavior to better inference, with downstream decision benefits demonstrated in simulation.
summary.tldr: A tractable surrogate for a richer cognitive choice model improves preference inference and simulated decision utility.

title: Preference Learning of Latent Decision Utilities with a Human-like Model of Preferential Choice

abstract: In this work, we introduce a new approach to model group actions in autoencoders. Diverging from prior research in this domain, we propose to learn the group actions on the latent space rather than strictly on the data space. This adaptation enhances the versatility of our model, enabling it to learn a broader range of scenarios prevalent in the real world, where groups can act on latent factors. Our method allows a wide flexibility in the encoder and decoder architectures and does not require group-specific layers. In addition, we show that our model theoretically serves as a superset of methods that learn group actions on the data space. We test our approach on five image datasets with diverse groups acting on them and demonstrate superior performance to recently proposed methods for modeling group actions.

paragraphs: Group actions describe structured transformations and how they compose. In an autoencoder, an encoder maps observations into a latent representation, and a decoder maps those representations back to the data space. This paper proposes learning group actions on the latent representation, allowing the transformations to operate on underlying factors rather than strictly on observations.

That change expands the range of situations the model can represent, particularly when group structure belongs to hidden factors in the data. The method also permits broad choices of encoder and decoder architecture without requiring layers designed for a particular group. The authors establish theoretically that their formulation contains methods learning group actions in data space as a special case.

The approach is evaluated on five image datasets with different groups acting on them and achieves better performance than recently proposed methods for modeling group actions. These results support the practical value of the broader formulation. The theoretical inclusion result and architectural flexibility together explain why moving the learned action into latent space can generalize the modeling setup.
summary.tldr: Learning group actions in an autoencoder’s latent space broadens transformation modeling without requiring group-specific network layers.

title: Learning Group Actions on Latent Representations

abstract: As artificial intelligence systems proliferate as content creators, generating unprecedented volumes of media that exceed human attention capacity, we propose a speculative intervention: AI systems that serve as synthetic audiences. This paper presents "artificial spectatorship," a multi-modal language models simulate viewing experiences through emotional response generation, internal dialogue synthesis, and real-time facial expression rendering. Our implementation employs feedback loops between affective states and dialogue generation, creating autonomous viewing entities that process and respond to AI-generated content. This work challenges fundamental assumptions about attention, meaning-making, and the nature of aesthetic experience in an era where the exponential growth of synthetic media threatens to overwhelm human cognitive bandwidth. We position this as critical design intervention that interrogates whether machine-generated attention can constitute meaningful engagement, and what implications arise when both creation and consumption become automated processes.

paragraphs: Artificial Spectator asks what happens when AI becomes an audience for the media it helps produce. The project starts from a mismatch between growing volumes of synthetic content and limited human attention. It proposes artificial viewers as a speculative intervention through which to examine the meaning of attention and aesthetic engagement.

The implementation uses multimodal language models to simulate viewing experiences. These viewers generate emotional responses and internal dialogue, while facial expressions are rendered in real time. Feedback loops connect the simulated emotional state with dialogue generation, allowing each viewing entity’s responses to develop as it processes AI-generated content.

The resulting system gives a concrete form to questions about automated consumption. Producing facial reactions and commentary makes machine attention visible, but the paper treats whether such attention constitutes meaningful engagement as an open question. Its contribution is therefore both an implementation and a critical design exercise: it explores the implications of a media ecosystem in which machines can occupy the roles of creator and spectator.
summary.tldr: Artificial Spectator simulates AI viewers’ emotions, thoughts, and facial reactions to question what automated media engagement could mean.

title: "Artificial Spectator" Developing AI Audiences for Watching AI-Generated Films: A Speculative Exploration on the Future of Media and AI

abstract: We study reinforcement learning from human feedback in general Markov decision processes, where agents learn from trajectory-level preference comparisons. A central challenge in this setting is to design algorithms that select informative preference queries to identify the underlying reward while ensuring theoretical guarantees. We propose a meta-algorithm based on randomized exploration, which avoids the computational challenges associated with optimistic approaches and remains tractable. We establish both regret and last-iterate guarantees under mild reinforcement learning oracle assumptions. To improve query complexity, we introduce and analyze an improved algorithm that collects batches of trajectory pairs and applies optimal experimental design to select informative comparison queries. The batch structure also enables parallelization of preference queries, which is relevant in practical deployment as feedback can be gathered concurrently. Empirical evaluation confirms that the proposed method is competitive with reward-based reinforcement learning while requiring a small number of preference queries.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning when feedback consists of preferences between entire trajectories rather than numerical rewards. The agent must choose which pairs of experiences to compare so that the feedback reveals the underlying reward efficiently. The setting covers general Markov decision processes, making informative query selection a central algorithmic problem.

The authors propose a meta-algorithm based on randomized exploration that avoids computational difficulties associated with optimistic approaches. Under mild assumptions about access to a reinforcement learning oracle, they establish guarantees for regret and for the final policy produced. An improved version collects batches of trajectory pairs and uses optimal experimental design to choose informative comparisons, reducing the number of preference queries needed.

Batching also allows several feedback requests to be answered concurrently, a practical advantage when gathering preferences. Empirical evaluation finds the method competitive with reinforcement learning that receives rewards directly, despite using few preference queries. The contribution joins tractable exploration, principled query selection, and theoretical guarantees, showing how an agent can make more effective use of limited comparison feedback.
summary.tldr: Randomized exploration and experimental design enable theoretically supported reinforcement learning with a small number of informative trajectory-preference queries.

title: Efficient Preference-Based Reinforcement Learning: Randomized Exploration meets Experimental Design

abstract: We present WUKONG, a novel training-free framework for high-fidelity textured 3D morphing that takes a pair of source and target prompts (text or images) as input. Unlike conventional methods -- which rely on manual correspondence matching and deformation trajectory estimation (limiting generalization and requiring costly preprocessing) -- WUKONG leverages the generative prior of flow-based transformers to produce high-fidelity 3D transitions with rich texture details. To ensure smooth shape transitions, we exploit the inherent continuity of flow-based generative processes and formulate morphing as an optimal transport barycenter problem. We further introduce a sequential initialization strategy to prevent abrupt geometric distortions and preserve identity coherence. For faithful texture preservation, we propose a similarity-guided semantic consistency mechanism that selectively retains high-frequency details and enables precise control over blending dynamics. This avoids common artifacts like oversmoothing while maintaining semantic fidelity. Through extensive quantitative and qualitative evaluations, we demonstrate that WUKONG significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving superior results across diverse geometry and texture variations.

paragraphs: WUKONG generates textured three-dimensional transitions between source and target prompts supplied as text or images. It is a training-free framework that uses the generative prior of flow-based transformers. This addresses a difficulty in conventional morphing workflows, which depend on manual correspondence matching and deformation-trajectory estimation, requiring costly preprocessing and limiting generalization.

For geometry, the method uses continuity in the flow-based generative process and formulates morphing as an optimal transport barycenter problem. A sequential initialization strategy is designed to prevent abrupt shape distortions and preserve coherent identity through the transition. These components organize the intermediate shapes so that the transformation remains geometrically smooth.

For appearance, a similarity-guided semantic consistency mechanism selectively preserves high-frequency texture details and controls blending dynamics. This is intended to avoid oversmoothing while maintaining semantic fidelity. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations report significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods across varied geometry and texture changes. The contribution treats smooth shape evolution and faithful texture evolution as coordinated parts of the morphing problem.
summary.tldr: WUKONG uses pretrained flow models to generate smooth, richly textured 3D morphs between text or image prompts without additional training.

title: Wukong's 72 Transformations: High-fidelity Textured 3D Morphing via Flow Models

abstract: In this paper, we consider the related problems of multicalibration --- a multigroup fairness notion and omniprediction --- a simultaneous loss minimization paradigm, both in the distributional and online settings. The recent work of Garg et al. (2024) raised the open problem of whether it is possible to efficiently achieve $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{T})$ $\ell_{2}$-multicalibration error against bounded linear functions. In this paper, we answer this question in a strongly affirmative sense. We propose an efficient algorithm that achieves $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{\frac{1}{3}})$ $\ell_{2}$-swap multicalibration error (both in high probability and expectation). On propagating this bound onward, we obtain significantly improved rates for $\ell_{1}$-swap multicalibration and swap omniprediction for a loss class of convex Lipschitz functions. In particular, we show that our algorithm achieves $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{\frac{2}{3}})$ $\ell_{1}$-swap multicalibration and swap omniprediction errors, thereby improving upon the previous best-known bound of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{\frac{7}{8}})$. As a consequence of our improved online results, we further obtain several improved sample complexity rates in the distributional setting. In particular, we establish a $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\varepsilon ^ {-3})$ sample complexity of efficiently learning an $\varepsilon$-swap omnipredictor for the class of convex and Lipschitz functions, $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\varepsilon ^{-2.5})$ sample complexity of efficiently learning an $\varepsilon$-swap agnostic learner for the squared loss, and $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\varepsilon ^ {-5}), \tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\varepsilon ^ {-2.5})$ sample complexities of learning $\ell_{1}, \ell_{2}$-swap multicalibrated predictors against linear functions, all of which significantly improve on the previous best-known bounds.

paragraphs: This paper improves theoretical guarantees for two related prediction goals. Multicalibration concerns prediction reliability across multiple groups, while omniprediction seeks predictions useful for minimizing several losses. The authors study swap versions of these goals in both online learning, where observations arrive sequentially, and distributional learning, where sample requirements are central.

Their efficient algorithm achieves an l2-swap multicalibration error bound scaling as T^(1/3), up to logarithmic factors, against bounded linear functions. The guarantee holds both in expectation and with high probability. It improves on the T^(1/2) rate posed in the motivating open question. The result also yields T^(2/3) bounds for l1-swap multicalibration and swap omniprediction with convex Lipschitz losses, improving the previous T^(7/8) rate.

These online improvements translate into reduced sample requirements. Ignoring logarithmic factors, the stated bounds are epsilon^(-3) for swap omniprediction and epsilon^(-2.5) for swap agnostic learning with squared loss. For l1- and l2-swap multicalibration against linear functions, they are epsilon^(-5) and epsilon^(-2.5), respectively. The contribution is stronger efficient-learning guarantees for the specified function and loss classes.
summary.tldr: An efficient algorithm improves online error bounds and sample requirements for swap multicalibration and swap omniprediction.

title: Improved Bounds for Swap Multicalibration and Swap Omniprediction

abstract: We study the online multi-class selection problem with group fairness guarantees, where limited resources must be allocated to sequentially arriving agents. Our work addresses two key limitations in the existing literature. First, we introduce a novel lossless rounding scheme that ensures the integral algorithm achieves the same expected performance as any fractional solution. Second, we explicitly address the challenges introduced by agents who belong to multiple classes. To this end, we develop a randomized algorithm based on a relax-and-round framework. The algorithm first computes a fractional solution using a resource reservation approach---referred to as the *set-aside* mechanism---to enforce fairness across classes. The subsequent rounding step preserves these fairness guarantees without degrading performance. Additionally, we propose a learning-augmented variant that incorporates untrusted machine-learned predictions to better balance fairness and efficiency in practical settings.

paragraphs: This paper studies allocation when agents arrive sequentially, resources are limited, and selection must satisfy fairness requirements across groups. An additional complication is that one agent may belong to several classes. The method explicitly addresses overlapping memberships rather than treating the arriving population as a collection of disjoint groups.

The algorithm first constructs a fractional solution using a set-aside mechanism that reserves resources to enforce fairness. It then turns that solution into actual selection decisions through randomized rounding. The key theoretical contribution is a lossless rounding scheme: the integral algorithm matches the fractional solution’s expected performance while preserving the fairness guarantees.

The expectation qualifier matters because the performance guarantee concerns the randomized algorithm, rather than requiring every individual realization to have identical performance. The paper also proposes a learning-augmented version that incorporates untrusted machine-learning predictions to improve the practical balance between fairness and efficiency. Together, these contributions connect fair resource reservation, implementable discrete decisions, and the possible use of predictive guidance in one online allocation framework.
summary.tldr: A randomized reservation-and-rounding method preserves group fairness and fractional-solution performance in expectation when allocating resources online.

title: Online Multi-Class Selection with Group Fairness Guarantee

abstract: This paper explores a novel lightweight approach LightFair to achieve fair text-to-image diffusion models (T2I DMs) by addressing the adverse effects of the text encoder. Most existing methods either couple different parts of the diffusion model for full-parameter training or rely on auxiliary networks for correction. They incur heavy training or sampling burden and unsatisfactory performance. Since T2I DMs consist of multiple components, with the text encoder being the most fine-tunable and front-end module, this paper focuses on mitigating bias by fine-tuning text embeddings. To validate feasibility, we observe that the text encoder’s neutral embedding output shows substantial skewness across image embeddings of various attributes in the CLIP space. More importantly, the noise prediction network further amplifies this imbalance. To finetune the text embedding, we propose a collaborative distance-constrained debiasing strategy that balances embedding distances to improve fairness without auxiliary references. However, mitigating bias can compromise the original generation quality. To address this, we introduce a two-stage text-guided sampling strategy to limit when the debiased text encoder intervenes. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LightFair is effective and efficient. Notably, on Stable Diffusion v1.5, our method achieves SOTA debiasing at just $1/4$ of the training burden, with virtually no increase in sampling burden. The code is available at https://github.com/boyuh/LightFair.

paragraphs: LightFair investigates bias originating in the text encoder of a text-to-image diffusion model. The authors observe that supposedly neutral text embeddings have uneven relationships to image embeddings associated with different attributes in CLIP space. They also find that the noise prediction network amplifies this imbalance, making the text representation a useful intervention point.

The method fine-tunes text embeddings using a collaborative distance constraint that balances their distances without auxiliary references. Focusing on the text encoder reduces the burden associated with adapting multiple model components or adding correction networks. Experiments demonstrate effectiveness and efficiency. On Stable Diffusion v1.5, the authors report state-of-the-art debiasing with one-quarter of the training burden and virtually unchanged sampling burden. The findings support a targeted intervention at the text encoder, paired with control over its use during sampling, as an efficient way to address the evaluated biases while managing generation quality.
summary.tldr: LightFair debiases text embeddings and controls their influence during sampling, achieving strong reported fairness results with substantially less training.

title: LightFair: Towards an Efficient Alternative for Fair T2I Diffusion via Debiasing Pre-trained Text Encoders

abstract: In-context reinforcement learning (ICRL) has emerged as a promising paradigm for adapting RL agents to downstream tasks through prompt conditioning. However, two notable challenges remain in fully harnessing in-context learning within RL domains: the intrinsic multi-modality of the state-action-reward data and the diverse, heterogeneous nature of decision tasks. To tackle these challenges, we propose **T2MIR** (**T**oken- and **T**ask-wise **M**oE for **I**n-context **R**L), an innovative framework that introduces architectural advances of mixture-of-experts (MoE) into transformer-based decision models. T2MIR substitutes the feedforward layer with two parallel layers: a token-wise MoE that captures distinct semantics of input tokens across multiple modalities, and a task-wise MoE that routes diverse tasks to specialized experts for managing a broad task distribution with alleviated gradient conflicts. To enhance task-wise routing, we introduce a contrastive learning method that maximizes the mutual information between the task and its router representation, enabling more precise capture of task-relevant information. The outputs of two MoE components are concatenated and fed into the next layer. Comprehensive experiments show that T2MIR significantly facilitates in-context learning capacity and outperforms various types of baselines. We bring the potential and promise of MoE to ICRL, offering a simple and scalable architectural enhancement to advance ICRL one step closer toward achievements in language and vision communities. Our code is available at [https://github.com/NJU-RL/T2MIR](https://github.com/NJU-RL/T2MIR).

paragraphs: T2MIR improves reinforcement-learning agents that adapt to downstream tasks through prompt conditioning. Such models must interpret several kinds of information—states, actions, and rewards—while handling tasks with different decision requirements. The paper treats these as two distinct sources of diversity and introduces separate mixture-of-experts components to address them within a transformer decision model.

The token-wise component specializes in the meanings of different input modalities. The task-wise component directs tasks to specialized experts, aiming to reduce conflicts between their training gradients. Both operate in parallel in place of the usual feedforward layer, and their outputs are concatenated before passing onward. A contrastive learning objective encourages the task router’s representation to retain information relevant to task identity.

Experiments report improved in-context learning capacity and stronger performance than several types of baselines. The architectural contribution is the explicit combination of specialization by token and specialization by task. This gives the shared decision model separate mechanisms for interpreting heterogeneous experience and accommodating a broad distribution of decision problems.
summary.tldr: T2MIR combines token-wise and task-wise expert routing to improve prompt-based adaptation in reinforcement learning.

title: Mixture-of-Experts Meets In-Context Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We propose a novel AutoRegressive Generation-based paradigm for image Segmentation (ARGenSeg), achieving multimodal understanding and pixel-level perception within a unified framework. Prior works integrating image segmentation into multimodal large language models (MLLMs) typically employ either boundary points representation or dedicated segmentation heads. These methods rely on discrete representations or semantic prompts fed into task-specific decoders, which limits the ability of the MLLM to capture fine-grained visual details. To address these challenges, we introduce a segmentation framework for MLLM based on image generation, which naturally produces dense masks for target objects. We leverage MLLM to output visual tokens and detokenize them into images using an universal VQ-VAE, making the segmentation fully dependent on the pixel-level understanding of the MLLM. To reduce inference latency, we employ a next-scale-prediction strategy to generate required visual tokens in parallel. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method surpasses prior state-of-the-art approaches on multiple segmentation datasets with a remarkable boost in inference speed, while maintaining strong understanding capabilities.
