paragraphs: GAN training is difficult because the interacting objectives are nonconvex, and optimization-based analyses typically provide only local convergence results. This paper changes the formulation by considering mixed Nash equilibria. In this perspective, the players can use distributions over strategies, expanding the object being learned beyond a single strategy for each player.

Using a classical lifting construction, the authors show that essentially all existing GAN objectives can be relaxed into mixed-strategy forms whose global optima can be solved through sampling. They then propose a mean-approximation sampling scheme. This makes methods for bi-affine games available as a systematic basis for practical GAN training algorithms.

The distinction between the relaxed formulation and its practical algorithms is central to interpreting the result. The global-optimum claim concerns the mixed-strategy forms; the experiments provide evidence about the proposed training approach. Those experiments show comparable or superior results to contemporary training algorithms and improvements over SGD, Adam, and RMSProp. The work thus links a game-theoretic reformulation to empirically effective training procedures.
summary.tldr: Reformulating GAN objectives as mixed-strategy games motivates sampling-based training methods with competitive or improved experimental performance.

title: Finding Mixed Nash Equilibria of Generative Adversarial Networks

abstract: In this paper, we develop a new variant of k-means++ seeding that in expectation achieves a constant approximation guarantee. We obtain this result by a simple combination of k-means++ sampling with a local search strategy. We evaluate our algorithm empirically and show that it also improves the quality of a solution in practice.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we develop a new variant of k-means++ seeding that in expectation achieves a constant approximation guarantee. We obtain this result by a simple combination of k-means++ sampling with a local search strategy. We evaluate our algorithm empirically and show that it also improves the quality of a solution in practice.

paragraphs: This paper improves the seeding stage of k-means++, where an algorithm chooses the starting centers for a clustering solution. The proposed variant combines k-means++ sampling with a local search strategy. Its central idea is to bring these two procedures together so that the selected centers come with a stronger guarantee on solution quality.

The main theoretical result is a constant approximation guarantee in expectation. This means that, averaged over the algorithm’s randomness, its objective value is bounded by a fixed multiplicative factor of the best possible value. The expectation qualifier matters: the claim concerns average behavior across random choices, rather than promising that every individual run meets the same bound.

The authors also evaluate the algorithm empirically and report improved solution quality in practice. This supplies a practical counterpart to the approximation result: the combination is useful both as an object of mathematical analysis and as a method for obtaining better clustering solutions in the reported evaluation.
summary.tldr: Combining k-means++ sampling with local search gives a constant approximation guarantee in expectation and improves solution quality empirically.

title: A Better k-means++ Algorithm via Local Search

abstract: Principal component analysis (PCA) is one of the most fundamental procedures in exploratory data analysis and is the basic step in applications ranging from quantitative finance and bioinformatics to image analysis and neuroscience. However, it is well-documented that the applicability of PCA in many real scenarios could be constrained by an "immune deficiency" to outliers such as corrupted observations. We consider the following algorithmic question about the PCA with outliers. For a set of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$, how to learn a subset of points, say 1% of the total number of points, such that the remaining part of the points is best fit into some unknown $r$-dimensional subspace? We provide a rigorous algorithmic analysis of the problem. We show that the problem is solvable in time $n^{O(d^2)}$. In particular, for constant dimension the problem is solvable in polynomial time. We complement the algorithmic result by the lower bound, showing that unless Exponential Time Hypothesis fails, in time $f(d)n^{o(d)}$, for any function $f$ of $d$, it is impossible not only to solve the problem exactly but even to approximate it within a constant factor.

We complement the algorithmic result by the lower bound, showing that unless Exponential Time Hypothesis fails, in time $f(d)n^{o(d)}$, for any function $f$ of $d$, it is impossible not only to solve the problem exactly but even to approximate it within a constant factor.

paragraphs: Principal component analysis fits data with a lower-dimensional subspace, but corrupted observations can undermine that fit. This paper studies the computational problem of jointly identifying a subset of points to exclude and finding the best-fitting subspace for those that remain. Both the outlier selection and the subspace are unknown, so the task involves more than applying ordinary PCA after a supplied cleanup.

For n points in d dimensions, the authors give an algorithm with running time n raised to O(d squared). Consequently, when the ambient dimension is held constant, the problem can be solved in polynomial time. The dependence on dimension is central: the result establishes tractability for fixed dimension while allowing the polynomial exponent to grow with dimension.

The paper also gives a conditional lower bound under the Exponential Time Hypothesis. Unless that hypothesis fails, no algorithm running in f(d) times n raised to o(d), for any function f, can solve the problem exactly or even approximate it within a constant factor. Together, the bounds clarify the computational cost of outlier-resistant subspace fitting and the difficulty of substantially reducing its dimension dependence.
summary.tldr: PCA with outliers is polynomial-time solvable in fixed dimension, but a conditional lower bound rules out much faster dimension dependence even for constant-factor approximation.

title: Refined Complexity of PCA with Outliers

abstract: We present Zeno, a technique to make distributed machine learning, particularly Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), tolerant to an arbitrary number of faulty workers. Zeno generalizes previous results that assumed a majority of non-faulty nodes; we need assume only one non-faulty worker. Our key idea is to suspect workers that are potentially defective. Since this is likely to lead to false positives, we use a ranking-based preference mechanism. We prove the convergence of SGD for non-convex problems under these scenarios. Experimental results show that Zeno outperforms existing approaches.

Zeno generalizes previous results that assumed a majority of non-faulty nodes; we need assume only one non-faulty worker. Our key idea is to suspect workers that are potentially defective. Since this is likely to lead to false positives, we use a ranking-based preference mechanism. We prove the convergence of SGD for non-convex problems under these scenarios. Experimental results show that Zeno outperforms existing approaches.

paragraphs: Distributed training relies on multiple workers contributing to optimization, but some workers may be faulty. Zeno studies how stochastic gradient descent can continue under this kind of failure. Its central assumption is unusually permissive: it requires only one non-faulty worker, extending earlier results that assumed a majority of workers were reliable.

The method treats potentially defective workers with suspicion and uses a ranking-based preference mechanism. Ranking matters because suspicion can produce false positives, mistakenly treating a functioning worker as defective. The design explicitly accommodates that uncertainty when deciding which contributions to prefer, rather than relying on a reliable-worker majority as its starting assumption.

The authors prove convergence of SGD for nonconvex problems under the scenarios they consider and report experimental performance above existing approaches. The theoretical result concerns continued optimization despite extensive worker faults, while the experiments provide evidence of practical benefit in the tested comparisons. The one-good-worker assumption remains essential to how the stated tolerance claim should be understood.
summary.tldr: Zeno uses suspicion-based ranking to support convergent distributed SGD with faulty workers, assuming only one worker is non-faulty.

title: Zeno: Distributed Stochastic Gradient Descent with Suspicion-based Fault-tolerance

abstract: In this paper, we propose a new theoretical analysis of unsupervised domain adaptation that relates notions of large margin separation, adversarial learning and optimal transport. This analysis generalizes previous work on the subject by providing a bound on the target margin violation rate, thus reflecting a better control of the quality of separation between classes in the target domain than bounding the misclassification rate. The bound also highlights the benefit of a large margin separation on the source domain for adaptation and introduces an optimal transport (OT) based distance between domains that has the virtue of being task-dependent, contrary to other approaches. From the obtained theoretical results, we derive a novel algorithmic solution for domain adaptation that introduces a novel shallow OT-based adversarial approach and outperforms other OT-based DA baselines on several simulated and real-world classification tasks.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we propose a new theoretical analysis of unsupervised domain adaptation that relates notions of large margin separation, adversarial learning and optimal transport. This analysis generalizes previous work on the subject by providing a bound on the target margin violation rate, thus reflecting a better control of the quality of separation between classes in the target domain than bounding the misclassification rate. The bound also highlights the benefit of a large margin separation on the source domain for adaptation and introduces an optimal transport (OT) based distance between domains that has the virtue of being task-dependent, contrary to other approaches. From the obtained theoretical results, we derive a novel algorithmic solution for domain adaptation that introduces a novel shallow OT-based adversarial approach and outperforms other OT-based DA baselines on several simulated and real-world classification tasks.

paragraphs: Unsupervised domain adaptation seeks to transfer a classifier from a source domain to a target domain. This paper analyzes that transfer through class separation, adversarial learning, and optimal transport. Its focus is the margin: how well examples are separated between classes, beyond whether their predicted labels happen to be correct.

The authors derive a bound on the target domain's margin violation rate. This generalizes earlier work and provides control over the quality of target class separation. The bound highlights the benefit of strong separation in the source domain and introduces an optimal-transport distance between domains that depends on the classification task.

From this analysis, the authors derive a shallow adversarial adaptation algorithm based on optimal transport. It outperforms other optimal-transport adaptation baselines on several simulated and real-world classification tasks. The theoretical and empirical contributions align around the same idea: domain comparison should reflect the task and the separation between classes, so the adaptation procedure is guided by more than a bound on classification errors alone.
summary.tldr: A margin-based adaptation bound leads to a task-dependent optimal-transport algorithm that improves on tested transport-based baselines.

title: Margin-aware Adversarial Domain Adaptation with Optimal Transport

abstract: Many applications require sparse neural networks due to space or inference time restrictions. There is a large body of work on training dense networks to yield sparse networks for inference, but this limits the size of the largest trainable sparse model to that of the largest trainable dense model. In this paper we introduce a method to train sparse neural networks with a fixed parameter count and a fixed computational cost throughout training, without sacrificing accuracy relative to existing dense-to-sparse training methods. Our method updates the topology of the sparse network during training by using parameter magnitudes and infrequent gradient calculations. We show that this approach requires fewer floating-point operations (FLOPs) to achieve a given level of accuracy compared to prior techniques. We demonstrate state-of-the-art sparse training results on a variety of networks and datasets, including ResNet-50, MobileNets on Imagenet-2012, and RNNs on WikiText-103. Finally, we provide some insights into why allowing the topology to change during the optimization can overcome local minima encountered when the topology remains static.

There is a large body of work on training dense networks to yield sparse networks for inference, but this limits the size of the largest trainable sparse model to that of the largest trainable dense model. In this paper we introduce a method to train sparse neural networks with a fixed parameter count and a fixed computational cost throughout training, without sacrificing accuracy relative to existing dense-to-sparse training methods. Our method updates the topology of the sparse network during training by using parameter magnitudes and infrequent gradient calculations. We show that this approach requires fewer floating-point operations (FLOPs) to achieve a given level of accuracy compared to prior techniques. We demonstrate state-of-the-art sparse training results on a variety of networks and datasets, including ResNet-50, MobileNets on Imagenet-2012, and RNNs on WikiText-103. Finally, we provide some insights into why allowing the topology to change during the optimization can overcome local minima encountered when the topology remains static.

paragraphs: Sparse neural networks are useful when storage or inference time is constrained. A common route trains a dense network and then makes it sparse, but this requires enough resources to train the dense model first. That requirement limits how large a sparse model can be trained through the dense-to-sparse route.

The paper introduces a method that trains with a fixed parameter count and fixed computational cost while allowing the sparse network’s connectivity to change. It uses parameter magnitudes and occasional gradient calculations to update this topology. The network can therefore change which connections it uses during learning without increasing its parameter budget.

The authors report reaching a given accuracy with fewer floating-point operations than prior techniques, without sacrificing accuracy relative to existing dense-to-sparse methods. They demonstrate leading sparse-training results across ResNet-50, MobileNets, and recurrent networks on the stated image and language datasets. They also provide insight into how changing connectivity can overcome local minima encountered with a fixed topology, connecting the efficiency results to greater flexibility during optimization.
summary.tldr: Updating sparse network connectivity during training achieves strong accuracy with a fixed parameter budget and fewer floating-point operations than prior techniques.

title: Rigging the Lottery: Making All Tickets Winners

abstract: Learning a good representation is an essential component for deep reinforcement learning (RL). Representation learning is especially important in multitask and partially observable settings where building a representation of the unknown environment is crucial to solve the tasks. Here we introduce Predictions of Bootstrapped Latents (PBL), a simple and flexible self-supervised representation learning algorithm for multitask deep RL. PBL builds on multistep predictive representations of future observations, and focuses on capturing structured information about environment dynamics. Specifically, PBL trains its representation by predicting latent embeddings of future observations. These latent embeddings are themselves trained to be predictive of the aforementioned representations. These predictions form a bootstrapping effect, allowing the agent to learn more about the key aspects of the environment dynamics. In addition, by defining prediction tasks completely in latent space, PBL provides the flexibility of using multimodal observations involving pixel images, language instructions, rewards and more. We show in our experiments that PBL delivers across-the-board improved performance over state of the art deep RL agents in the DMLab-30 multitask setting.

The contribution also provides flexibility in observation types because its prediction tasks operate on learned embeddings.
summary.tldr: PBL learns mutually predictive latent representations of future observations, improving multitask reinforcement learning performance in DMLab-30.

title: Bootstrap Latent-Predictive Representations for Multitask Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Robust perception relies on both bottom-up and top-down signals. Bottom-up signals consist of what’s directly observed through sensation. Top-down signals consist of beliefs and expectations based on past experience and the current reportable short-term memory, such as how the phrase ‘peanut butter and ...’ will be completed. The optimal combination of bottom-up and top-down information remains an open question, but the manner of combination must be dynamic and both context and task dependent. To effectively utilize the wealth of potential top-down information available, and to prevent the cacophony of intermixed signals in a bidirectional architecture, mechanisms are needed to restrict information flow. We explore deep recurrent neural net architectures in which bottom-up and top-down signals are dynamically combined using attention. Modularity of the architecture further restricts the sharing and communication of information. Together, attention and modularity direct information flow, which leads to reliable performance improvements in perceptual and language tasks, and in particular improves robustness to distractions and noisy data. We demonstrate on a variety of benchmarks in language modeling, sequential image classification, video prediction and reinforcement learning that the \emph{bidirectional} information flow can improve results over strong baselines.

summary.tldr: Attention and modularity help recurrent networks combine observations with expectations, improving performance and robustness across the evaluated tasks.

title: Learning to Combine Top-Down and Bottom-Up Signals in Recurrent Neural Networks with Attention over Modules

abstract: \emph{Is there a classifier that ensures optimal robustness against all adversarial attacks?} This paper tackles this question by adopting a game-theoretic point of view. We present the adversarial attacks and defenses problem as an \emph{infinite} zero-sum game where classical results (\emph{e.g.} Nash or Sion theorems) do not apply. We demonstrate the non-existence of a Nash equilibrium in our game when the classifier and the Adversary are both deterministic, hence giving a negative answer to the above question in the deterministic regime. Nonetheless, the question remains open in the randomized regime. We tackle this problem by showing that any deterministic classifier can be outperformed by a randomized one. This gives arguments for using randomization, and leads us to a simple method for building randomized classifiers that are robust to state-or-the-art adversarial attacks. Empirical results validate our theoretical analysis, and show that our defense method considerably outperforms Adversarial Training against strong adaptive attacks, by achieving 0.55 accuracy under adaptive PGD-attack on CIFAR10, compared to 0.42 for Adversarial training.

They also show that any deterministic classifier can be outperformed by a randomized classifier within their framework. These results motivate a simple method for constructing randomized classifiers. summary.tldr: Game-theoretic analysis and adaptive-attack experiments support randomized defenses, while universal optimal robustness in the randomized regime remains unresolved.

title: Randomization matters How to defend against strong adversarial attacks

abstract: Conditional selective inference (SI) has been actively studied as a new statistical inference framework for data-driven hypotheses. The basic idea of conditional SI is to make inferences conditional on the selection event characterized by a set of linear and/or quadratic inequalities. Conditional SI has been mainly studied in the context of feature selection such as stepwise feature selection (SFS). The main limitation of the existing conditional SI methods is the loss of power due to over-conditioning, which is required for computational tractability. In this study, we develop a more powerful and general conditional SI method for SFS using the homotopy method which enables us to overcome this limitation. The homotopy-based SI is especially effective for more complicated feature selection algorithms. As an example, we develop a conditional SI method for forward-backward SFS with AIC-based stopping criteria and show that it is not adversely affected by the increased complexity of the algorithm. We conduct several experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed method.

paragraphs: When hypotheses arise from selecting features in data, statistical inference must account for that selection. Conditional selective inference does this by conditioning on the event that produced the chosen features. The paper focuses on stepwise feature selection, where this event can be described using linear or quadratic inequalities.

Existing approaches often condition on extra information to keep the calculations manageable. That over-conditioning reduces statistical power, weakening the ability to detect effects. The authors introduce a homotopy-based method that overcomes this limitation and supports more general selection procedures. Its purpose is to make the required conditional analysis tractable without the same loss of power.

As a concrete example, the paper develops inference for forward-backward stepwise selection with an AIC-based stopping rule. The authors show that their approach is not adversely affected by this procedure’s increased complexity, and experiments demonstrate effectiveness and efficiency. The contribution links computational technique to statistical usefulness: handling a richer selection process need not impose the same power penalty associated with earlier tractability choices.
summary.tldr: A homotopy-based selective-inference method reduces power loss from over-conditioning and handles more complex stepwise feature selection.

title: More Powerful and General Selective Inference for Stepwise Feature Selection using Homotopy Method

abstract: There has been much interest in recent years in developing learning algorithms that can learn accurate classifiers from data with noisy labels. A widely-studied noise model is that of \emph{class-conditional noise} (CCN), wherein a label $y$ is flipped to a label $\tilde{y}$ with some associated noise probability that depends on both $y$ and $\tilde{y}$. In the multiclass setting, all previously proposed algorithms under the CCN model involve changing the training process, by introducing a ‘noise-correction’ to the surrogate loss to be minimized over the noisy training examples. In this paper, we show that this is really unnecessary: one can simply perform class probability estimation (CPE) on the noisy examples, e.g. using a standard (multiclass) logistic regression algorithm, and then apply noise-correction only in the final prediction step. This means that the training algorithm itself does not need any change, and one can simply use standard off-the-shelf implementations with no modification to the code for training. Our approach can handle general multiclass loss matrices, including the usual 0-1 loss but also other losses such as those used for ordinal regression problems. We also provide a quantitative regret transfer bound, which bounds the target regret on the true distribution in terms of the CPE regret on the noisy distribution; in doing so, we extend the notion of strong properness introduced for binary losses by Agarwal (2014) to the multiclass case. Our bound suggests that the sample complexity of learning under CCN increases as the noise matrix approaches singularity. We also provide fixes and potential improvements for noise estimation methods that involve computing anchor points. Our experiments confirm our theoretical findings.

Their experiments support the theoretical findings.
summary.tldr: Under class-conditional label noise, standard probability-estimation training can be retained by applying noise correction only when making predictions.

title: Learning from Noisy Labels with No Change to the Training Process

abstract: The performance of Beta-Variational-Autoencoders and their variants on learning semantically meaningful, disentangled representations is unparalleled. On the other hand, there are theoretical arguments suggesting the impossibility of unsupervised disentanglement. In this work, we shed light on the inductive bias responsible for the success of VAE-based architectures. We show that in classical datasets the structure of variance, induced by the generating factors, is conveniently aligned with the latent directions fostered by the VAE objective. This builds the pivotal bias on which the disentangling abilities of VAEs rely. By small, elaborate perturbations of existing datasets, we hide the convenient correlation structure that is easily exploited by a variety of architectures. To demonstrate this, we construct modified versions of standard datasets in which (i) the generative factors are perfectly preserved; (ii) each image undergoes a mild transformation causing a small change of variance; (iii) the leading VAE-based disentanglement architectures fail to produce disentangled representations whilst the performance of a non-variational method remains unchanged.

paragraphs: Variational autoencoders can learn representations whose coordinates correspond to meaningful factors in data, despite theoretical arguments against unrestricted unsupervised disentanglement. This paper investigates the inductive bias behind that apparent tension. Its central finding is that, in classical datasets, variance created by the generating factors aligns conveniently with latent directions encouraged by the VAE objective.

The authors test this explanation by constructing carefully modified versions of standard datasets. The modifications preserve the generative factors perfectly while applying mild transformations to images that make small changes to variance. These changes hide the convenient correlation structure that VAE-based architectures would otherwise exploit, separating the presence of meaningful factors from the statistical arrangement that helps reveal them.

On the modified datasets, leading VAE-based disentanglement architectures fail to produce disentangled representations, while a non-variational method retains its performance. This supports the claim that favorable variance structure is pivotal to the observed VAE successes. It also shows why preserving a dataset's underlying factors does not necessarily preserve a particular model family's ability to discover them.
summary.tldr: Carefully altered datasets reveal how VAE disentanglement depends on favorable alignment between data variance and the training objective.

title: Demystifying Inductive Biases for (Beta-)VAE Based Architectures

abstract: As the computational requirements for machine learning systems and the size and complexity of machine learning frameworks increases, essential framework innovation has become challenging. While computational needs have driven recent compiler, networking, and hardware advancements, utilization of those advancements by machine learning tools is occurring at a slower pace. This is in part due to the difficulties involved in prototyping new computational paradigms with existing frameworks. Large frameworks prioritize machine learning researchers and practitioners as end users and pay comparatively little attention to systems researchers who can push frameworks forward — we argue that both are equally important stakeholders. We introduce Flashlight, an open-source library built to spur innovation in machine learning tools and systems by prioritizing open, modular, customizable internals and state-of-the-art, research-ready models and training setups across a variety of domains. Flashlight allows systems researchers to rapidly prototype and experiment with novel ideas in machine learning computation and has low overhead, competing with and often outperforming other popular machine learning frameworks. We see Flashlight as a tool enabling research that can benefit widely used libraries downstream and bring machine learning and systems researchers closer together.

Flashlight is an open-source library designed around that goal. It provides modular, customizable internals together with research-ready models and training setups across multiple domains. They position Flashlight as infrastructure for research whose results could later benefit widely used libraries. Its broader contribution is to connect framework experimentation with practical model training, helping systems and machine learning researchers work on shared computational problems.
summary.tldr: Flashlight pairs customizable framework internals with research-ready models to make machine learning systems experimentation easier and computationally competitive.

title: Flashlight: Enabling Innovation in Tools for Machine Learning

abstract: The word mover’s distance (WMD) is a fundamental technique for measuring the similarity of two documents. As the crux of WMD, it can take advantage of the underlying geometry of the word space by employing an optimal transport formulation. The original study on WMD reported that WMD outperforms classical baselines such as bag-of-words (BOW) and TF-IDF by significant margins in various datasets. In this paper, we point out that the evaluation in the original study could be misleading. We re-evaluate the performances of WMD and the classical baselines and find that the classical baselines are competitive with WMD if we employ an appropriate preprocessing, i.e., L1 normalization. In addition, we introduce an analogy between WMD and L1-normalized BOW and find that not only the performance of WMD but also the distance values resemble those of BOW in high dimensional spaces.

paragraphs: Word Mover’s Distance measures document similarity using an optimal transport formulation that incorporates the geometry of word representations. Its original evaluation reported substantial advantages over bag-of-words and TF-IDF. This paper revisits that comparison and asks whether the apparent advantage depends on how the classical baseline representations were preprocessed.

The authors find that bag-of-words and TF-IDF become competitive with Word Mover’s Distance when L1 normalization is applied appropriately. Normalization changes the scale of the document representations being compared, so it is part of the evaluation setup with meaningful consequences for the result. The finding challenges the interpretation of the original performance margins without asserting that Word Mover’s Distance never offers an advantage.

The paper also develops an analogy between Word Mover’s Distance and L1-normalized bag-of-words. In high-dimensional spaces, the resemblance extends beyond predictive performance to the distance values themselves. Together, these findings show that a geometry-aware document distance can behave more like a classical representation than its formulation might suggest, and that preprocessing must be considered when assessing the benefit of the more elaborate method.
summary.tldr: Appropriate L1 normalization makes classical document-similarity baselines competitive with Word Mover’s Distance in the paper’s re-evaluation.

title: Re-evaluating Word Mover’s Distance

abstract: We propose multirate training of neural networks: partitioning neural network parameters into "fast" and "slow" parts which are trained on different time scales, where slow parts are updated less frequently. By choosing appropriate partitionings we can obtain substantial computational speed-up for transfer learning tasks. We show for applications in vision and NLP that we can fine-tune deep neural networks in almost half the time, without reducing the generalization performance of the resulting models. We analyze the convergence properties of our multirate scheme and draw a comparison with vanilla SGD. We also discuss splitting choices for the neural network parameters which could enhance generalization performance when neural networks are trained from scratch. A multirate approach can be used to learn different features present in the data and as a form of regularization. Our paper unlocks the potential of using multirate techniques for neural network training and provides several starting points for future work in this area.

paragraphs: Standard training need not update every neural-network parameter at the same frequency. This paper divides parameters into fast and slow groups, with the slow group updated less often. The aim is to reduce computation by assigning different update schedules to different parts of a network, especially during transfer learning.

With suitable parameter partitions, the authors show that vision and language models can be fine-tuned in almost half the time without reducing their resulting generalization performance. They also analyze convergence and compare the multirate scheme with ordinary stochastic gradient descent. These results connect the practical speed improvement to a study of the underlying optimization procedure.

The paper additionally considers how parameter splits might improve generalization when training from scratch. It discusses multirate updates as a way to learn different features and as a form of regularization. Those possibilities broaden the motivation beyond speed, while the concrete reported timing result concerns transfer-learning applications and depends on choosing appropriate partitions.
summary.tldr: Updating different parameter groups at different frequencies nearly halves fine-tuning time in reported applications without reducing generalization.

title: Multirate Training of Neural Networks

abstract: This paper considers the learning of logical (Boolean) functions with focus on the generalization on the unseen (GOTU) setting, a strong case of out-of-distribution generalization. This is motivated by the fact that the rich combinatorial nature of data in certain reasoning tasks (e.g., arithmetic/logic) makes representative data sampling challenging, and learning successfully under GOTU gives a first vignette of an ’extrapolating’ or ’reasoning’ learner. We then study how different network architectures trained by (S)GD perform under GOTU and provide both theoretical and experimental evidence that for a class of network models including instances of Transformers, random features models, and diagonal linear networks, a min-degree-interpolator is learned on the unseen. We also provide evidence that other instances with larger learning rates or mean-field networks reach leaky min-degree solutions. These findings lead to two implications: (1) we provide an explanation to the length generalization problem (e.g., Anil et al. 2022); (2) we introduce a curriculum learning algorithm called Degree-Curriculum that learns monomials more efficiently by incrementing supports.

This paper studies generalization on the unseen, a strong out-of-distribution setting for Boolean functions. Success in this setting provides an initial view of extrapolation or reasoning when the training examples do not adequately represent the combinations encountered later.

The authors investigate networks trained with gradient descent or stochastic gradient descent. They provide theoretical and experimental evidence that certain instances of Transformers, random feature models, and diagonal linear networks learn minimum-degree interpolators on unseen inputs. This identifies a preference for particular low-degree solutions among functions compatible with the training data.

Other model instances, including some using larger learning rates or mean-field networks, show evidence of leaky minimum-degree solutions. The findings help explain length generalization and motivate Degree-Curriculum, which learns monomials more efficiently by progressively increasing their supports. The conclusions distinguish architecture and training settings, rather than claiming that every neural network exhibits the same extrapolation behavior.
summary.tldr: Evidence of low-degree extrapolation in certain networks motivates a curriculum that learns monomials by progressively increasing their supports.

title: Generalization on the Unseen, Logic Reasoning and Degree Curriculum

abstract: Hypersphere classification is a classical and foundational method that can provide easy-to-process explanations for the classification of real-valued as well as binary data. However, obtaining an (ideally concise) explanation via hypersphere classification is much more difficult when dealing with binary data as opposed to real-valued data. In this paper, we perform the first complexity-theoretic study of the hypersphere classification problem for binary data. We use the fine-grained parameterized complexity paradigm to analyze the impact of structural properties that may be present in the input data as well as potential conciseness constraints. Our results include not only stronger lower bounds but also a number of new fixed-parameter algorithms for hypersphere classification of binary data, which can find an exact and concise explanation when one exists.

However, obtaining an (ideally concise) explanation via hypersphere classification is much more difficult when dealing with binary data as opposed to real-valued data. In this paper, we perform the first complexity-theoretic study of the hypersphere classification problem for binary data. We use the fine-grained parameterized complexity paradigm to analyze the impact of structural properties that may be present in the input data as well as potential conciseness constraints. Our results include not only stronger lower bounds but also a number of new fixed-parameter algorithms for hypersphere classification of binary data, which can find an exact and concise explanation when one exists.

paragraphs: Hypersphere classification can express classification decisions through geometric regions, offering explanations that are easy to process. Finding a concise explanation is substantially harder for binary data than for real-valued data. This paper investigates that difficulty through a complexity-theoretic study focused on binary inputs.

The analysis uses fine-grained parameterized complexity to separate the effects of different aspects of the problem. It considers structural properties in the data alongside restrictions on how concise the explanation must be. This perspective asks which features of an instance drive computational difficulty and which can support more efficient exact methods.

The results include stronger lower bounds and new fixed-parameter algorithms. The lower bounds sharpen the understanding of computational barriers, while the algorithms can find an exact, concise explanation when one exists. These contributions give a more differentiated account than treating all binary classification instances as equally difficult. They connect the demand for understandable explanations to the structure that makes finding those explanations algorithmically feasible under suitable parameterizations.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes computational barriers and fixed-parameter algorithms for finding exact, concise hypersphere explanations of binary data.

title: The Computational Complexity of Concise Hypersphere Classification

abstract: We investigate the extent to which offline demonstration data can improve online learning. It is natural to expect some improvement, but the question is how, and by how much? We show that the degree of improvement must depend on the quality of the demonstration data. To generate portable insights, we focus on Thompson sampling (TS) applied to a multi-armed bandit as a prototypical online learning algorithm and model. The demonstration data is generated by an expert with a given competence level, a notion we introduce. We propose an informed TS algorithm that utilizes the demonstration data in a coherent way through Bayes’ rule and derive a prior-dependent Bayesian regret bound. This offers insight into how pretraining can greatly improve online performance and how the degree of improvement increases with the expert’s competence level. We also develop a practical, approximate informed TS algorithm through Bayesian bootstrapping and show substantial empirical regret reduction through experiments.

Their informed Thompson sampling algorithm incorporates the demonstrations through Bayes’ rule. This provides a coherent way to let prior observations shape online decisions. The theoretical and empirical contributions together explain why demonstrations should be evaluated by their quality as well as their availability, with the formal analysis grounded in the stated bandit and expert-competence model.
summary.tldr: An informed Thompson sampling method uses demonstrations through Bayesian updating, with benefits that increase with expert competence.

title: Leveraging Demonstrations to Improve Online Learning: Quality Matters

abstract: We analyze the Nyström approximation of a positive definite kernel associated with a probability measure. We first prove an improved error bound for the conventional Nyström approximation with i.i.d. sampling and singular-value decomposition in the continuous regime; the proof techniques are borrowed from statistical learning theory. We further introduce a refined selection of subspaces in Nyström approximation with theoretical guarantees that is applicable to non-i.i.d. landmark points. Finally, we discuss their application to convex kernel quadrature and give novel theoretical guarantees as well as numerical observations.

Finally, we discuss their application to convex kernel quadrature and give novel theoretical guarantees as well as numerical observations.

paragraphs: Nyström approximation represents a kernel using selected landmark points and an associated lower-dimensional subspace. This paper analyzes the approximation of a positive definite kernel tied to a probability measure. Its focus is on understanding approximation error and improving how the representing subspace is selected, including when landmark sampling differs from the conventional independent setup.

The first result improves the error bound for conventional Nyström approximation using independently sampled landmarks and singular-value decomposition in the continuous setting. The proof draws on statistical learning theory. The authors then introduce a refined subspace-selection method with theoretical guarantees that also apply to landmark points that are not independently and identically distributed.

Finally, the paper connects these approximation results to convex kernel quadrature, where kernel methods support numerical integration. It supplies new theoretical guarantees for that application alongside numerical observations. The contribution links two questions: how accurately sampled landmarks represent a kernel, and how that representation can support integration. Its guarantees extend the analysis beyond one standard sampling arrangement without claiming unrestricted accuracy for every landmark choice.
summary.tldr: The paper strengthens Nyström error guarantees, refines subspace selection for non-i.i.d. landmarks, and applies the results to kernel quadrature.

title: Sampling-based Nyström Approximation and Kernel Quadrature

abstract: Identifying prognostic genes associated with patient survival is an important goal in cancer genomics, as this information could inform treatment approaches and improve patient outcomes. However, the identification of prognostic genes is complicated by the high dimensionality of genetic data, which makes their identification computationally intensive. Furthermore, most cancer genomics studies lack appropriate low-risk groups against which to compare. To address these issues, we present a framework that identifies candidate prognostic genes by integrating representation learning and statistical analysis approaches. Specifically, we propose a collaborative filtering-derived mechanism to represent patients in order of their survival risk, facilitating their dichotomization. We also propose a mechanism that allows embedded gene vectors to be polarized on the extremities of, or centered on, both reference axes to facilitate recommendations. Restricting our analysis to a few representative genes within each cluster allowed for the efficient identification of prognostic genes. Finally, we demonstrate the potential of this proposed framework for identifying prognostic genes.

paragraphs: Finding genes associated with cancer-patient survival can help identify candidates with prognostic value. The task is difficult because genetic datasets have many dimensions and studies often lack an appropriate low-risk comparison group. SurProGenes combines representation learning and statistical analysis to make candidate-gene identification more manageable.

The framework uses a mechanism derived from collaborative filtering to represent patients in an order reflecting survival risk. This ordering supports dividing patients into two groups for comparison. A second mechanism organizes embedded gene vectors toward the ends or centers of reference axes to facilitate recommendations. The learned representations therefore serve both patient grouping and the organization of gene candidates.

To reduce the amount of analysis, the method examines a few representative genes from each cluster. This focuses statistical work on a smaller collection while using the broader representation to organize the search. The authors demonstrate the framework’s potential for identifying prognostic genes. The stated outcome concerns candidate identification and efficient analysis, with possible treatment relevance motivating the work rather than constituting a demonstrated clinical benefit.
summary.tldr: SurProGenes organizes patients by survival risk and genes into learned groups to support efficient identification of candidate prognostic genes.

title: SurProGenes: Survival Risk-Ordered Representation of Cancer Patients and Genes for the Identification of Prognostic Genes

abstract: Text-to-audio (TTA) systems have recently gained attention for their ability to synthesize general audio based on text descriptions. However, previous studies in TTA have limited generation quality with high computational costs. In this study, we propose AudioLDM, a TTA system that is built on a latent space to learn continuous audio representations from contrastive language-audio pretraining (CLAP) embeddings. The pretrained CLAP models enable us to train LDMs with audio embeddings while providing text embeddings as the condition during sampling. By learning the latent representations of audio signals without modelling the cross-modal relationship, AudioLDM improves both generation quality and computational efficiency. Trained on AudioCaps with a single GPU, AudioLDM achieves state-of-the-art TTA performance compared to other open-sourced systems, measured by both objective and subjective metrics. AudioLDM is also the first TTA system that enables various text-guided audio manipulations (e.g., style transfer) in a zero-shot fashion. Our implementation and demos are available at https://audioldm.github.io.

Its central choice is to learn audio generation in a continuous latent representation. The system uses embeddings supplied by pretrained contrastive language-audio models, called CLAP, to connect the representations available during training and generation.

This connection allows the latent diffusion model to train using audio embeddings and then receive text embeddings as its condition when generating samples. These findings show that the approach supports both generating audio from descriptions and modifying audio through textual guidance.
summary.tldr: AudioLDM uses pretrained language-audio embeddings and latent diffusion to generate and manipulate audio efficiently from text.

title: AudioLDM: Text-to-Audio Generation with Latent Diffusion Models

abstract: To improve the efficiency and sustainability of learning deep models, we propose CREST, the first scalable framework with rigorous theoretical guarantees to identify the most valuable examples for training non-convex models, particularly deep networks. To guarantee convergence to a stationary point of a non-convex function, CREST models the non-convex loss as a series of quadratic functions and extracts a coreset for each quadratic sub-region. In addition, to ensure faster convergence of stochastic gradient methods such as (mini-batch) SGD, CREST iteratively extracts multiple mini-batch coresets from larger random subsets of training data, to ensure nearly-unbiased gradients with small variances. Finally, to further improve scalability and efficiency, CREST identifies and excludes the examples that are learned from the coreset selection pipeline. Our extensive experiments on several deep networks trained on vision and NLP datasets, including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, TinyImageNet, and SNLI, confirm that CREST speeds up training deep networks on very large datasets, by 1.7x to 2.5x with minimum loss in the performance. By analyzing the learning difficulty of the subsets selected by CREST, we show that deep models benefit the most by learning from subsets of increasing difficulty levels.

paragraphs: CREST seeks to reduce deep-network training costs by selecting the examples most useful for learning. It constructs coresets, or selected training subsets, for nonconvex models. The framework models the loss through a sequence of quadratic functions and selects a coreset within each quadratic sub-region to support convergence to a stationary point.

For stochastic training, CREST repeatedly selects multiple mini-batch coresets from larger random subsets. This aims to provide nearly unbiased gradients with low variance, supporting faster convergence. It further reduces selection overhead by identifying examples already learned and excluding them from the coreset-selection pipeline, so selection effort changes as training progresses.

Experiments across vision and language datasets report training speedups of 1.7 to 2.5 times with minimal performance loss. The tested datasets include CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, TinyImageNet, and SNLI. Analysis of selected examples also finds that the models benefit most from subsets of increasing difficulty, connecting the efficiency gains with how useful training data changes over learning.
summary.tldr: CREST selects changing training subsets with convergence guarantees and achieves reported deep-network training speedups of 1.7 to 2.5 times.

title: Towards Sustainable Learning: Coresets for Data-efficient Deep Learning

abstract: The successes of modern deep machine learning methods are founded on their ability to transform inputs across multiple layers to build good high-level representations. It is therefore critical to understand this process of representation learning. However, standard theoretical approaches (formally NNGPs) involving infinite width limits eliminate representation learning. We therefore develop a new infinite width limit, the Bayesian representation learning limit, that exhibits representation learning mirroring that in finite-width models, yet at the same time, retains some of the simplicity of standard infinite-width limits. In particular, we show that Deep Gaussian processes (DGPs) in the Bayesian representation learning limit have exactly multivariate Gaussian posteriors, and the posterior covariances can be obtained by optimizing an interpretable objective combining a log-likelihood to improve performance with a series of KL-divergences which keep the posteriors close to the prior. We confirm these results experimentally in wide but finite DGPs. Next, we introduce the possibility of using this limit and objective as a flexible, deep generalisation of kernel methods, that we call deep kernel machines (DKMs). Like most naive kernel methods, DKMs scale cubically in the number of datapoints. We therefore use methods from the Gaussian process inducing point literature to develop a sparse DKM that scales linearly in the number of datapoints. Finally, we extend these approaches to NNs (which have non-Gaussian posteriors) in the Appendices.

Yet standard infinite-width theories remove this learning of representations, making them a poor fit for explaining that part of deep learning. This paper develops a different infinite-width limit that retains representation learning resembling finite-width models while preserving some mathematical simplicity.

For deep Gaussian processes, the new limit produces exactly multivariate Gaussian posterior distributions. Their covariances come from optimizing an interpretable objective: a likelihood term rewards predictive performance, while a sequence of divergence terms discourages departures from the prior. Experiments with wide but finite deep Gaussian processes support these theoretical results.

The authors also turn this framework into deep kernel machines, a flexible extension of kernel methods with multiple learned representation stages. The straightforward version has computational cost growing cubically with dataset size. A sparse version uses inducing-point techniques to make that dependence linear. Extensions to neural networks are also presented, although their posterior distributions are not Gaussian.
summary.tldr: A new infinite-width theory preserves representation learning and leads to deep kernel machines with a scalable sparse variant.

title: A theory of representation learning gives a deep generalisation of kernel methods

abstract: Disentangling the factors of variation in data is a fundamental concept in machine learning and has been studied in various ways by different researchers, leading to a multitude of definitions. Despite the numerous empirical studies, more theoretical research is needed to fully understand the defining properties of disentanglement and how different definitions relate to each other. This paper presents a meta-analysis of existing definitions of disentanglement, using category theory as a unifying and rigorous framework. We propose that the concepts of the cartesian and monoidal products should serve as the core of disentanglement. With these core concepts, we show the similarities and crucial differences in dealing with (i) functions, (ii) equivariant maps, (iii) relations, and (iv) stochastic maps. Overall, our meta-analysis deepens our understanding of disentanglement and its various formulations and can help researchers navigate different definitions and choose the most appropriate one for their specific context.

paragraphs: Disentanglement concerns separating the factors that account for variation in data. Researchers have formalized this idea in many ways, making it difficult to tell whether two definitions describe the same property or impose different requirements. This paper examines those definitions together, using category theory to give their comparison a shared mathematical language.

The authors propose cartesian and monoidal products as central concepts for describing disentanglement. These provide ways to express how separate components combine into a larger structure. The analysis then distinguishes four settings: functions, equivariant maps, relations, and stochastic maps. Examining each setting within the same framework exposes both common structure and consequential differences between formulations.

The contribution is conceptual: it clarifies what different definitions commit a researcher to when describing a representation as disentangled. The authors argue that this comparison can help researchers choose a definition suited to their context. Their proposal supplies a framework for navigating existing formulations rather than establishing one universally appropriate definition for every application.
summary.tldr: A category-theoretic framework clarifies the shared structure and important differences among definitions of disentanglement.

title: A Category-theoretical Meta-analysis of Definitions of Disentanglement

abstract: The non-clairvoyant scheduling problem has gained new interest within learning-augmented algorithms, where the decision-maker is equipped with predictions without any quality guarantees. In practical settings, access to predictions may be reduced to specific instances, due to cost or data limitations. Our investigation focuses on scenarios where predictions for only $B$ job sizes out of $n$ are available to the algorithm. We first establish near-optimal lower bounds and algorithms in the case of perfect predictions. Subsequently, we present a learning-augmented algorithm satisfying the robustness, consistency, and smoothness criteria, and revealing a novel tradeoff between consistency and smoothness inherent in the scenario with a restricted number of predictions.

paragraphs: Non-clairvoyant scheduling concerns decisions made without knowing job sizes in advance. Predictions can help, but obtaining them may be costly or impossible for some jobs. This paper studies a restricted-information setting in which the scheduling algorithm receives size predictions for only B of its n jobs, rather than assuming predictions are available throughout the workload.

The authors first analyze perfect predictions for that limited subset. They establish lower bounds and algorithms that are near-optimal in this setting. This separates the consequences of incomplete prediction coverage from the consequences of inaccurate predictions: even correct information is available for only part of the scheduling problem.

They then introduce a learning-augmented algorithm with robustness, consistency, and smoothness guarantees. These criteria concern protection when predictions are poor, performance when they are accurate, and how performance changes as prediction quality worsens. The analysis reveals a tradeoff between consistency and smoothness when prediction coverage is restricted. The result shows that designing for partial access requires balancing distinct benefits of prediction, beyond merely accounting for prediction errors.
summary.tldr: Scheduling with predictions for only some jobs admits near-optimal guarantees and exposes a tradeoff between consistency and smoothness.

title: Non-clairvoyant Scheduling with Partial Predictions

abstract: We address the challenge of utilizing large language models (LLMs) for complex embodied tasks, in the environment where decision-making systems operate timely on capacity-limited, off-the-shelf devices. We present DeDer, a framework for decomposing and distilling the embodied reasoning capabilities from LLMs to efficient, small language model (sLM)-based policies. In DeDer, the decision-making process of LLM-based strategies is restructured into a hierarchy with a reasoning-policy and planning-policy. The reasoning-policy is distilled from the data that is generated through the embodied in-context learning and self-verification of an LLM, so it can produce effective rationales. The planning-policy, guided by the rationales, can render optimized plans efficiently. In turn, DeDer allows for adopting sLMs for both policies, deployed on off-the-shelf devices. Furthermore, to enhance the quality of intermediate rationales, specific to embodied tasks, we devise the embodied knowledge graph, and to generate multiple rationales timely through a single inference, we also use the contrastively prompted attention model. Our experiments with the ALFRED benchmark demonstrate that DeDer surpasses leading language planning and distillation approaches, indicating the applicability and efficiency of sLM-based embodied policies derived through DeDer.

paragraphs: Embodied agents need to make timely decisions while operating on devices with limited capacity. DeDer addresses this by transferring reasoning capabilities from a large language model into policies built with small language models. The aim is to make complex task planning practical on ordinary devices while retaining useful reasoning from the larger model.

The framework separates decision-making into a reasoning policy and a planning policy. The reasoning policy learns from data produced through an LLM’s embodied in-context learning and self-verification, and generates rationales. The planning policy uses those rationales to produce plans efficiently. Small language models can implement both parts of this hierarchy.

DeDer also introduces an embodied knowledge graph to improve intermediate rationales and uses a contrastively prompted attention model to generate multiple rationales in one inference. On the ALFRED benchmark, it surpasses leading language-planning and distillation approaches. These experiments support the applicability and efficiency of its distilled policies, showing how separating reasoning from planning can help bring LLM-derived capabilities to smaller systems.
summary.tldr: DeDer distills LLM reasoning into small reasoning and planning policies for efficient embodied agents on ordinary devices.

title: Embodied CoT Distillation From LLM To Off-the-shelf Agents

abstract: One of the biggest challenges to modern deep reinforcement learning (DRL) algorithms is sample efficiency. Many approaches learn a world model in order to train an agent entirely in imagination, eliminating the need for direct environment interaction during training. However, these methods often suffer from either a lack of imagination accuracy, exploration capabilities, or runtime efficiency. We propose HIEROS, a hierarchical policy that learns time abstracted world representations and imagines trajectories at multiple time scales in latent space. HIEROS uses an S5 layer-based world model, which predicts next world states in parallel during training and iteratively during environment interaction. Due to the special properties of S5 layers, our method can train in parallel and predict next world states iteratively during imagination. This allows for more efficient training than RNN-based world models and more efficient imagination than Transformer-based world models. We show that our approach outperforms the state of the art in terms of mean and median normalized human score on the Atari 100k benchmark, and that our proposed world model is able to predict complex dynamics very accurately. We also show that HIEROS displays superior exploration capabilities compared to existing approaches.

paragraphs: World-model reinforcement learning uses learned predictions of the environment to train an agent through imagined experience. Its usefulness depends on accurate predictions, effective exploration, and manageable computation. HIEROS addresses these concerns with a hierarchical policy that learns representations at different temporal scales and imagines trajectories within a latent space.

The world model uses S5 layers, which support parallel prediction during training and iterative prediction during interaction and imagination. This combination matters because learning from sequences and generating future steps have different computational needs. The authors report more efficient training than recurrent-network world models and more efficient imagination than Transformer-based world models.

The hierarchy allows imagined behavior to be considered at multiple time scales, alongside the sequence model’s computational design. On Atari 100k, HIEROS exceeds the reported state of the art in both mean and median normalized human score. The authors also report accurate prediction of complex dynamics and stronger exploration than existing approaches. These findings support the combined architecture in the evaluated reinforcement-learning setting.
summary.tldr: HIEROS combines hierarchical imagination with an S5 world model to improve computational efficiency, exploration, and reported Atari 100k performance.

title: Hieros: Hierarchical Imagination on Structured State Space Sequence World Models

abstract: In this position paper, we argue that application-driven research has been systemically under-valued in the machine learning community. As applications of machine learning proliferate, innovative algorithms inspired by specific real-world challenges have become increasingly important. Such work offers the potential for significant impact not merely in domains of application but also in machine learning itself. In this paper, we describe the paradigm of application-driven research in machine learning, contrasting it with the more standard paradigm of methods-driven research. We illustrate the benefits of application-driven machine learning and how this approach can productively synergize with methods-driven work. Despite these benefits, we find that reviewing, hiring, and teaching practices in machine learning often hold back application-driven innovation. We outline how these processes may be improved.

Its central point is that a real-world challenge can inspire algorithmic innovation with significance beyond the original application. As machine learning spreads into more domains, the authors regard this source of new ideas as increasingly important to the field itself.

The paper describes application-driven research and compares it with the more conventional practice of starting from a method. It emphasizes that the two approaches can strengthen one another. Under this view, solving an application problem can contribute to machine-learning methodology, while methods research can supply ideas that help address the application’s demands.

The authors also identify reviewing, hiring, and teaching practices as obstacles to application-driven innovation and outline improvements to those processes. The contribution is an argument about research priorities and institutional evaluation, supported by an account of the approach’s benefits. It asks the community to recognize potential methodological contributions arising from applications, rather than judging their value only within the application domain.
summary.tldr: The authors argue that application-driven research can advance machine learning itself and deserves stronger support in evaluation, hiring, and teaching.

title: Position: Application-Driven Innovation in Machine Learning

abstract: Implicit Neural Representations (INRs) have gained popularity for encoding signals as compact, differentiable entities. While commonly using techniques like Fourier positional encodings or non-traditional activation functions (e.g., Gaussian, sinusoid, or wavelets) to capture high-frequency content, their properties lack exploration within a unified theoretical framework. Addressing this gap, we conduct a comprehensive analysis of these activations from a sampling theory perspective. Our investigation reveals that, especially in shallow INRs, $\mathrm{sinc}$ activations—previously unused in conjunction with INRs—are theoretically optimal for signal encoding. Additionally, we establish a connection between dynamical systems and INRs, leveraging sampling theory to bridge these two paradigms.

title: A sampling theory perspective on activations for implicit neural representations

abstract: Forecasting of Irregular Multivariate Time Series (IMTS) is critical for numerous areas, such as healthcare, biomechanics, climate science, and astronomy. Despite existing research addressing irregularities in time series through ordinary differential equations, the challenge of modeling correlations between asynchronous IMTS remains underexplored. To bridge this gap, this study proposes Transformable Patching Graph Neural Networks (t-PatchGNN), which transforms each univariate irregular time series into a series of transformable patches encompassing a varying number of observations with uniform temporal resolution. It seamlessly facilitates local semantics capture and inter-time series correlation modeling while avoiding sequence length explosion in aligned IMTS. Building on the aligned patching outcomes, we then present time-adaptive graph neural networks to model dynamic intertime series correlation based on a series of learned time-varying adaptive graphs. We demonstrate the remarkable superiority of t-PatchGNN on a comprehensive IMTS forecasting benchmark we build, which contains four real-world scientific datasets covering healthcare, biomechanics and climate science, and seventeen competitive baselines adapted from relevant research fields.

paragraphs: Irregular multivariate time series contain several signals observed at uneven and potentially different times. Forecasting them requires handling both irregular timing and relationships among asynchronous signals. This paper focuses on the latter challenge, which the authors identify as underexplored in existing approaches to irregular time series.

The proposed t-PatchGNN groups each individual signal into transformable patches. Patches share a uniform temporal resolution but can contain different numbers of observations. This provides an aligned representation for capturing local patterns and relationships across signals without the sequence-length explosion associated with aligning individual observations. Time-adaptive graph neural networks then model changing relationships using learned graphs that vary over time.

The authors also assemble a forecasting benchmark containing four real-world scientific datasets from healthcare, biomechanics, and climate science. They compare against seventeen competitive baselines adapted from related research areas and report strong superiority. The results support combining temporal patch alignment with changing graph connections to represent both the local content of each signal and its evolving relationships with other signals.
summary.tldr: t-PatchGNN aligns irregular signals through flexible temporal patches and learns changing graph relationships to improve forecasting.

title: Irregular Multivariate Time Series Forecasting: A Transformable Patching Graph Neural Networks Approach

abstract: Optimization with orthogonality constraints frequently arises in various fields such as machine learning. Riemannian optimization offers a powerful framework for solving these problems by equipping the constraint set with a Riemannian manifold structure and performing optimization intrinsically on the manifold. This approach typically involves computing a search direction in the tangent space and updating variables via a retraction operation. However, as the size of the variables increases, the computational cost of the retraction can become prohibitively high, limiting the applicability of Riemannian optimization to large-scale problems. To address this challenge and enhance scalability, we propose a novel approach that restricts each update on a random submanifold, thereby significantly reducing the per-iteration complexity. We introduce two sampling strategies for selecting the random submanifolds and theoretically analyze the convergence of the proposed methods. We provide convergence results for general nonconvex functions and functions that satisfy Riemannian Polyak–{Ł}ojasiewicz condition as well as for stochastic optimization settings. Additionally, we demonstrate how our approach can be generalized to quotient manifolds derived from the orthogonal manifold. Extensive experiments verify the benefits of the proposed method, across a wide variety of problems.

Riemannian optimization handles these constraints by treating valid solutions as a geometric space and moving within that space. A standard update computes a direction in a tangent space and then uses a retraction to produce another valid point. For large variables, that retraction can become expensive.

The authors reduce this cost by restricting each update to a randomly selected submanifold, a smaller part of the constraint geometry. They introduce two ways to sample these submanifolds. The central computational benefit is lower complexity per iteration, making individual updates less costly while retaining an optimization method built around the constraint.

It also extends the approach to quotient manifolds derived from the orthogonal manifold. Experiments across varied problems support its practical benefits. Together, the analysis and evaluations show how smaller randomized geometric updates can improve scalability under the settings studied.
summary.tldr: Randomly restricting updates to smaller submanifolds lowers iteration costs for orthogonality-constrained optimization, with convergence results across several settings.

title: Efficient Optimization with Orthogonality Constraint: a Randomized Riemannian Submanifold Method

abstract: Protein Language Models (PLMs), pre-trained on extensive evolutionary data from natural proteins, have emerged as indispensable tools for protein design. While powerful, PLMs often struggle to produce proteins with precisely specified functionalities or properties due to inherent challenges in controlling their outputs. In this work, we investigate the potential of Activation Steering, a technique originally developed for controlling text generation in Large Language Models (LLMs), to direct PLMs toward generating protein sequences with targeted properties. We propose a simple yet effective method that employs activation editing to steer PLM outputs, and extend this approach to protein optimization through a novel editing site identification module. Through comprehensive experiments on lysozyme-like sequence generation and optimization, we demonstrate that our methods can be seamlessly integrated into both auto-encoding and autoregressive PLMs without requiring additional training. These results highlight a promising direction for precise protein engineering using foundation models. Code is available at https://github.com/Long-Kai/Steering-PLMs.

paragraphs: Protein language models learn from large collections of natural protein sequences, but directing them toward precisely specified properties remains challenging. This paper investigates activation steering as a way to control their outputs. The technique adapts an approach developed for text language models to the generation and optimization of protein sequences.

The proposed method edits internal activations to steer the model toward targeted properties. The authors also extend the approach to protein optimization through a module that identifies editing sites. This adds a mechanism for deciding where edits should be directed when using the model to improve a protein sequence.

Experiments focus on generating and optimizing lysozyme-like sequences. The authors demonstrate integration with both auto-encoding and autoregressive protein language models without additional training. That compatibility matters because the control mechanism can be applied across these two model families without retraining them for the steering procedure. The stated results present activation editing as a promising route toward more precise protein engineering, with the empirical evidence centered on the sequence tasks studied.
summary.tldr: Activation editing steers protein language models toward targeted properties and supports sequence optimization without additional training.

title: Steering Protein Language Models

abstract: Effective search methods are crucial for improving the performance of deep generative models at test time. In this paper, we introduce a novel test-time search method, Neural Genetic Search (NGS), which incorporates the evolutionary mechanism of genetic algorithms into the generation procedure of deep models. The core idea behind NGS is its crossover, which is defined as parent-conditioned generation using trained generative models. This approach offers a versatile and easy-to-implement search algorithm for deep generative models. We demonstrate the effectiveness and flexibility of NGS through experiments across three distinct domains: routing problems, adversarial prompt generation for language models, and molecular design.
