paragraphs: Generalized zero-shot learning must recognize both categories seen during training and categories absent from training. Models often favor familiar categories when these groups appear together at test time. PUFE addresses this bias by treating inference as a positive-unlabeled learning problem, with seen categories supplying positives and the mixed test data remaining unlabeled.

The framework builds a classifier in semantic space using a network with two output heads. Maximum likelihood estimation jointly learns the probability of belonging to a seen class and the propensity for labeling. The classifier then identifies high-confidence pseudo-instances, which guide adaptive calibration of semantic prototypes so that those prototypes better match the underlying test distribution.

PUFE operates as a plug-and-play post-processing framework and improves diverse generalized zero-shot learning baselines across multiple architectural families. Experiments report gains of up to 11.2 percentage points in harmonic mean performance. The results support combining an explicit estimate of seen-class membership with prototype adjustment to reduce the imbalance between recognition of familiar and unfamiliar categories.
summary.tldr: PUFE reduces seen-class bias in generalized zero-shot learning through positive-unlabeled classification and adaptive semantic-prototype calibration.

title: When Generalized Zero-Shot Learning Meets PU Learning: A Plug-and-Play Framework for Seen-Class Bias Mitigation

abstract: Protein language models (pLMs) have emerged as powerful predictors of protein structure and function. However, the computational circuits underlying their predictions remain poorly understood. Recent mechanistic interpretability methods decompose pLM representations into interpretable features, but they treat each layer independently and thus fail to capture cross-layer computation, limiting their ability to approximate the full model. We introduce ProtoMech, a framework for discovering computational circuits in pLMs using cross-layer transcoders that learn sparse latent representations jointly across layers to capture the model’s full computational circuitry. Applied to the pLM ESM2, ProtoMech recovers 82–89% of the original performance on protein family classification and function prediction tasks. ProtoMech then identifies compressed circuits that use $<$1% of the latent space while retaining up to 79% of model accuracy, revealing correspondence with structural and functional motifs, including binding, signaling, and stability. Steering along these circuits enables high-fitness protein design, surpassing baseline methods in more than 70% of cases. These results establish ProtoMech as a principled framework for protein circuit tracing.

Interpreting each layer independently can reveal features without explaining how information moves through the network. title: Protein Circuit Tracing via Cross-layer Transcoders

abstract: Emotional expression in human speech is nuanced and compositional, often involving multiple, sometimes conflicting, affective cues that may diverge from linguistic content. In contrast, most expressive text-to-speech (TTS) systems enforce a single utterance-level emotion, collapsing affective diversity and suppressing mixed or text–emotion–misaligned expression. While activation steering via latent direction vectors offers a promising solution, it remains unclear whether emotion representations are linearly steerable in TTS, where steering should be applied within hybrid TTS architectures, and how such complex emotion behaviors should be evaluated. This paper presents the first systematic analysis of activation steering for emotional control in hybrid TTS models, introducing a quantitative, controllable steering framework, and multi-rater evaluation protocols that enable composable mixed-emotion synthesis and reliable text–emotion mismatch synthesis. Our results demonstrate, for the first time, that emotional prosody and expressive variability are primarily synthesized by the TTS language module instead of the flow-matching module, and also provide a lightweight steering approach for generating natural, human-like emotional speech.

paragraphs: Human speech can convey several emotions at once, and its emotional delivery can differ from the literal meaning of the words. Many expressive text-to-speech systems instead assign one emotion to an entire utterance. CoCoEmo investigates how steering a model’s internal activations can give speech synthesis more flexible and composable emotional control.

The paper systematically studies activation steering in hybrid text-to-speech architectures. It examines whether internal emotion representations can be adjusted through direction vectors and where those adjustments should occur. The proposed framework makes steering quantitatively controllable and introduces evaluation protocols involving multiple raters. These protocols assess mixed emotions and cases where the spoken emotion intentionally diverges from the text’s emotional content.

The results attribute emotional prosody and expressive variation primarily to the language module in the studied systems, rather than the flow-matching module. This finding helps identify where emotional control should be applied. The work also provides a lightweight steering approach for natural, human-like emotional speech, supporting mixtures and mismatches that a single utterance-level emotion label would suppress.
summary.tldr: CoCoEmo steers internal TTS activations to compose emotions and control delivery even when it differs from the text’s emotional content.

title: CoCoEmo: Composable and Controllable Human-Like Emotional TTS via Activation Steering

abstract: Transfer across diverse task compositions and unseen behaviors remains a significant challenge for vision-language action (VLA) models. Skills are repeatable and atomic components for various tasks, and similarities shared with different skills provide evidence for transferability across behaviors. However, existing skill-centric methods have two problems. First, skills are often loosely organized, lacking a hierarchy that can capture similarities and differences across skills. Second, they lack a mechanism which has the capacity to express transferable skill attributes in a structured parametric space. To this end, we propose SkillNet, which models skill attributes in a hierarchical way and regulates compositional model structure with transferable skill attributes. SkillNet exploits motion code and VerbNet Framework to explicitly model similarities of skills on mechanical properties and semantic roles, and organizes skills in a hierarchical way. Based on this hierarchy, SkillNet leverages the scalability of the mixture-of-experts (MoE) mechanism and develops skill embeddings as soft constraints to enable compositional generalization via similar expert activations on similar skills. On zero-shot and few-shot transfer experiments in simulators and real-world environments, SkillNet achieves an improvement of performance by 16.0% and 23.9%. Meanwhile, SkillNet achieves state-of-the-art performance on in-domain settings.

paragraphs: SkillNet addresses transfer to unfamiliar behaviors and new combinations of tasks in vision-language action models. Its starting point is that repeatable, atomic skills share useful attributes. Existing skill-based approaches can leave those relationships loosely organized and lack a structured parameter representation through which shared attributes influence transfer.

SkillNet also reaches state-of-the-art performance in the in-domain settings. The findings support connecting an explicit organization of skill relationships to expert activation as a route toward learning behaviors that can be recombined and transferred.
summary.tldr: SkillNet organizes skills hierarchically and guides expert activation with shared attributes to improve compositional action transfer.

title: SkillNet: Hierarchical Skill Modeling for Compositional Generalization in Vision-Language Action Models

abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has become a cornerstone for improving the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, its rollout phase constitutes a significant efficiency bottleneck, mainly arising from the long-tail bubbles across data parallel ranks, particularly in long-context scenarios where faster GPUs remain idle while waiting for stragglers. Existing solutions, such as partial rollout or asynchronous RL, mitigate these bubbles by compromising the algorithm’s strict synchronous nature. Instead, we propose BubbleSpec, a novel framework that accelerates RL rollouts while strictly keeping the mathematical exactness. Instead of attempting to eliminate bubbles, BubbleSpec exploits them. We exploit the idle time windows of faster ranks to pre-generate rollout results for subsequent steps, serving as drafts for speculative decoding. Unlike prior speculative methods that rely on historical epoch similarity and warm-ups, BubbleSpec is agnostic to dataset size and provides immediate acceleration from the onset of training. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that BubbleSpec reduces decoding steps by $\sim$50% and increases rollout throughput by up to 1.8$\times$. Critically, BubbleSpec is seamlessly compatible with various RL frameworks and strategies as it sustains the strict synchronous property of RL algorithms.

paragraphs: Synchronous reinforcement learning can leave fast GPUs idle while slower workers finish generating responses. These waiting periods become a substantial bottleneck for long-context language-model training. BubbleSpec uses those idle windows to prepare useful work for later training steps while retaining the algorithm's strict synchronization and mathematical exactness.

Faster workers pre-generate prospective rollout results during the wait. Those results become drafts for speculative decoding in subsequent steps, reducing the decoding work needed then. The framework turns uneven completion times into an opportunity for preparation. Unlike speculative methods that depend on similarity with historical epochs or require warm-up, it is designed to accelerate training immediately and without depending on dataset size.

The framework also supports different reinforcement-learning systems and strategies because it preserves synchronous behavior. Its practical significance is the ability to recover value from otherwise idle hardware time while keeping the training procedure's synchronization requirements intact.
summary.tldr: BubbleSpec uses idle GPU time to draft future rollouts, accelerating decoding while preserving exact synchronous reinforcement learning.

title: BubbleSpec: Turning Long-Tail Bubbles into Speculative Rollout Drafts for Synchronous Reinforcement Learning

abstract: One of the most common complaints about large language models (LLMs) is their prompt sensitivity—that is, the fact that their ability to perform a task or provide a correct answer to a question can depend unpredictably on the way the question is posed. We investigate this variation by comparing two very different but commonly-used styles of prompting: instruction-based prompts, which describe the task in natural language, and example-based prompts, which provide in-context few-shot demonstration pairs to illustrate the task. We find that, despite large variation in performance as a function of the prompt, the model engages some common underlying mechanisms across different prompts of a task. Specifically, we identify task-specific attention heads whose outputs literally describe the task — which we dub lexical task heads—and show that these heads are shared across prompting styles and trigger subsequent answer production. We further find that behavioral variation between prompts can be explained by the degree to which these heads are activated, and that failures are at least sometimes due to competing task representations that dilute the signal of the target task. Our results together present an increasingly clear picture of how LLMs’ internal representations can explain behavior that otherwise seems idiosyncratic to users and developers.

paragraphs: A language model may succeed or fail on the same task depending on how the prompt is written. This paper investigates that sensitivity by comparing natural-language instructions with prompts that demonstrate the task through example pairs. Despite substantial performance differences, the authors find shared internal mechanisms across these prompting styles.

They identify task-specific attention heads whose outputs describe the task in words, calling them lexical task heads. The same heads appear across instruction-based and example-based prompts and trigger later answer production. Variation in their activation helps explain why different prompts produce different behavior, linking visible performance changes to an identifiable internal task signal.

The study also finds that some failures involve competing task representations that weaken the intended task’s signal. This is a qualified explanation for at least some errors, rather than a claim that all prompt sensitivity has one cause. The findings make apparently unpredictable behavior more interpretable by connecting prompt wording, activation of shared task representations, and the subsequent production of answers.
summary.tldr: Shared attention heads encode tasks across prompting styles, and differences in their activation help explain prompt-sensitive behavior.

title: Shared Lexical Task Representations Explain Behavioral Variability In LLMs

abstract: Recently, the physics reasoning capabilities of (M)LLMs have attracted growing attention. However, existing physics benchmarks lack systematic coverage of recent physics Olympiads and direct comparison with human contestants. We present HiPhO, the first benchmark dedicated to high school physics Olympiads with human-aligned evaluation. HiPhO highlights three key innovations. (1) Comprehensive data: it compiles 13 latest Olympiads from 2024–2025, covering international and regional competitions and spanning mixed modalities from text-only to diagram-based problems. (2) Professional evaluation: it adopts official rubrics for fine-grained answer- and step-level grading aligned with human examiners. (3) Human-level comparison: it assigns gold, silver, and bronze medals to models based on official medal scores, enabling direct comparison with human contestants. Evaluating 30 (M)LLMs across 13 exams, we find that most open-source MLLMs remain at or below the bronze level, open-source LLMs demonstrate notable progress with multiple gold medals, and closed-source MLLMs achieve 6-13 gold medals, while most models still fall well short of full marks. These results underscore the substantial gap between current (M)LLMs and top human contestants, as well as the room for further improvement. The dataset and leaderboard are available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/SciYu/HiPhO and https://phyarena.github.io, respectively.

paragraphs: HiPhO evaluates language and multimodal models using high school physics Olympiad exams, with scoring designed to support comparison with human contestants. It collects 13 competitions from 2024–2025, including international and regional events. The problems span text-only questions and questions requiring diagrams, making the benchmark relevant to both textual and visual physics reasoning.

The evaluation follows official grading rubrics at the answer and reasoning-step levels. It then assigns models gold, silver, or bronze medals using the competitions’ official score thresholds. This gives performance a concrete interpretation tied to existing human examinations, while step-level grading provides more detail than checking only whether a final answer is correct.

Across 30 models and 13 exams, most open-source multimodal models reach bronze level or below. Open-source language models earn multiple gold medals, while closed-source multimodal models earn between 6 and 13. Most models nevertheless remain well below full marks. The results show substantial progress alongside the reported gap between evaluated models and top human contestants.
summary.tldr: HiPhO uses official physics Olympiad grading and medal thresholds to compare 30 models with human contestants.

title: HiPhO: How Far Are (M)LLMs from Humans in the Latest High School Physics Olympiad Benchmark?

abstract: Current Large Language Models have achieved Olympiad-level logic, yet Vision-Language Models paradoxically falter on elementary spatial tasks like block counting. This capability mismatch reveals a critical "spatial intelligence gap," where models fail to construct coherent 3D mental representations from 2D observations. We uncover this gap via diagnostic analyses showing the bottleneck is a missing view-consistent spatial interface rather than insufficient visual features or weak reasoning. To bridge this, we introduce 3ViewSense, a framework that grounds spatial reasoning in Orthographic Views. Drawing on engineering cognition, we propose a "Simulate-and-Reason" mechanism that decomposes complex scenes into canonical orthographic projections to resolve geometric ambiguities. By aligning egocentric perceptions with these allocentric references, our method facilitates explicit mental rotation and reconstruction. Empirical results on spatial reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing baselines, with consistent gains on occlusion-heavy counting and view-consistent spatial reasoning. The framework also improves the stability and consistency of spatial descriptions, offering a scalable path toward stronger spatial intelligence in multimodal systems.

paragraphs: 3ViewSense addresses a gap between recognizing visual content and reasoning consistently about three-dimensional space. A model may have useful visual features and strong general reasoning yet still struggle to count partly hidden blocks. The paper’s diagnostic analyses identify the missing connection as an interface that keeps spatial information consistent across different views.

The framework uses a Simulate-and-Reason mechanism to decompose scenes into canonical orthographic projections. These provide standardized views that help resolve geometric ambiguity. It then aligns the observer’s perspective with these scene-centered references, supporting explicit mental rotation and reconstruction. The approach gives spatial reasoning a shared geometric representation on which to operate.

On spatial reasoning benchmarks, the authors report significant improvements over existing baselines, including consistent gains in counting with heavy occlusion and reasoning across views. Spatial descriptions also become more stable and consistent. These findings support the value of organizing visual evidence into coordinated projections when a task requires reconstructing spatial relationships from two-dimensional observations.
summary.tldr: 3ViewSense organizes visual scenes into orthographic views to improve spatial reconstruction, counting, and reasoning across perspectives.

title: 3ViewSense: Spatial and Mental Perspective Reasoning from Orthographic Views in Vision-Language Models

abstract: We introduce a formal active learning methodology for guiding the placement of Lagrangian observers to infer time-dependent vector fields – a key task in oceanography, marine science, and ocean engineering – using a physics-informed spatio-temporal Gaussian process surrogate model. The majority of existing placement campaigns either follow standard ‘space-filling’ designs or relatively ad-hoc expert opinions. A key challenge to applying principled active learning in this setting is that Lagrangian observers are continuously advected through the vector field, so they make measurements at different locations and times. It is, therefore, important to consider the likely future trajectories of placed observers to account for the utility of candidate placement locations. To this end, we present BALLAST: Bayesian Active Learning with Look-ahead Amendment for Sea-drifter Trajectories. We observe noticeable benefits of BALLAST-aided sequential observer placement strategies on both synthetic and high-fidelity ocean current models. In addition, we developed a novel GP inference method – the Vanilla SPDE Exchange (VaSE) – to boost the GP posterior sampling efficiency, which is also of independent interest.

paragraphs: BALLAST studies where to place drifting observers to learn a vector field that changes over space and time, such as ocean currents. Placement is complicated because the observers move with the field. A deployment location therefore determines a future measurement trajectory, making its usefulness depend on more than the information available at the starting point.

The method combines Bayesian active learning with a physics-informed spatiotemporal Gaussian process model. Its lookahead component considers observers’ likely future paths when assessing candidate placements. This supplies a formal basis for sequential deployment decisions in a setting where existing campaigns often use spatial coverage rules or relatively informal expert judgment.

The authors observe benefits from BALLAST-guided placement in both synthetic and high-fidelity ocean current models. They also introduce Vanilla SPDE Exchange, or VaSE, an inference method that improves posterior sampling efficiency for the Gaussian process. The two contributions address complementary needs: choosing informative deployments and making the underlying probabilistic computation more efficient.
summary.tldr: BALLAST chooses sea-drifter placements by considering the information their future trajectories are likely to provide.

title: BALLAST: Bayesian Active Learning with Look-ahead Amendment for Sea-drifter Trajectories under Spatio-Temporal Vector Fields

abstract: Medical time series are central to healthcare, enabling continuous monitoring and supporting timely clinical decisions. Despite recent progress, existing methods struggle to jointly model local-global dynamics and handle nonstationarities like baseline drift, while often failing to capture latent channel interactions. To address these challenges, we propose MedMamba, an end-to-end architecture that integrates state space models with domain-specific inductive biases. Specifically, MedMamba first employs multi-scale convolutional embeddings to capture discriminative local morphology. Second, to mitigate nonstationarity, we introduce a tri-branch differential state space encoder that processes raw, temporal-difference, and frequency-domain views, fusing them to emphasize informative patterns while suppressing drift. Furthermore, to uncover latent channel correlations, we design a spatial graph Mamba module that learns a directed dependency structure regularized toward sparsity and acyclicity, which obviates the need for predefined graphs. Extensive experiments on five real-world datasets demonstrate that MedMamba achieves state-of-the-art performance while maintaining linear computational complexity, and ablation studies validate each component’s contribution.Code is available at https://github.com/zhangda1018/MedMamba.

paragraphs: Medical time-series classification requires recognizing local signal shapes, following longer-range dynamics, and accounting for relationships among measurement channels. Changes such as baseline drift can obscure useful patterns. MedMamba combines several architectural components to address these issues within an end-to-end state-space model.

First, convolutions at multiple scales encode local morphology. A three-branch encoder then processes the raw signal, temporal differences, and a frequency-domain view, combining them to emphasize informative patterns and suppress drift. A spatial graph Mamba module learns directed dependencies among channels. Its regularization encourages sparse connections and acyclicity, allowing the model to discover a dependency structure without requiring a predefined graph.

Across five real-world datasets, the authors report state-of-the-art classification performance while maintaining linear computational complexity. Ablation studies support the contribution of each component. The findings indicate that complementary signal views and learned channel relationships can work together: the temporal branches address changing signal behavior, while the graph component captures dependencies that treating channels independently would leave unmodeled.
summary.tldr: MedMamba combines multiple signal views with learned channel dependencies to improve medical time-series classification at linear computational complexity.

title: MedMamba: Multi-View State Space Models with Adaptive Graph Learning for Medical Time Series Classification

abstract: The stochastic minimax optimization problem has widespread applications in machine learning. Recently, numerous distributed minimax optimization algorithms have been developed to handle distributed training data. However, most of these algorithms suffer from high communication costs. To address this issue, we develop a novel communication-efficient decentralized stochastic gradient descent ascent with momentum algorithm based on the error feedback mechanism. Importantly, our algorithm demonstrates how to balance the full-precision update and the compression residual with novel designs for coefficients regarding variables and gradients to guarantee convergence. However, compressing the primal and dual variables (and their gradients) of stochastic minimax optimization problems with the error feedback mechanism presents significant challenges for convergence analysis. In particular, it incurs the circle dependence among consensus errors and compression errors. To overcome this challenge, we propose novel strategies that enable the establishment of the convergence rate for our algorithm. Our theoretical results demonstrate how the compression operator influences the convergence rate. Finally, extensive experimental results confirm the efficacy of our proposed algorithm.

To address this issue, we develop a novel communication-efficient decentralized stochastic gradient descent ascent with momentum algorithm based on the error feedback mechanism. Importantly, our algorithm demonstrates how to balance the full-precision update and the compression residual with novel designs for coefficients regarding variables and gradients to guarantee convergence. However, compressing the primal and dual variables (and their gradients) of stochastic minimax optimization problems with the error feedback mechanism presents significant challenges for convergence analysis. paragraphs: Distributed minimax learning requires workers to coordinate updates for variables being minimized and maximized. Communicating those updates can be expensive. This paper develops a decentralized stochastic gradient descent-ascent algorithm with momentum that compresses communication and uses error feedback to account for information lost through compression.

The method introduces coefficients that balance full-precision updates against compression residuals for both variables and gradients. The central analytical difficulty is circular dependence between consensus errors and compression errors: disagreement among workers and inaccuracies from compression affect one another. The authors develop strategies to handle that dependence and establish a convergence rate for their algorithm.

The theoretical results explicitly show how the compression operator affects convergence. This matters because communication savings must be considered together with their effect on optimization progress. Extensive experiments confirm the proposed method’s efficacy. The contribution therefore combines a communication-efficient update design with an analysis of the coupled errors created when both sides of a minimax problem are compressed.
summary.tldr: The paper develops compressed decentralized minimax optimization with error feedback and establishes how compression affects its convergence rate.

title: On the Convergence of Decentralized Stochastic Minimax Optimization Algorithm with Compressed Communication

abstract: Implicit Neural Representation (INR) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for continuous MRI reconstruction. However, standard self-supervised INR requires time-consuming optimization from scratch for each scan, hindering clinical deployment. This work presents IPOD, a Reference-Free Meta-Learning framework designed to learn generalized parameter initializations for INR directly from undersampled data. Distinct from conventional meta-learning that relies on fully-sampled ground truth, IPOD operates in an inverse-problem-driven manner, leveraging diverse reconstruction tasks with varying sampling patterns to capture a robust prior. Furthermore, we introduce an adaptive meta-update strategy modulated by task-specific performance to ensure optimal parameter distribution for diverse anatomical structures. Extensive experiments demonstrate that IPOD provides a superior initialization that enables rapid adaptation and achieves high-fidelity reconstruction across various imaging protocols, significantly outperforming existing INR baselines. By eliminating the dependence on reference images, IPOD offers a scalable and efficient solution for a wide range of imaging inverse problems. Code and data available at: https://github.com/zhn00310/RFML4MRI

paragraphs: Implicit neural representations offer a continuous representation for MRI reconstruction, but optimizing a new model from scratch for every scan takes time. IPOD learns an initialization that can adapt rapidly to a scan, addressing this computational burden without relying on fully sampled reference images during meta-learning.

The framework learns directly from undersampled measurements across reconstruction tasks with different sampling patterns. This variation is used to capture a prior that generalizes across tasks. An adaptive meta-update strategy changes the learning update according to task-specific performance, with the aim of producing suitable initial parameters for diverse anatomical structures.

Experiments report faster adaptation and high-fidelity reconstruction across several imaging protocols, substantially outperforming existing implicit-representation baselines. The stated findings link the learned initialization to both efficiency and reconstruction quality. Removing the need for fully sampled training references also changes the data requirements of meta-learning, supporting the authors’ proposal of a scalable approach to imaging inverse problems while retaining scan-specific adaptation as part of reconstruction.
summary.tldr: IPOD learns MRI reconstruction initializations directly from undersampled data, enabling rapid adaptation without fully sampled training references.

title: Reference-Free Meta-Learning for Generalized Implicit Neural Representation in Efficient MRI Reconstruction

abstract: Class-incremental semantic segmentation learns new classes while retaining old ones without access to past data. Although existing methods alleviate catastrophic forgetting on old classes, new-class performance remains limited. We identify that the key bottleneck arises from low-margin regions, where the logit of the ground-truth class is close to that of the most competitive non-ground-truth class. Our theoretical analysis suggests that optimization in these regions is characterized by high second-order margin sensitivity and a small stability radius, making learning prone to class confusion. Based on the above analysis, we propose Learnability-Driven Knowledge Assimilation (LDKA), which targets low-margin learning via three complementary optimization strategies: (i) Progressive Margin Learning continuously reallocates pixel-wise optimization budget in a threshold-free manner, shifting emphasis from high-margin to low-margin regions; (ii) Smooth Knowledge Distillation applies second-order sensitivity damping along the margin direction and perturbation stabilization to suppress high-frequency updates and increase the stability radius; (iii) Misclassification-Aware Decoupling measures inter-class confusion with a competition matrix and decouples highly competitive class representations. Experiments show that LDKA improves mIoU on new classes while preserving performance on old classes across 9 incremental protocols.

paragraphs: Class-incremental semantic segmentation must learn to label new categories of pixels while retaining older categories without access to past data. This paper focuses on a bottleneck in learning the new classes: regions where the correct class score barely exceeds, or competes closely with, another class score. Its analysis suggests these low-margin regions are sensitive to optimization and have limited stability.

LDKA combines three strategies aimed at this difficulty. Progressive Margin Learning gradually shifts pixel-level optimization effort from high-margin regions toward low-margin ones without a threshold. Smooth Knowledge Distillation dampens second-order sensitivity along the margin direction and stabilizes behavior under perturbations. Misclassification-Aware Decoupling uses a competition matrix to identify confusing classes and separate their representations.

Together, these mechanisms address where learning effort goes, how sharply updates behave, and which class representations interfere. Experiments across nine incremental protocols show improved mean intersection-over-union for new classes while preserving old-class performance. The findings indicate that improving the learnability of ambiguous regions can complement efforts aimed primarily at preventing forgetting.
summary.tldr: LDKA targets ambiguous pixel regions with coordinated optimization strategies, improving new-class segmentation while preserving old-class performance.

title: Learnability-Driven Knowledge Assimilation for Class-Incremental Semantic Segmentation

abstract: This position paper argues that the machine learning community should prioritize speech-native architectures that treat audio as a first-class modality, anticipating the inevitable shift from text-dominated to speech-first data distributions. Text dominates human-computer interaction not because it is cognitively natural, but because decades of interface design conditioned users to express knowledge through keyboards and search boxes. Recent advances in speech recognition and multimodal foundation models have removed the technical barriers to voice-based interaction; what remains is primarily a habit problem. As voice becomes habitual, the data ecosystem underlying machine learning will shift toward speech-native knowledge—with profound implications for model architecture, training efficiency, and evaluation paradigms. This paper examines the technical readiness of speech systems, identifies habit inertia as the primary adoption barrier, addresses alternative views that favor text-centric approaches, and outlines a research agenda for ML systems that anticipate speech-first data distributions.

paragraphs: This paper argues that machine learning should prepare for a future in which speech becomes the dominant form of interaction and data. The authors attribute today’s reliance on text largely to habits established by keyboards and search interfaces. In their account, text’s current prominence reflects the history of interface design rather than its cognitive naturalness.

The paper examines the readiness of speech recognition and multimodal foundation models and argues that technical barriers to voice interaction have been removed. It identifies persistent user habits as the main remaining adoption obstacle. As those habits change, the authors anticipate a shift toward knowledge expressed directly through speech, with consequences for model architecture, training efficiency, and evaluation.

The proposed research agenda prioritizes architectures that treat audio as a primary modality. The paper also considers competing arguments favoring text-centered approaches. Its contribution is a forward-looking position about where research effort should go, based on its assessment of technical readiness and expected adoption. The projected speech-first transition is the authors’ premise and forecast, rather than a reported measurement of an already completed shift.
summary.tldr: The authors urge speech-native model development, arguing that changing interaction habits will shift future data distributions toward audio.

abstract: The integration of diverse forms of informative data by learning an optimal combination of base kernels in classification or regression problems can provide enhanced performance when compared to that obtained from any single data source. We present a Bayesian hierarchical model which enables kernel learning and present effective variational Bayes estimators for regression and classification. Illustrative experiments demonstrate the utility of the proposed method. Matlab code replicating results reported is available at http://www.dcs.gla. ac.uk/∼srogers/kernel comb.html.
originalAbstract: The integration of diverse forms of informative data by learning an optimal combination of base kernels in classification or regression problems can provide enhanced performance when compared to that obtained from any single data source. We present a Bayesian hierarchical model which enables kernel learning and present effective variational Bayes estimators for regression and classification. Illustrative experiments demonstrate the utility of the proposed method. Matlab code replicating results reported is available at http://www.dcs.gla. ac.uk/∼srogers/kernel comb.html.

paragraphs: Different sources of data can provide different kinds of useful information for a prediction task. This paper considers integrating them by learning a combination of base kernels. Each kernel supplies a way to represent information for learning, and choosing a useful combination can improve performance relative to using a single data source.

The authors introduce a hierarchical Bayesian model that makes kernel learning part of the modeling process. They also present variational Bayes estimators for both regression and classification. These estimators provide the computational machinery for applying the proposed Bayesian approach to predicting numerical values or class labels.

Illustrative experiments demonstrate the method's utility. The reported contribution joins a model for learning kernel combinations with effective estimation procedures for two major prediction settings. Its motivation is the possible benefit of integrating informative sources, rather than a claim that every combination must outperform every individual source. The authors also provide Matlab code to reproduce the reported results.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical Bayesian model learns combinations of kernels, with variational estimators for regression and classification.

title: Hierarchic Bayesian models for kernel learning

abstract: In this paper we introduce a novel approach to manifold alignment, based on Procrustes analysis. Our approach differs from "semi-supervised alignment" in that it results in a mapping that is defined everywhere - when used with a suitable dimensionality reduction method - rather than just on the training data points. We describe and evaluate our approach both theoretically and experimentally, providing results showing useful knowledge transfer from one domain to another. Novel applications of our method including cross-lingual information retrieval and transfer learning in Markov decision processes are presented.
originalAbstract: In this paper we introduce a novel approach to manifold alignment, based on Procrustes analysis. Our approach differs from "semi-supervised alignment" in that it results in a mapping that is defined everywhere - when used with a suitable dimensionality reduction method - rather than just on the training data points. We describe and evaluate our approach both theoretically and experimentally, providing results showing useful knowledge transfer from one domain to another. Novel applications of our method including cross-lingual information retrieval and transfer learning in Markov decision processes are presented.

paragraphs: Manifold alignment seeks to connect representations from different domains so that knowledge can transfer between them. This paper introduces an approach based on Procrustes analysis. Its emphasis is both on aligning the available data and on obtaining a mapping that can be used beyond the particular examples supplied during training.

The scope of that mapping is a central distinction. When paired with a suitable dimensionality reduction method, the approach produces a mapping defined everywhere, rather than only at the training points. The qualification is essential: this extension depends on the dimensionality reduction method used. It makes the choice of representation part of what enables the alignment to generalize.

The authors study the approach theoretically and experimentally, reporting useful knowledge transfer between domains. Applications include cross-lingual information retrieval and transfer learning in Markov decision processes. These examples show the alignment idea being used in different kinds of transfer tasks, while the broader contribution is a route to mappings that remain usable outside the original training set.
summary.tldr: Procrustes-based manifold alignment enables useful knowledge transfer and, with suitable dimensionality reduction, mappings beyond training points.

title: Manifold alignment using Procrustes analysis

abstract: In this paper, we investigate a simple, mistake-driven learning algorithm for discriminative training of continuous density hidden Markov models (CD-HMMs). Most CD-HMMs for automatic speech recognition use multivariate Gaussian emission densities (or mixtures thereof) parameterized in terms of their means and covariance matrices. For discriminative training of CD-HMMs, we reparameterize these Gaussian distributions in terms of positive semidefinite matrices that jointly encode their mean and covariance statistics. We show how to explore the resulting parameter space in CD-HMMs with perceptron-style updates that minimize the distance between Viterbi decodings and target transcriptions. We experiment with several forms of updates, systematically comparing the effects of different matrix factorizations, initializations, and averaging schemes on phone accuracies and convergence rates. We present experimental results for context-independent CD-HMMs trained in this way on the TIMIT speech corpus. Our results show that certain types of perceptron training yield consistently significant and rapid reductions in phone error rates.

These are commonly parameterized by means and covariance matrices. This paper changes that representation to support a simple, mistake-driven approach to discriminative training.

The authors encode the Gaussian mean and covariance information together in positive semidefinite matrices. They then develop perceptron-style updates within the resulting parameter space. The updates seek to reduce the distance between the transcription produced by Viterbi decoding and the target transcription, connecting parameter changes directly to decoding mistakes.

The study compares different update forms, matrix factorizations, initialization choices, and averaging schemes, examining phone accuracy and convergence rates. The contribution shows how a matrix representation of Gaussian emissions can enable effective mistake-driven learning for these sequence models.
summary.tldr: Matrix-based Gaussian parameterizations enable perceptron training that rapidly reduces phone errors for certain hidden Markov model update schemes.

title: Matrix updates for perceptron training of continuous density hidden Markov models

abstract: In real sequence labeling tasks, statistics of many higher order features are not sufficient due to the training data sparseness, very few of them are useful. We describe Sparse Higher Order Conditional Random Fields (SHO-CRFs), which are able to handle local features and sparse higher order features together using a novel tractable exact inference algorithm. Our main insight is that states and transitions with same potential functions can be grouped together, and inference is performed on the grouped states and transitions. Though the complexity is not polynomial, SHO-CRFs are still efficient in practice because of the feature sparseness. Experimental results on optical character recognition and Chinese organization name recognition show that with the same higher order feature set, SHO-CRFs significantly outperform previous approaches.

paragraphs: Sequence labeling can benefit from features involving larger patterns of labels, but training data often provides insufficient evidence for many such higher-order features. This paper starts from the observation that only a small number are useful. Sparse Higher Order Conditional Random Fields combine local features with a sparse collection of higher-order features.

The central computational insight is to group states and transitions that share the same potential functions. Exact inference then operates on those groups. This exploits shared structure in the model's scoring functions and supports practical efficiency when higher-order features are sparse. The authors explicitly note that the complexity is still not polynomial.

Experiments cover optical character recognition and Chinese organization name recognition. Using the same higher-order feature set, the proposed models significantly outperform previous approaches. These results show the value of the inference formulation in the tested tasks: sparse higher-order information can be incorporated alongside local information without giving up exact inference, even though the general computational complexity remains nonpolynomial.
summary.tldr: Grouping equivalent states and transitions enables practically efficient exact inference for CRFs with sparse higher-order features.

title: Sparse higher order conditional random fields for improved sequence labeling

abstract: There has been a recent focus in reinforcement learning (RL) on addressing continuous state and action problems by optimizing parameterized policies. PI2 is a recent example of this approach. It combines a derivation from first principles of stochastic optimal control with tools from statistical estimation theory. In this paper, we consider PI2 as a member of the wider family of methods which share the concept of probability-weighted averaging to iteratively update parameters to optimize a cost function. We compare PI2 to other members of the same family – Cross-Entropy Methods and CMA-ES – at the conceptual level and in terms of performance. The comparison suggests the derivation of a novel algorithm which we call PI2-CMA for “Path Integral Policy Improvement with Covariance Matrix Adaptation”. PI2-CMA's main advantage is that it determines the magnitude of the exploration noise automatically.

paragraphs: For reinforcement learning with continuous states and actions, one approach is to optimize a policy's parameters directly. PI2 follows this route, drawing on stochastic optimal control and statistical estimation. This paper places it within a broader family of optimization methods that update parameters through probability-weighted averaging.

The authors compare PI2 with Cross-Entropy Methods and CMA-ES, examining both their conceptual relationships and their performance. The shared averaging perspective makes it possible to connect methods with different derivations through the operation they use to improve parameters. This comparison motivates a new algorithm, PI2-CMA.

PI2-CMA combines path integral policy improvement with covariance matrix adaptation. Its main stated advantage is automatic determination of exploration-noise magnitude. That magnitude controls the size of the perturbations used to explore policy parameters, so adapting it makes exploration scale part of the optimization procedure. The abstract presents this automatic adjustment as the central benefit of the new algorithm, without claiming that it universally outperforms the other methods.
summary.tldr: PI2-CMA combines path integral policy improvement with covariance adaptation to determine exploration-noise magnitude automatically.

title: Path Integral Policy Improvement with Covariance Matrix Adaptation

abstract: We consider supervised learning in the presence of very many irrelevant features, and study two different regularization methods for preventing overfitting. Focusing on logistic regression, we show that using L_1 regularization of the parameters, the sample complexity (i.e., the number of training examples required to learn "well,") grows only logarithmically in the number of irrelevant features. This logarithmic rate matches the best known bounds for feature selection, and indicates that L_1 regularized logistic regression can be effective even if there are exponentially many irrelevant features as there are training examples. We also give a lower-bound showing that any rotationally invariant algorithm---including logistic regression with L_2 regularization, SVMs, and neural networks trained by backpropagation---has a worst case sample complexity that grows at least linearly in the number of irrelevant features.

paragraphs: This paper examines supervised learning when many input features are irrelevant to prediction. Its central question is how the number of training examples needed for effective learning changes as irrelevant features accumulate. Focusing on logistic regression, it compares the implications of L1 regularization with those of methods whose behavior is invariant to rotations of the feature space.

For L1-regularized logistic regression, the authors show that sample complexity grows only logarithmically with the number of irrelevant features. This matches the best known feature-selection bounds described in the abstract. The result indicates that effective learning can remain possible even when the number of irrelevant features is exponential in the number of training examples.

The contrasting result is a worst-case lower bound: rotationally invariant algorithms require sample complexity that grows at least linearly with irrelevant features. The abstract includes L2-regularized logistic regression, SVMs, and neural networks trained by backpropagation in this comparison. This is a theoretical distinction about vulnerability to irrelevant dimensions, not a claim that L1 wins on every dataset.
summary.tldr: L1-regularized logistic regression has logarithmic sample complexity in irrelevant features, while rotationally invariant methods face a linear worst-case lower bound.

title: Feature selection, L1 vs. L2 regularization, and rotational invariance
